blurb: A `Bearer` actor's identity is minted from the token's `sub` claim, which is a string, so the identity type must be one a string can become: a refined or opaque `String`. Any other type has no way to be built from the claim, and an actor with no `identity` at all is refused for the same reason. Declare a type over `String`, such as `type UserId = String where NonEmpty`, and name it as the `identity`. An `Oidc` actor has the same rule under `bynk.actor.oidc_identity_not_string_constructible`.
example:
type Age = Int where NonNegative
actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = Age }      // ✗ a token's `sub` is a string, not an `Int`

type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = UserId }   // ✓ minted from `sub`
summary: A `Bearer` actor's identity is not a string-constructible type.

blurb: A `Bearer` actor checks a JWT signed with a shared key, so the compiler needs to know which key. Name the environment variable that holds it: `Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY")`. The string is the variable's name, never the key itself, so no secret is written in the source; the `Secrets` capability reads the value at run time. An `Oidc` actor needs no secret, because it checks the provider's public keys, and a `Signature` actor has its own `bynk.actor.signature_missing_secret`.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty

actor User { auth = Bearer, identity = UserId }                         // ✗ no signing secret named

actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = UserId }     // ✓ the env var that holds the key
summary: A `Bearer` actor does not name its signing secret.

blurb: A `by` clause with a binder, `by who: Visitor`, adds a name to the handler body beside its parameters. If the binder is spelt like a parameter it would hide it, so a body that read `body` would silently get the actor instead of the request body. The compiler refuses the clash rather than choose one. Rename the binder or the parameter. A `by` with no binder, `by Visitor`, adds no name and cannot clash.
example:
on POST("/echo") (body: String) -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by body: Visitor {   // ✗ `body` is already a parameter

on POST("/echo") (body: String) -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by who: Visitor {   // ✓ a name of its own
summary: A `by` actor binder collides with a handler parameter of the same name.

blurb: `by` names who is calling and has the compiler verify it at the edge of the program: an HTTP request, a queue message, a cron tick. An agent handler is not an edge. It is reached only from a service or another agent, which has already been through its own check, so there is no caller left to verify and the clause would be silently ignored. The compiler refuses it instead of letting it look like protection. Remove the clause, and put the `by` on the service handler that calls the agent, passing on whatever the agent needs as an argument.
example:
on call bump() -> Effect[Int] by v: Visitor {   // ✗ an agent handler has no actor

on call bump() -> Effect[Int] {                // ✓ the service in front of it holds the `by`
summary: A `by` actor clause was placed on an agent `on call` handler, which has no actor.

blurb: Peers in a `by who: A | B` clause are told apart by their authentication scheme, so two peers of the same scheme can't both be reached: the second would never be chosen. Keep one peer per scheme, or fold the two into a single actor. A catch-all peer placed too early is a different mistake, `bynk.actor.unreachable_sum_arm`.
summary: Two peers in a multi-actor sum share an authentication scheme.

blurb: A foreign caller signs its calls under a key named from the context's name, `BYNK_CALL_TO_<CONTEXT>`. The name must therefore be lower-case letters and digits in dot-separated segments, each starting with a letter, with single underscores between runs: no `__`, and no trailing `_`. Rename the context, or move the foreign actor to one whose name qualifies.
example:
context shop.orders_
actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }   // ✗ no key can be named from `shop.orders_`

context shop.orders
actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }   // ✓
summary: A context declaring a `Foreign` actor has a name no call key can be named from.

blurb: A context tells its foreign callers apart by the secret their calls are signed under, and `bynk deploy` mints one secret per name. Two actors on one secret could each pass for the other, so a foreign actor's secret may be no other actor's. Give each its own variable.
summary: A `Foreign` actor's secret is also another actor's secret in the same context.

blurb: A `Foreign` actor is its own identity: a handler tells foreign callers apart by matching on its `by` sum, not by a value carried in. So `identity` is refused, where a `Bearer` actor takes one from its token. Remove it.
example:
type Who = String where NonEmpty

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY"), identity = Who }   // ✗ the actor is the identity

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }                   // ✓
summary: A `Foreign` actor declares an `identity`.

blurb: A `Foreign` actor is a caller that is not Bynk. Its calls are signed, and the context checks each one against a secret, so the actor must name the environment variable that holds it. The string is the variable's name, never the key, and `bynk deploy` mints the key and sets it. With no name the context has nothing to check a call against. A secret that is not a string is `bynk.actor.foreign_secret_not_string`.
example:
actor Legacy { auth = Foreign }                                // ✗ no secret named

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }    // ✓ the env var that holds the key
summary: A `Foreign` actor does not name the secret its calls are signed with.

blurb: A foreign caller sends its actor's name as its caller, and a Bynk context's name is lower case. An actor named like a context could pass for one. Start the actor's name with a capital letter.
example:
actor legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }   // ✗ reads as a context name

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }   // ✓ capitalised
summary: A `Foreign` actor's name could be read as a context's name.

blurb: `bynk deploy` mints the keys that Bynk contexts sign their calls to each other with, and names them `BYNK_CALL_FROM_…` and `BYNK_CALL_TO_…`. A foreign caller's secret in that range could collide with one of them, so those names are kept for contexts. Pick another name, such as `LEGACY_CALL_KEY`.
example:
actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "BYNK_CALL_FROM_LEGACY") }   // ✗ a `BYNK_CALL_` key name

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }         // ✓ any other name
summary: A `Foreign` actor's secret uses a `BYNK_CALL_` edge key's name.

blurb: A `Foreign` actor's `secret` is the name of an environment variable, so it is written as a string. A number or any other expression names no variable. Put the variable's name in quotes. A `secret` left out altogether is `bynk.actor.foreign_missing_secret`.
example:
actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = 42) }                   // ✗ not a variable name

actor Legacy { auth = Foreign(secret = "LEGACY_CALL_KEY") }    // ✓ a string
summary: A `Foreign` actor's secret is not a string.

blurb: An actor's identity is a value only its context can mint, from a verified token or caller, so its type has to be one that context owns. A built-in such as `Int`, or a type from another context, could be built by anyone, so the identity would prove nothing. Declare the identity as a type in this context, such as `type PrincipalId = Int where NonNegative`, and name that.
example:
actor Principal { auth = Internal, identity = Int }   // ✗ `Int` is not owned by this context

type PrincipalId = Int where NonNegative
actor Principal { auth = Internal, identity = PrincipalId }   // ✓ minted only here
summary: An actor identity type is not a context-ownable (sealed) value type.

blurb: An `on call` handler is reachable by every context that consumes this one, and which of them may call it is an access decision, so the handler must say, with a `by` clause. `by Caller` is the explicit "any consuming context"; a refinement over `Caller`, a `Foreign` actor or a sum narrows it. The error's fix inserts `by Caller`, which is what the handler did before the clause was required, and `bynk check --fix=bynk.actor.missing_by_on_call` migrates a whole project. A header default, `service pay by Caller`, covers every handler without its own `by`. Agents, cron, queue and `Events` handlers have no caller to name, so they are unchanged.
summary: An `on call` handler lacks the required `by` actor clause.

blurb: An HTTP handler can be reached by anyone, and Bynk has no safe default for who is calling, so each one must say, with a `by` clause, which actor it expects. The compiler then emits the verification before the body runs. A public route writes `by v: Visitor`; an authenticated one names an `actor` it declares. Set it once on the header, `service api from http by Visitor`, and every handler without its own `by` inherits it. A WebSocket `on open` handler needs one too. `call` handlers need one too (`bynk.actor.missing_by_on_call`); cron and queue have a default.
summary: An HTTP handler lacks the required `by` actor clause.

blurb: An `Oidc` actor's identity is minted from the verified token's `sub` claim, which is a string, so the identity type must be a refined or opaque `String`. An actor with no `identity` is refused too. Declare a type over `String`, such as `type UserId = String where NonEmpty`, and name it. A `Bearer` actor has the same rule under `bynk.actor.bearer_identity_not_string_constructible`.
example:
type Age = Int where NonNegative
actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = Age }   // ✗ `sub` is a string, not an `Int`

type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✓ minted from `sub`
summary: An `Oidc` actor's identity is not a string-constructible type.

blurb: A provider signs tokens for many services, and each token is issued for one. An `Oidc` actor therefore names its `audience`, the `aud` claim a token must carry, so a token issued for some other API is refused here even though its signature is valid. Add `audience = "…"` with the identifier your provider uses for this API. The issuer and key set have their own codes, `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_issuer` and `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_jwks`.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✗ no audience

actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✓ the `aud` this API accepts
summary: An `Oidc` actor does not name its `audience`.

blurb: A valid signature shows that some key signed a token, not that your provider issued it. An `Oidc` actor therefore names its `issuer`, the `iss` claim a token must carry, and refuses any other. Add `issuer = "…"` with the provider's issuer URL. The other required settings have their own codes, `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_audience` and `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_jwks`.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Oidc(audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✗ no issuer

actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✓ the `iss` a token must carry
summary: An `Oidc` actor does not name its `issuer`.

blurb: An `Oidc` actor holds no shared secret. It checks a token's signature against the provider's public keys, a JSON Web Key Set that the verifier fetches from a URL, so the actor must say where it is. Add `jwks = "…"`, for example the provider's `/.well-known/jwks.json`. The `issuer` and `audience` are required as well, under `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_issuer` and `bynk.actor.oidc_missing_audience`.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api"), identity = UserId }   // ✗ nowhere to fetch the public keys

actor User { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://issuer.example", audience = "my-api", jwks = "https://issuer.example/jwks"), identity = UserId }   // ✓ the provider's key set
summary: An `Oidc` actor does not name its `jwks` endpoint.

blurb: A multi-actor `by` clause tries its peers in turn on a request it reads once. An `Oidc` actor must first fetch the provider's keys, which that path does not yet support, so an `Oidc` actor stands alone on its route. Give the route a single `by who: Member`, and serve any anonymous route separately.
summary: An `Oidc` actor appears as a member of a multi-actor sum.

blurb: `trustFrom` names a variable that holds trust roots as JSON. A variable an actor uses as its `secret` holds a signing key, and one variable cannot be both. Give `trustFrom` a variable of its own.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
type WorkloadId = String where NonEmpty

actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = UserId }
actor Workload { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://i.test", audience = "a", jwks = "https://i.test/jwks", trustFrom = "JWT_KEY"), identity = WorkloadId }   // ✗ `JWT_KEY` is a key

actor Workload { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://i.test", audience = "a", jwks = "https://i.test/jwks", trustFrom = "OIDC_TRUST"), identity = WorkloadId }   // ✓
summary: An `Oidc` actor's `trustFrom` names an environment variable that an actor uses as its `secret`.

blurb: `trustFrom` names an environment variable whose JSON, when set, replaces the actor's declared trust roots at run time, as in a test or staging deployment. A variable is named by a string, so a number or other expression names nothing. Write the variable's name in quotes.
example:
type WorkloadId = String where NonEmpty

actor Workload { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://i.test", audience = "a", jwks = "https://i.test/jwks", trustFrom = 5), identity = WorkloadId }   // ✗ not a name

actor Workload { auth = Oidc(issuer = "https://i.test", audience = "a", jwks = "https://i.test/jwks", trustFrom = "OIDC_TRUST"), identity = WorkloadId }   // ✓
summary: An `Oidc` actor's `trustFrom` isn't a string naming an environment variable.

blurb: An `actor` says who may call a handler and what the compiler then knows about them. Only a context has handlers, and an actor's identity is sealed to the context that declares it, so only a context may declare one. A `commons` is shared code that other units `uses`. Move the `actor` into the context whose services take it.
example:
commons shop

actor User { auth = None }   // ✗ a commons has no handlers

context shop

actor User { auth = None }   // ✓ declared where it is used
summary: An `actor` was declared outside a context (e.g. in a commons).

blurb: `actor Admin = User where …` adds an authorisation check on a token's claims, and only a `Bearer` actor carries claims. So the base must be a declared `Bearer` actor: not `Visitor`, `Internal` or `Signature`, and not another refinement. Name a `Bearer` actor as the base, declaring it if need be.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = UserId }

actor Admin = Visitor where hasClaim("admin")   // ✗ `Visitor` carries no claims

actor Admin = User where hasClaim("admin")   // ✓ a `Bearer` actor
summary: A refinement actor's base is not a `Bearer` actor (no claims to authorise against).

blurb: A refinement actor has its base's scheme and only narrows it, and peers of a sum are told apart by scheme, so it can't stand beside its base as another choice. Name the base as the peer and test the extra condition in its arm, or give the refined route its own `by who: Admin`.
summary: A refinement actor appears as a member of a multi-actor sum.

blurb: A refinement actor's `where` is checked against a token's claims, which are untyped JSON, so the predicate is a closed vocabulary: `hasClaim("name")` and `claimEquals("name", "value")`, composed with `&&`, `||` and `!`. Express the condition with those. Anything else, such as a call to a function of your own, is refused.
example:
type UserId = String where NonEmpty
actor User { auth = Bearer(secret = "JWT_KEY"), identity = UserId }

actor Admin = User where isAdmin(user)   // ✗ not a claim predicate

actor Admin = User where hasClaim("admin")   // ✓
summary: A refinement actor's `where` predicate is outside the closed claim-predicate set.

blurb: A scheme's config values are strings and integers, except that a `SignedCookie` also takes a duration (`ttl = 12.hours`) and a bare name (`sameSite = Lax`). Every other scheme reads a string or an integer, so a duration or a bare name would be dropped without a word: a `Signature` `tolerance = 5.minutes` would read as no tolerance at all, and the replay window would be off. Write a `Signature` tolerance in whole seconds, and quote a string.
example:
actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "K", header = "X-Sig", timestamp = "X-Ts", tolerance = 5.minutes) }   // ✗ a duration

actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "K", header = "X-Sig", timestamp = "X-Ts", tolerance = 300) }   // ✓ seconds
summary: A scheme config value other than `SignedCookie`'s is a duration or a bare name, which only `SignedCookie` takes.

blurb: Each protocol admits only the schemes that can be verified on it. HTTP takes `None` (`Visitor`), `Bearer`, `Signature` and `Oidc`; a WebSocket takes `None` and `Bearer`; `call` takes `Internal` and `Foreign`; cron and queue take `Internal`. A `Visitor` on cron is wrong because nothing public calls a cron handler: the platform does. Use the actor made for the protocol: `Scheduler` for cron, `Producer` for queue, `Caller` for `on call`. `Caller` is admitted on `on call` only.
summary: An actor's scheme is not admissible on this handler's protocol.

blurb: A signature shows that a request is authentic, not who sent it, so a `Signature` actor has no principal to give an identity. The event is the handler's `body`. Remove `identity`. For an actor that carries a principal, see `bynk.actor.bearer_identity_not_string_constructible`.
example:
actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig"), identity = String }   // ✗ no principal

actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig") }                       // ✓
summary: A `Signature` actor declared an `identity`, which is not yet supported.

blurb: A `Signature` actor reads the sender's signature from a request header, and the header's name is the sender's choice, so the actor must say which one. Add `header = "…"` with the name of the header that carries the HMAC. Without it the compiler has no way to find the signature to check the body against.
example:
actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY") }   // ✗ which header holds the signature?

actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig") }   // ✓
summary: A `Signature` actor does not name its signature header.

blurb: A `Signature` actor checks an HMAC of the request body, so the compiler needs the key to check it against. Name the environment variable that holds it: `secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY"`. The string is the variable's name, never the key itself, so no secret is written in the source. A `Bearer` actor has its own `bynk.actor.bearer_missing_secret`.
example:
actor Hook { auth = Signature(header = "X-Sig") }   // ✗ no signing secret named

actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig") }   // ✓ the env var that holds the key
summary: A `Signature` actor does not name its signing secret.

blurb: A `Signature` is an HMAC over the raw request body, so the handler must take that body: one with no `body` parameter would vouch for data it never reads. Add `(body: T)`, where `T` is the payload's type. A route that takes no payload has nothing for a signature to protect.
summary: A `Signature` handler does not take a `body` parameter.

blurb: `tolerance` is how many seconds old a signed request may be before it is refused, which limits replay of a captured one. The age is read from a timestamp header, so `tolerance` needs `timestamp = "…"` naming it; alone it has nothing to compare against. Add the `timestamp`, or drop `tolerance` and accept that a captured request can be replayed.
example:
actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig", tolerance = 300) }   // ✗ age of what?

actor Hook { auth = Signature(secret = "WEBHOOK_KEY", header = "X-Sig", timestamp = "X-Time", tolerance = 300) }   // ✓
summary: A `Signature` actor set `tolerance` without a `timestamp` header.

blurb: Each `SignedCookie` key takes one kind of value: `secret`, `previous` and `cookie` are strings, `ttl` is a duration, and `sameSite` is `Lax`, `Strict` or `Unrestricted`. Fix the value or remove the key.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = 5, ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` config value has the wrong kind.

blurb: A cookie name is an RFC 6265 token: letters, digits and a few punctuation characters, with no space, `=`, `;`, `,` or quote. A browser would drop or misread anything else. The default, `__Host-session`, is always legal.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours, cookie = "my session"), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` `cookie` is not a legal cookie name.

blurb: `ttl` must be a `Duration` literal that is positive and a whole number of seconds, because it becomes both a `Max-Age` and a signed expiry in seconds. Write `12.hours` or `30.minutes`.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 1500.milliseconds), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` `ttl` is not a positive whole number of seconds.

blurb: A `SignedCookie` config names each key once. A repeated `secret` or `ttl` would have the first value win and the second ignored without a word, in the scheme that guards a session. Keep the one you mean.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "A", secret = "B", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✗ two secrets

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "A", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` config repeats a key.

blurb: The identity is minted from the cookie's `sub` claim, which is a string, so it must be a refined or opaque `String` type that this context owns. Declare `identity = T`.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours) }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` actor's identity is missing or not a string-constructible type.

blurb: `User.issue(identity)` signs a cookie that expires, so it reads the current time from the `Clock` capability, and a handler's dependencies are always visible in its `given` clause (and a test can stub the clock to know exactly the cookie it gets). Add `consumes bynk { Clock }` to the context and `given Clock` to the handler.
example:
let c <- User.issue(body)   // ✗ the handler lists no `given Clock`

let c <- User.issue(body)   // ✓ with `given Clock` on the handler
summary: `Actor.issue(identity)` on a `SignedCookie` actor is called where the handler does not list `Clock` in `given`.

blurb: The signing key reaches a service handler, which is where a request arrives and a `Set-Cookie` is sent. A provider or an agent holds only the capabilities in its `given`, so `User.issue(identity)` there would find no key and fault on every request. Issue the cookie in the handler.
example:
User.issue(id)   // ✗ in a provider or an agent

let c <- User.issue(body)   // ✓ in a service handler
summary: `Actor.issue(identity)` on a `SignedCookie` actor is called outside a service handler (in a provider or an agent).

blurb: A `SignedCookie` actor signs the session cookies it issues and verifies the ones it receives, so it needs a key. `secret` names the environment variable holding it, never the key itself. `bynk deploy` mints a random 32-byte key for it when the variable is unset, so you never choose one.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` actor does not name its signing secret.

blurb: A session cookie that never expires is the failure a language should not allow by omission, so `ttl` is required. It is how long an issued cookie is valid: the browser's `Max-Age` and the signed expiry both come from it. A stateless cookie cannot be revoked before it expires, so keep it short.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY"), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` actor does not declare a `ttl`.

blurb: A multi-actor `by` clause tries its peers in turn. A cookie is an ambient credential, so the CSRF check must apply only when the cookie is what authenticated the request, and that per-arm rule is not built yet. A `SignedCookie` actor therefore stands alone on its route: give it a single `by who: User` and serve any anonymous route separately.
example:
on POST("/x") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by who: User | Visitor {   // ✗ a `SignedCookie` peer in a sum

on POST("/x") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by who: User {   // ✓ alone
summary: A `SignedCookie` actor appears as a member of a multi-actor sum.

blurb: A route guarded by a session cookie answers one user, so a shared cache must not store its response, or it would serve one user's answer to another. Use `scope: private`, which lets only the browser keep it, or drop `@cache`.
example:
@cache(maxAge: 5.minutes, scope: public)   // ✗ a shared cache would replay it

@cache(maxAge: 5.minutes, scope: private)   // ✓
summary: A `@cache(scope: public)` route is guarded by a `SignedCookie` actor.

blurb: A `SignedCookie` actor reads its session cookie at the boundary, verifies it and hands the handler only the identity, so the signed value never reaches handler code. A `cookies` record on the same route that names that cookie (by its own name or `@name`) would ask for the raw value, so it is refused, and the router leaves the cookie out of a raw `RequestCookies` view too. Read the identity from the `by` binder, and keep other cookies (a theme, a language) in the record.
summary: A typed `cookies` field reads the session cookie that a route's `SignedCookie` actor consumes.

blurb: A session key signs one actor's cookies and nothing else. If two actors shared a variable, a cookie issued for one would verify for the other, and a Bearer token could be replayed as a cookie. Give each actor its own variable; `previous` is the key being rotated out, so it differs from `secret` too.
summary: A `SignedCookie` actor's `secret` or `previous` is also used by another actor, or by itself.

blurb: A stateless signed cookie cannot be revoked before it expires: a copy a user already took keeps working for the whole `ttl`. Beyond 30 days that is a long exposure, so it warns. Shorten the `ttl`, or keep the session on the server (see `examples/sessions`) if you need to log out everywhere.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 31.days), identity = UserId }   // ⚠ long-lived

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` `ttl` is longer than 30 days (warning).

blurb: A `SignedCookie` takes `secret`, `ttl`, `cookie`, `previous` and `sameSite`, and nothing else. The set is closed so a misspelt option is refused rather than ignored. The cookie's `Domain` and `Path` are not configurable on purpose: the issued cookie is always host-only and `Path=/`, which keeps a `__Host-` name valid.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours, domain = "example.com"), identity = UserId }   // ✗

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓
summary: A `SignedCookie` config has a key outside the closed set.

blurb: A `__Host-` cookie name tells the browser to keep the cookie only if it is `Secure`, host-only and `Path=/`, so a sibling subdomain cannot set or overwrite it. An unprefixed session cookie is open to cookie tossing from any subdomain, which is rarely intended. The default is `__Host-session`; drop `cookie` or give it a `__Host-` name.
example:
actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours, cookie = "session"), identity = UserId }   // ⚠ not `__Host-`

actor User { auth = SignedCookie(secret = "SESSION_KEY", ttl = 12.hours), identity = UserId }   // ✓ `__Host-session` by default
summary: A `SignedCookie` `cookie` does not start with `__Host-` (warning).

blurb: A `SignedCookie` actor's session cookie is minted by `Actor.issue(identity)`, which signs it with the actor's key, and removed by `Actor.expire()`, and the CSRF check keys off that actor. A cookie record's `R.field.cookie(v)` or `R.field.expire()` whose field is read under the session cookie's name would write or clear the credential without any of that, so it is refused. Keep the session cookie out of the record and use the actor's own members.
summary: A cookie record's typed write names the session cookie that a `SignedCookie` actor consumes.

blurb: A `Cookie { name: "__Host-session", … }` literal named like a `SignedCookie` actor's session cookie would write or clear the credential by hand, without the actor's signing key, expiry or CSRF seam, so it is refused. Write it with `Actor.issue(identity)` and remove it with `Actor.expire()`.
example:
Ok("x").withCookie(Cookie { name: "__Host-session", value: "forged" })   // ✗ the actor's cookie

Ok("x").withCookie(Cookie { name: "theme", value: "dark" })            // ✓ another cookie
summary: An untyped `Cookie` literal is named like a `SignedCookie` actor's session cookie.

blurb: `by A | B` tries the actors in order and the first that verifies the caller wins. Which one that was is only known when a request arrives, so the handler learns it through the binder and `match`es on it. With no binder the answer would be thrown away and the sum would do nothing a single actor does not. Add one, `by who: A | B`, and match `who` in the body. A single actor needs no binder.
example:
on GET("/x") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by User | Visitor {       // ✗ which one was it?

on GET("/x") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by who: User | Visitor {   // ✓ `who` is the resolved actor
summary: A multi-actor sum `by` clause has no binder to match the resolved actor.

blurb: A `by` clause must name an actor the compiler can find: one declared with `actor` in this context, or a prelude actor (`Visitor`, `Caller`, `Scheduler` or `Producer`). Anything else is a misspelling or a missing declaration. The compiler will not guess, because the actor decides how callers are verified. Fix the spelling, or declare the actor first with `actor Name { auth = … }`.
example:
on GET("/health") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by v: Visitr {     // ✗ no actor of that name

on GET("/health") () -> Effect[HttpResult[String]] by v: Visitor {   // ✓ the prelude actor
summary: A handler's `by` clause names an actor that is not declared.

blurb: An actor's `auth` names how its callers are verified, and the compiler writes that check itself, so the scheme must be one it knows: `None`, `Internal`, `Bearer`, `Signature`, `Oidc`, `Foreign` or `SignedCookie`. There are no user-defined schemes, and a name outside the set is usually a typo or a scheme borrowed from another framework. Choose the one that matches how callers prove who they are, such as `Bearer` for a JWT signed with a shared key; the actors page lists what each one needs.
example:
actor Robot { auth = Bogus }   // ✗ not a scheme the compiler knows

actor Robot { auth = None }    // ✓ one of the seven
summary: An actor declares an authentication scheme that is not compiler-known.

blurb: In `by who: A | B` the peers are tried in order and the first to verify wins. `Visitor`, or any other `None` peer, accepts everyone, so a peer after it can never be reached and its check would never run. Put the catch-all last. A repeated scheme is a different mistake, `bynk.actor.duplicate_sum_scheme`.
summary: A multi-actor sum has an arm unreachable after a catch-all (`None`) peer.

blurb: Adapter dependencies run from adapter to adapter. An adapter sits at the host boundary and is wired in process beside its binding, but a context is a deployment unit with services of its own, so it cannot be consumed from there. Consume a capability that another adapter exports, or put the code that needs a context in a context.
summary: An `adapter` consumed a context; adapter dependencies are adapter-to-adapter.

blurb: An adapter depends on another adapter's capabilities, never on its services, so its `consumes` must say which: `consumes logging { Log }`. The whole-unit form and `as Alias` belong to contexts. Braces that select only types are refused too, since they name no capability. List the capabilities the adapter needs.
summary: An `adapter` used a whole-unit or aliased `consumes`; adapters must select capabilities with `consumes U { Cap, … }`.

blurb: An adapter wraps foreign code, so it holds only what describes that boundary: capabilities, the types that cross it, external providers and helper functions. A `service`, an `agent` or an `actor` has behaviour, state and an address of its own, and those belong to a context. Move the item into a context that `consumes` the adapter's capability, and leave the adapter as an interface to the foreign code.
summary: An `adapter` declared a `service`, `agent`, or other item it may not contain.

blurb: An adapter's `binding` names the one TypeScript module that supplies its external providers, so there is one clause. With two, the compiler would have no way to say which module a provider comes from. Merge them into one clause; the module it names can import whatever others it needs.
summary: An `adapter` declared more than one `binding` clause.

blurb: Each module is listed once: the compiler generates one loader, `./x.wasm.js`, per file. Two entries for one file add nothing, and `./a.wasm` and `a.wasm` are the same file once the path is normalised. Remove the repeat, or correct the name if a different module was meant.
summary: An adapter `binding … includes [ … ]` list names one file more than once.

blurb: `includes` is for WebAssembly modules. The compiler generates a loader for each, `./x.wasm.js`, that gives the binding a compiled module, and it picks them by the `.wasm` extension. Any other file has no such loader. Name a `.wasm` module.
summary: An adapter `binding … includes [ … ]` entry is not a `.wasm` file; only WebAssembly modules can be included.

blurb: `includes` ships WebAssembly modules beside the binding, so each file it names has to exist: the path is read relative to the adapter's source file. A misspelt name, or a module left out of the tree, is the usual cause. Correct the path, or add the file.
summary: An adapter `binding … includes [ … ]` entry names a file that could not be read.

blurb: An included module is part of the adapter's own tree, and, for a dependency, of the tree the lock checksums. So each path is relative to the adapter's file and stays inside its directory: no absolute path, and no `..`. Move the module into the adapter's directory, or a subdirectory of it, and name it from there.
summary: An adapter `binding … includes [ … ]` path is absolute or climbs out of the adapter's directory with `..`.

blurb: An external provider, `provides Jwt = JoseJwt` with no body, is written in TypeScript, not Bynk. The adapter's `binding` clause names that TypeScript module, resolved relative to the adapter's source file, and the compiler reads it to wire the provider in. The code fires when the clause is missing, and when the named file cannot be read. Add `binding "./tokens.binding.ts"` and create the file, exporting a class named for the provider.
summary: An `adapter` declares an external provider but no `binding` module to supply it.

blurb: An adapter wraps code written in TypeScript. Its provider has no body: `provides Jwt = JoseJwt`, and the binding exports a class of that name. A Bynk body would be a second implementation beside the binding's. Remove the body and implement the operations in the binding, or, for a provider written in Bynk, move it to a context. An external provider in a context is `bynk.context.external_provider`.
summary: A provider inside an `adapter` has a Bynk body; adapter providers must be external.

blurb: An agent class that bynk.schema.lock records can't just disappear from source: it must be given one fate, either `agent New replaces Old` (its data moves) or `removed agent Old` (its data is deleted). Giving a name two fates is a conflict: renamed twice, renamed and removed, or removed twice. A rename onto a class that already has recorded history of its own is also refused, since it would merge two histories and Cloudflare refuses a rename onto an existing namespace. Decide what becomes of the old class, and declare that once.
summary: An agent class has more than one fate: it is renamed twice, both renamed and removed, or renamed onto a class that already has its own recorded history in `bynk.schema.lock`.

An agent class recorded in `bynk.schema.lock` is no longer declared, so a deployment's stored instances of it would be orphaned. If the class was never deployed, delete its `[agents]` entry from the lock; renaming or removing a deployed class gets its own declaration in a later state-migrations slice.

blurb: An agent is addressed by its key, so constructing one takes exactly one argument: the value of its single `key` field. `Counter("a")` names the instance with key `"a"`. Two arguments or none do not say which instance is meant. Pass the one key. A key of the wrong type is `bynk.agent.key_mismatch`.
summary: An agent was constructed with the wrong number of key arguments.

blurb: A handler call is checked against the handler's declaration, as a function call is: it must pass one argument for each parameter, no more and no fewer. The agent's key is not one of them, since it was given when the agent was constructed. Match the call to the parameter list. If the handler is missing a parameter it needs, add it to the declaration and update every caller.
summary: An agent handler was called with the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: An agent is used through the handlers it declares with `on call`, so a method name it does not declare is a mistake: usually a misspelling, or a handler that was never written. Check the name against the agent's declaration, or add the handler. To read a `store` field from a caller, add a handler that returns it.
summary: Called a handler the agent does not declare.

blurb: The key is what picks an instance, so its type is fixed by the agent: the type of its `key` field. An agent keyed by `String` cannot be addressed by an `Int`, because `1` and `"1"` would otherwise be easy to confuse and could name different instances. Pass a value of the key's type. The number of key arguments is `bynk.agent.construction_arity`.
summary: An agent key argument has the wrong type.

A `migrate` step reads a schema version below the agent's floor. A complete `bynk migrate sweep` raised the floor past it, so no stored instance can hold that version: the step emits nothing and can be deleted (warning).

blurb: A stored record carries the schema version it was written at, and is loaded through the one `migrate from N` step for that version. Two steps for the same `N` would leave the compiler to choose between them, so the second is refused. Merge them into one step that assigns every field the move from version `N` needs. A step that assigns one field twice is `bynk.agent.migrate_duplicate_assignment`.
summary: Two `migrate` steps in one agent read the same schema version.

blurb: A migration step builds the new state like a record literal: each `store` field takes at most one value. A bare field name in the body reads the value carried over, never an earlier assignment, so a second `:=` to a field cannot build on the first and is refused. Combine the two into one expression of `old` and the carried fields. Two steps for one version is `bynk.agent.migrate_duplicate`.
summary: A `migrate` step assigns the same `store` field more than once; each field takes at most one value per step (record-literal semantics).

blurb: A migration step must be pure and must not read the agent's key. A migration sweep wakes each stored instance by its object ID, which does not recover the key, so a step cannot depend on who the instance is, and it cannot use `?`, `expect` or `Effect.pure`. Compute the new value from `old` and the carried fields. If it needs the key, do that in a handler after the migration.
summary: A `migrate` step uses an effect, a capability, `?`, `expect`, or the agent's `key`; steps are pure and key-free so a migration sweep can run them by object ID.

blurb: A `migrate from N` step must account for every change between version `N` and the agent's current shape. A field that is gone has to be read through `old` or discarded on purpose with `drop`, and a field that changed type has to be assigned. Otherwise stored data would be carried over silently incomplete. A `Set`, `Log` or `Cache` field that changed can only be dropped, which starts it afresh. The message lists what the step leaves out. Read each removed field, `drop` the ones you mean to lose, and assign the retyped ones.
summary: A `migrate` step does not account for every change between its version and the current shape: a removed field must be read (`old.f`) or dropped, and a retyped or re-kinded field must be assigned (or dropped, for a `Set`, `Log` or `Cache` field).

blurb: A `migrate from N (old: T)` step reads a stored record through `T`, so `T` must describe the shape version `N` recorded in bynk.schema.lock, which is not necessarily the shape the code has now. The compiler checks each field of `T` against that record: its storage kind and its type must match what was stored, and a field the class never had is refused too. A `drop` of a field that exists neither then nor now is refused as well. Declare the old type exactly as version `N` stored it, and give a nested type that has changed since its own copy. Keep such types for the step alone.
example:
type CartV1 = { owner: Int }      // ✗ version 1 recorded `owner` as a `String`

type CartV1 = { owner: String }   // ✓ as version 1 stored it
summary: A `migrate` step's declared old shape (or a `drop`) names a field the lock does not record at that version, or records with a different structure.

blurb: A migrate step reads an older recorded version of the agent's state and carries it to the current shape. bynk.schema.lock records the versions an agent class has had, so `from N` must name one of them below the current version, which needs no step. A step from the current version, or from one the lock never recorded, has nothing to read. The message gives the range the lock holds. A class with no history yet, and an unchanged shape, need no step at all. Change the shape first, build to record the new version, then write the step `from` the version it replaces.
summary: A `migrate` step reads a schema version the lock does not record below the agent's current version.

blurb: bynk.schema.lock records the stored shape of every agent class, version by version, and a build compares the new shape against it. A deployed instance holds data in the recorded shape, so a change that data can still be read through, such as a new field, is additive and just bumps the version. A change it cannot be read through, such as a field removed, retyped or renamed, would orphan or misread what is stored, so the build refuses it. A rename looks like a removal plus an addition, and the message names the pairing it infers. Give an added record field a default, keep the old field and add the new one, or carry the data across with a `migrate from N` step, which records the change as a non-additive version. For a class that was never deployed, delete its entry from the schema lock, and the next build records the new shape afresh.
summary: An agent's stored state changed in a way deployed data cannot be read through — a `store` field was removed, retyped (including inside a stored record or sum), or changed storage kind. A renamed field is a removed field plus an added one. If the class was never deployed, delete its `[agents]` entry from `bynk.schema.lock`; otherwise widen rather than narrow, or stage the change through a new field.

blurb: An agent holds state, and a context is the unit that owns it. A `commons` is code shared between contexts, which each `uses` it, so it is not given an agent, a service, an actor or a capability: those are only allowed in a `context`. Declare the agent in a context. A type the agent and other contexts both need can stay in the commons.
example:
commons shop

agent Counter { … }   // ✗ a commons has no state

context shop

agent Counter { … }   // ✓ a context owns it
summary: An `agent` was declared outside a context.

A stored `store` field's refinement changed while its structure did not. A widening is safe; a narrowing faults on load for any stored value that no longer satisfies it (`RehydrationViolation`), so migrate the data first (warning).

blurb: `removed agent Cart` tells the next deploy to delete the class `Cart` and all of its stored data. While `Cart` is still declared, that would delete the data of a class the code still uses, so the two together are refused. Delete the `agent Cart` declaration; the data goes at the next deploy, once you confirm it by name. If the class should stay, delete the `removed agent` line instead.
example:
removed agent Cart    // ✗ `Cart` is still declared
agent Cart { … }

removed agent Cart
agent Basket { … }    // ✓ `Cart` is gone
summary: A `removed agent` declaration names a class that is still declared; removing a class deletes its stored data.

blurb: `agent New replaces Old` renames a class: `Old`'s stored data moves to `New`. While `Old` is still declared, both would claim that data, so it is refused. To rename, delete the `Old` declaration. If the two are separate classes, drop `replaces`. Each old name has one fate, as `bynk.agent.class_conflict` says.
summary: `agent New replaces Old` names an `Old` that is still declared; a rename moves the old class's data to the new one.

blurb: `agent New replaces Old` renames a class: `Old`'s stored data and its recorded history move to `New`. That only works for a class bynk.schema.lock records for this context, so a misspelt old name, or a class that was never built with this context, is refused rather than quietly starting `New` from nothing. Check the old name against the `[agents."…"]` entries in the lock. The old class must also be gone from source, as `bynk.agent.replaces_live` requires.
example:
agent Basket replaces Trolley {   // ✗ the lock records no class `shop.Trolley`

agent Basket replaces Cart {      // ✓ a recorded class, and no longer declared
summary: `agent New replaces Old` names an `Old` that `bynk.schema.lock` does not record for this context, so there is no recorded class to rename.

blurb: An agent handler reads and writes the agent's stored state, and may call other agents and capabilities, so it does work in the world, not just compute a value. Bynk marks that in the type: a handler must return `Effect[T]`, and its caller takes the result with `<-`. A bare `Int` would claim the handler is pure. Wrap the return type in `Effect`. A plain `fn`, which really is pure, returns an ordinary value.
summary: An agent handler's return type is not an `Effect`.

blurb: Inside an agent's handlers and invariants, `<Agent>State` names the record of the agent's `Cell` fields: for agent `Counter`, `CounterState`. A type you declare with that name would be silently replaced there, so the compiler refuses it instead of renaming anything: unlike the names it derives elsewhere, this one can be written in a program. Rename your type.
summary: A type is named `<Agent>State` beside agent `<Agent>`; that name is the agent's state record (its `Cell` fields), which its handlers and invariants see in place of the type.

A schema version between the agent's floor and its current version has no way forward: no `migrate` step covers it and its path to the current shape is not entirely additive, so a stored record at that version faults on load with `NoMigrationPath` (warning).

blurb: A key's state is initialised automatically the first time it is used, before any handler runs, so a `store` field's `= value` must be fixed when the program compiles: a literal, a variant, `Some`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`, a record, or `T.unsafe(lit)` for an opaque type. It cannot read `self`, a parameter or a capability, or call anything. The code is also reported for a static value of the wrong type. Write the starting value out, and set the real one from a handler. A field with no initialiser and no zero is `bynk.agents.non_zeroable_state_field`.
example:
store label: Cell[String] = self.id   // ✗ `self` is not available to an initialiser

store label: Cell[String] = ""   // ✓ a static starting value
summary: An agent `store` field initialiser is not a static value of the field's type.

blurb: A key that has never been used is initialised automatically the first time it is touched, so every `store Cell[T]` field needs a starting value. With no initialiser, the compiler supplies a zero (`0`, `false`, `""`, `None`, or a record of zeroed fields), but only where that zero is a valid value of the type. An opaque type, a sum other than `Option`, and a refined type that rules its zero out have none, and the compiler will not invent a value that the type's own constructors might refuse. Say what "not set yet" means: wrap the type in `Option`, where `None` is the zero, give the field an initialiser, `store name: Cell[T] = value`, or relax a refinement so that its zero is allowed (`NonNegative` admits `0`; `Positive` does not).
example:
type Secret = opaque String

store secret: Cell[Secret]                // ✗ no zero value for an opaque type

store secret: Cell[Option[Secret]]        // ✓ `None` until it is set
summary: An agent `store` field has no initialiser and no implicit zero value.

blurb: An asset is a name for a file, read as a value (`style.url`), so a unit declares each name once: a second `asset style` would leave `style` meaning two files. Give each asset its own name, or drop the repeat when it names the same file. An asset whose name is a function's or a type's is `bynk.resolve.name_conflict` instead.
example:
asset style = "assets/board.css"
asset style = "assets/print.css"    // ✗ `style` is already declared

asset style = "assets/board.css"
asset print = "assets/print.css"    // ✓ one name each
summary: An `asset` name is declared more than once in the same unit.

blurb: `at` serves an asset at a fixed URL, for clients that ask for a file by name, such as `/favicon.ico`, so the path must be the URL of one file: it starts with `/`, does not end in `/`, and uses only letters, digits and `._~-` between its slashes. It may not be under `/_assets/` or `/_bynk/`, which Bynk uses itself, nor be `/_headers`, `/_redirects` or `/.assetsignore`, which the platform reads as configuration. Write the path of a single file.
example:
asset favicon = "assets/favicon.ico" at "/icons/"          // ✗ a folder, not a file

asset favicon = "assets/favicon.ico" at "/favicon.ico"    // ✓
summary: An `asset`'s `at` path is not a URL path naming one file, or lies under `/_assets/` or `/_bynk/`, or is a file the platform reads as configuration.
A parameterised HTTP route matches a fixed asset path, so it never sees requests for that path (a warning).

blurb: An `asset` is a file the build ships, and the compiler reads it to hash its contents into the asset's URL, so the file must exist when the project is built. The path is relative to the project root and must name a regular file; a symbolic link is not followed. Create the file under `assets/`, or correct the path. A file that exists but cannot be read is `bynk.asset.unreadable_file`.
example:
asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✗ no such file in the project
asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✓ once assets/board.css exists
summary: An `asset` names a file that is not in the project's `assets/` folder.
A single-file build met an `asset` declaration; assets need a project build.
A deployable Bundle build met an `asset`; a Bundle ships no files, so its `.url` would not be served (a warning).

blurb: An asset is served to anyone who asks, without the Worker running, so it may come only from the project's `assets/` folder. If any path were allowed, a declaration could publish `.env` or a source file just by naming it. Move or copy the file into `assets/` and name it there. A path that is absolute or contains `..` is `bynk.asset.unsafe_path` instead.
example:
asset style = "styles/board.css"        // ✗ not in the assets/ folder
asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✓
summary: An `asset` path does not name a file in the project's `assets/` folder.

blurb: An `asset` is a file the platform serves, shipped with each context that declares it or `uses` a commons that does. An adapter is the host boundary, not a deployed unit of its own, so an `asset` there is refused. Declare it in a context or a commons. For text compiled into the program rather than served, see `bynk.embed.outside_context_or_commons`.
example:
// app/host.bynk
adapter app.host

binding "./host.binding.ts"

asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✗ an adapter cannot declare an asset

// app/page.bynk
commons app.page

asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✓ in a commons
summary: An `asset` declaration appears outside a context or commons.

blurb: A fixed asset path names one file, and a Worker serves one file at it, so two assets cannot both claim `/legal.txt`. One path cannot be a folder of another either, as `/logo` and `/logo/icon.png` would be: a name cannot be both a file and a directory. Give each asset its own path. Two assets for the same file at the same path are no conflict. A route at an asset's path is `bynk.asset.shadows_route`.
example:
asset terms = "assets/a.txt" at "/legal.txt"
asset privacy = "assets/b.txt" at "/legal.txt"    // ✗ a second file at `/legal.txt`

asset terms = "assets/a.txt" at "/terms.txt"
asset privacy = "assets/b.txt" at "/privacy.txt"    // ✓
summary: Two different asset files would be served at one fixed path by the same Worker.

blurb: The platform answers a fixed asset's path before the Worker runs, and it does so for every method, so an HTTP handler at exactly that path can never be reached. The compiler refuses it rather than ship a route that never runs. Move the route, or give the asset another path. A route with a parameter that matches the asset's path, such as `/:page`, still serves every other path, and is only the warning `bynk.asset.may_shadow_route`. The members of a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group share one assets directory, so an asset in one member shadows a route of the same path in another.
summary: A fixed asset path equals a literal HTTP route, in the same context or in another member of the same `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group, which the platform-served asset makes unreachable.
An `asset` names a file in the project's `assets/` folder that could not be read.

blurb: An asset's path must stay inside the project: it may not be empty or absolute, and it may not contain a `..` segment. Assets are public, so a path that starts at the filesystem root or climbs out of the project could publish a file that was never meant to ship. Write the path relative to the project root, inside `assets/`. A relative path that is only outside `assets/` is `bynk.asset.outside_assets_dir`.
example:
asset style = "assets/../board.css"     // ✗ a `..` segment
asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✓
summary: An `asset` path is empty, absolute, or contains a `..` segment.

blurb: A context can export a record whose field has a type it does not export. Reading that field through a value you got from it needs the field's type, and if two contexts you consume each declare a type of that name with different shapes, the compiler cannot tell which is meant. Rename one of the two so a name stands for one shape across the contexts you consume.
summary: A value's type is declared, with different shapes, by more than one consumed context, so its fields cannot be read.

blurb: A value that crosses a context boundary, as an argument to a consumed context's service or as its result, is matched by shape, not by name. So where both contexts declare a `Box`, the two must have the same shape, or the value is not a `Box` on the other side. Give them the same fields, or rename one so the names stop meeting. A type both sides need can live in a `commons` that each `uses`.
summary: Data crossing a context boundary did not match the expected shape.

blurb: A derived capability is another instance of a platform resource, with a namespace, bucket or limiter of its own. Only a platform resource kind, such as `Kv` or `R2`, has instances. A capability such as `Clock` has no resource to separate, so there is nothing to derive; use it bare, with `given Clock`.
summary: A derived capability's base is not a platform resource that can be instantiated.

blurb: A derived capability is an instance of a platform resource, and the resource's data belongs to a context. An adapter only describes a boundary to foreign code, so it has no data to own. Declare the instance in a context that selects the base with `consumes`.
summary: A derived capability was declared outside a context.

blurb: A few platform capabilities (`Service`, `R2`, `RateLimit`, `Queue`, `Analytics`, `D1` and `EdgeCache`) are never used as the bare kind. Each stands for a particular resource of its own: a database, a bucket, a limiter with a limit and a window, a Worker. So you declare a named instance, `capability Orders = D1`, which gets a binding and a double of its own, and a handler asks for that instance in `given` instead of the kind. Two instances of one kind never share data. Some kinds need options on the instance, such as `RateLimit @limit(20) @period(60.seconds)`.
example:
on call() -> Effect[()] by Caller given D1 {            // ✗ the bare kind names no database

capability Orders = D1
on call() -> Effect[()] by Caller given Orders {        // ✓ a named instance
summary: A platform capability that is used only through named instances (`Service`, `R2`, `RateLimit`, `Queue`, `Analytics`, `D1`, `EdgeCache`) was used bare, in a `given` clause.

blurb: A derived capability, `capability Name = Kind`, can take options after the kind, each one positional literal that the compiler reads while it checks the program: `Service` takes `@worker("name")`, `R2` an optional `@jurisdiction("eu")`, `RateLimit` a `@limit(n)` and a `@period(d)`, and `Queue` a `@name("queue")`. The value must be a literal of the option's kind, and one the platform accepts: `@limit` a positive `Int`, `@period` `10.seconds` or `60.seconds`, `@jurisdiction` `"eu"` or `"fedramp"`, `@tls` (on a `MySql`) `"required"`, `"verify-ca"` or `"verify-identity"`, `@worker` a Worker name and `@name` a queue name, each of 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits and `-` (a Worker name may also hold `_`). Each option is given once, and an `@worker` must name a Worker outside the project, since a context of your own is reached with `consumes`. A bad value would otherwise surface only when the platform refuses the deployment, so it is refused here. Use one of the values the note lists. `RateLimit` is experimental, so the project opts in under `[unstable]` in `bynk.toml`.
summary: A derived capability's option is not a single positional literal of its kind (string, positive `Int`, or an offered window), is given twice, or is a value the kind refuses (an `@worker` that is not a well-formed Worker name outside the project, a malformed queue `@name`, an unknown `@jurisdiction`).

blurb: A derived capability, `capability Name = Kind`, takes its configuration from options after the kind, and some kinds cannot work without them: a `Service` needs the Worker it reaches, `@worker(…)`, a `Queue` its `@name(…)`, a `RateLimit` its `@limit(…)` and `@period(…)`, and a `StoredSecret` its `@store(…)` and `@secret(…)`. There is no default. Write the options the note shows. A value the platform would refuse is `bynk.capability.invalid_option`; an option the kind does not take is `bynk.capability.unknown_option`.
summary: A derived capability lacks an option its base requires, such as a `Service` instance's `@worker`.

blurb: On the Workers target, each context is its own Worker, and a Worker builds every capability its handlers are given. A handler's `given Mailer` therefore needs a `provides Mailer = …` in the same context, which says what the capability does there. Without one the Worker has nothing to hand the handler, so the compiler refuses it here and does not leave it to fail in the generated TypeScript. The bundle target (the default) asks only when the program has a composition root (`composeApp`), which it has once a context consumes another context's service or capability, emits events, or derives a capability: `composeApp` builds every context itself, so nothing else can supply the capability, and a test `stub` covers only the cases that stub it. Without a root, the host program can supply the capability when it builds the surface. A capability declared in another context is that context's to provide, and an exported capability with no provider has its own `bynk.exports.capability_not_provided`. Add a provider to the context, or, on Workers, build for `--target bundle` when the bundle has no composition root.
summary: A capability a context requires has no provider in it, on the Workers target or in a bundle with a composition root.

blurb: A call to a capability operation passes exactly the parameters its declaration lists, so `Clock.now(1)` against `fn now() -> Effect[Int]` has one argument too many. Pass the declared number of arguments. If the operation really needs another parameter, add it to the capability's declaration and to every provider of it.
summary: A capability operation was called with the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: A capability is a typed interface to the outside world: a context declares it, provides it and asks for it in `given`, and the compiler wires the provider to the services that need it. A commons holds only pure declarations, so it cannot declare one. Move the capability into the context that uses it, or, for one several contexts share, into a context that exports it.
example:
commons demo

capability Logger {                     // ✗ a commons cannot declare a capability
  fn log(message: String) -> Effect[()]
}

context demo

capability Logger {                     // ✓ a context can
  fn log(message: String) -> Effect[()]
}
summary: A `capability` was declared outside a context.

blurb: On the Workers target, each context is its own Worker with its own `env`, and a Worker builds the capabilities its handlers are given. If a context requires a capability that another context provides, it builds that provider in its own Worker. When that provider constructs agents of the context it lives in, it needs the Durable Object bindings of that context, which the consumer's `env` does not have, so the build would fail, or `bynk dev` would quietly keep the agent's state in the isolate. The compiler refuses the requirement instead. Reach the agents through a service of the providing context, which runs in its own Worker beside its own bindings, or build for `--target bundle`, where every context shares one process.
summary: On the Workers target, a context requires a capability whose provider, in another context, constructs that context's agents; the consumer's Worker would build the provider without a binding for those agents' Durable Objects.

blurb: `capability Sessions = Kv` makes a separate instance of a platform capability, so the base has to be one the context has selected: `consumes bynk.cloudflare { Kv }`. A name that is not selected is a misspelling, or a `consumes` that was left out. Correct the name, or select the capability.
summary: A derived capability's base is not a capability the context consumes.

blurb: A capability is an interface: its operations are exactly the `fn` signatures in its declaration, and a provider supplies nothing more. Calling `Clock.nope()` asks for an operation the capability does not declare, which usually means a misspelt name. Call one of the declared operations, or add the new operation to the capability and to each provider of it.
summary: Referenced an operation the capability does not declare.

blurb: An option after the kind in `capability Name = Kind @option(…)` must be one that kind takes: `Service` takes `@worker`, `R2` `@jurisdiction`, `RateLimit` `@limit` and `@period`, `Queue` `@name`, `MySql` `@tls`, and `StoredSecret` `@store` and `@secret`, while `Kv`, `Analytics`, `D1`, `EdgeCache` and `Postgres` take none. One the kind does not take is refused rather than ignored, since it is probably a misspelling or the wrong kind. Drop it, or use one of the options the note lists. An option that is known but has a bad value is `bynk.capability.invalid_option`.
example:
capability Sessions = Kv @ttl          // ✗ `Kv` instances take no options
capability Sessions = Kv               // ✓
summary: A derived capability carries an option its base does not take.

blurb: A `:=` replaces the value of a `Cell`, the one store kind that holds a single value. A `Set`, `Map`, `Log` or `Cache` has no one value to replace; each changes through its own operations (`add`, `put`, `append`), and a name that is not a `store` field of the agent has nothing to write. Use the operation the field's kind offers, or declare the field `Cell[T]` if a single replaceable value is what you want. The same check covers a `migrate from` step that assigns a field.
example:
store ids: Set[Int]

ids := n               // ✗ a `Set` has no single value to replace

let _ <- ids.add(n)    // ✓ the operation the kind offers
summary: A `:=` write targets something that is not a `store Cell` field.

blurb: A `:=` writes a `Cell` store field, and its right-hand side may not read the cell it is writing. Computing the new value from the old one is a hidden read-modify-write; Bynk asks for `.update(fn)` instead, so the dependency on the prior value is written down where a reader (and a retry) can see it. A `:=` is for a value that does not depend on what the cell held.
example:
count := count + 1                       // ✗ reads `count` while writing it

let _ <- count.update((c) => c + 1)      // ✓ awaited, as an effect; the combiner gets the old value
summary: A `:=` right-hand side reads the cell being written (a read-modify-write); use `.update`.

blurb: Workers Cache is one setting for the whole Worker, and a context has one Worker, so a context declares at most one `EdgeCache` instance, which both turns the cache on and purges it. A second would be another handle on the same cache, so it is refused. Delete it and use the first instance wherever you need it, with `given`.
example:
capability Edge = EdgeCache
capability Cdn = EdgeCache    // ✗ one `EdgeCache` per context

capability Edge = EdgeCache   // ✓ use `Edge` everywhere
summary: A context declares a second `EdgeCache` instance; the edge cache is one setting for the whole Worker.

blurb: A capability you `export` is built by each context that consumes it, in that context's own Worker. A provider that reaches `EdgeCache` would purge from there, and a purge reaches only the cache of the Worker it runs in, so this context's cache would keep the stale response. Keep the capability inside the context and have a service route do the purge, which another context can reach by calling that service.
summary: An exported capability reaches an `EdgeCache` instance through its provider's `given`; a consuming context would build it in its own Worker, whose purge misses this one's cache.

blurb: A purge reaches the edge cache only when it runs in the Worker's own `fetch`. An agent runs in a Durable Object, so an agent handler that reaches `EdgeCache`, with `given Edge` or through a provider that does, would not reach this Worker's cache. Purge from the service handler that calls the agent. A queue consumer and an `on schedule` handler have the same rule: `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_queue`, `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_schedule`.
summary: An agent handler reaches an `EdgeCache` instance, directly or through a provider's `given`; an agent's purge would not reach the Worker's cache.

blurb: A purge reaches the edge cache only from the Worker's own `fetch`, the entrypoint that serves cached responses. A queue consumer is not that entrypoint, and its purge is not known to reach the cache, so a consumer that reaches `EdgeCache`, with `given Edge` or through a provider that does, is refused. Purge from a service handler instead. An agent and an `on schedule` handler have the same rule: `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_agent`, `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_schedule`.
summary: A queue consumer reaches an `EdgeCache` instance; purge from a service handler instead.

blurb: A purge reaches the edge cache only from the Worker's own `fetch`. Cloudflare accepts a purge from a cron run, but it clears nothing from the cache that `fetch` serves, so the stale responses would stay. An `on schedule` handler that reaches `EdgeCache`, with `given Edge` or through a provider that does, is refused. Purge from a service handler instead. An agent and a queue consumer have the same rule: `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_agent`, `bynk.cloudflare.edge_cache_in_queue`.
summary: An `on schedule` handler reaches an `EdgeCache` instance; a cron run's purge is accepted but clears nothing from the fetch cache, so purge from a service handler.

blurb: In a context with `EdgeCache`, the edge keys a response by its URL alone, and `scope: public` lets it share one response with every later caller. On a route whose actor authenticates, such as a `Bearer` one, that response belongs to one caller, so it would be served to the rest. Use `scope: private`, which is never shared at the edge, or serve the route `by Visitor`. See also `bynk.http.cache_public_reads_cookies`.
summary: In a context with `EdgeCache`, a `@cache(scope: public)` route is served by an actor that authenticates; its response would be shared at the edge with every caller.

`tsc` rejected the TypeScript the compiler generated for a program that passed the checker. This is a bug in the Bynk compiler, not in the program: the diagnostic points at the Bynk code the failing generated line came from, with the TypeScript error attached (#3068).

blurb: `consumes payment as Pay` gives a context one name to call a unit by, and a name for one unit. Two clauses with the same alias, a unit consumed under two aliases, or an alias that is also a type, function, capability, service or agent of this context, would leave a call such as `Pay.charge(…)` with no single meaning. Give each clause its own alias, or drop it. The same clause in another file of the context is fine.
example:
// shop.bynk
context shop

consumes payment as Pay
consumes shipping as Pay     // ✗ `Pay` already names `payment`

consumes payment as Pay
consumes shipping as Ship    // ✓ one name each
summary: Two `consumes` aliases collide.

blurb: `consumes payment { Gateway }` brings `Gateway` in by its bare name, so that `given Gateway` reads it. If the context already declares a capability of that name, or a second consumed unit supplies one, the bare name would mean two things. Reach it qualified instead, `given payment.Gateway`, rename the local one, or consume the unit under an alias instead of selecting names from it, `consumes payment as pay`, and write `given pay.Gateway`.
summary: Two flattened `consumes U { Cap }` capabilities collide, or one clashes with a local capability.

blurb: Imports are per file, for capabilities as for types. A braced `consumes U { Cap }` brings the capability `Cap` into scope as a bare name, but only in the file that writes it: a `given Cap` clause, a call `Cap.op(…)`, a `provides Cap = …`, a derived capability's base, or a suite's `stub Cap.op`. A file that names one its own `consumes` does not list is an error; `bynk check --fix=bynk.consumes.capability_not_selected` adds the name to this file's `consumes`, or adds one. The unit's wiring and deploy order still follow the union of its files' `consumes`.
summary: A capability a consumed unit exports is named (a `given` clause, a call, `provides`, a `stub`) in a file whose own `consumes` does not list it.

blurb: `consumes payment` brings every type that `payment` exports into scope under its own name, because the services' signatures use them. If this context already has something of that name, a type declared here or reached through `uses`, or a function, asset, service, agent or provider, a mention would mean two things, so the compiler refuses the clause. Rename the imported type with `as`: it is then in scope only under the alias, and is still the same type. `bynk.consumes.type_alias_conflict` is the same clash with an alias.
summary: A `consumes` name collides with another name in scope.

blurb: `consumes` declares that a context depends on a different one. A context's own declarations are already in scope, so consuming itself adds nothing, and a context that depends on itself is a cycle of length one. Delete the clause, or, if you meant another context, name it. A cycle through several contexts is `bynk.context.consumes_cycle`.
summary: A context `consumes` itself.

blurb: A cross-context call has the shape of the `on call` handler it reaches: one argument for each parameter. The consumed context owns that signature, so the caller adapts to it. Pass the arguments the handler declares (the note says where it is declared), or change the handler's parameters if the service needs different input.
summary: A consumed service was called with the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: A service you call may take or return a type declared in a third context. The value crosses the call as that context's type, so your context has to state the dependency itself: it does not inherit it from the service's context. Add `consumes` for the context the error names.
summary: A cross-context call reaches a service whose signature names a type the consumed context itself consumes from a third context, which the caller does not consume.

blurb: `consumes` is for depending on a context, or on an adapter: it is how you call a service and use the capabilities the other unit exports. A commons has neither. It is shared types and functions, brought in with `uses`. Replace `consumes` with `uses`.
example:
// money.bynk
commons money

type Amount = Int where NonNegative

// shop.bynk
context shop

consumes money                   // ✗ `money` is a commons
uses money                       // ✓ shared declarations come in with `uses`
summary: `consumes` targets a `commons` instead of a context.

blurb: `as` renames a type that the consumed context exports, for use in this one. A capability keeps its own name wherever it is used, in `given` and in calls. Select it bare, `consumes payment { Gateway }`, or consume the context without braces and write `given payment.Gateway`.
summary: A capability was aliased in `consumes U { Cap as Alias }`; only exported types can be aliased.

blurb: An alias is a name in this context, so it cannot be one that is already taken: by another alias, by a type or function the context declares or brings in with `uses`, or by a capability. Give each aliased type a name of its own. A consumed type that is not aliased, and clashes with one of these, is `bynk.consumes.name_conflict`.
example:
// shop.bynk
context shop

consumes payment { AuthId as Id, Receipt as Id }            // ✗ `Id` already names `AuthId`

consumes payment { AuthId as Id, Receipt as ReceiptId }     // ✓ distinct aliases
summary: A `consumes U { T as Alias }` alias collides with a type or value in scope, or with another alias.

blurb: A type is in scope under one name, so it is selected once in a file: the alias is that name. Selecting it twice, or both bare and aliased, would leave two names for it. Keep one selection. The bare selection of a type is not needed, since `consumes payment` already brings every exported type into scope.
example:
// shop.bynk
context shop

consumes payment { AuthId as A, AuthId as B }   // ✗ `AuthId` aliased twice

consumes payment { AuthId as Auth }             // ✓ one alias
summary: An exported type is aliased more than once, or is selected both bare and aliased, in `consumes U { … }`.

blurb: `consumes payment { AuthId as Auth }` brings a type that `payment` exports in under another name, so the type has to be one it exports. A misspelt name, or a type that `payment` keeps to itself, is the usual cause. Correct the name, or ask `payment` to export the type.
example:
// shop.bynk
context shop

consumes payment { AuthIdd as Auth }   // ✗ `payment` exports no `AuthIdd`

consumes payment { AuthId as Auth }    // ✓ a type it exports
summary: `consumes U { T as Alias }` names a type `U` does not export.

blurb: Imports are per file. A unit's own declarations are shared by all its files, but a name from another unit, a type or a bare variant of one of its sums, is in scope only in a file that itself has a `consumes` bringing it in, and where the list is braced, only if it is listed. Naming a type that this file's own `consumes` does not bring in is an error, whether the clause lists other names or only another file of the unit consumes the unit; `bynk check --fix=bynk.consumes.type_not_selected` adds the name to this file's `consumes`, or adds one. A bare `consumes U`, with no braces, brings in all of `U`'s names for that file.
summary: A type (or a bare variant of a sum) of a consumed unit is named in a file whose own `consumes` does not bring it in: it lists other names, or only another file of the unit consumes the unit.

blurb: Imports are per file. A call to another unit's service (`pay.charge(…)`, or through the alias of `consumes pay as P`) is in scope only in a file that itself `consumes` that unit, in any form, even when another file of the same context does. A call from a file that does not is an error; `bynk check --fix=bynk.consumes.unit_not_consumed` adds `consumes <unit>` to this file. The unit's wiring and deploy order still follow the union of its files' `consumes`.
