summary: A call to another unit's service is written in a file whose own `consumes` does not name that unit.

blurb: A `consumes` clause is how one context states that it depends on another, so it has to name a context in the project, and no unit of that name exists. Check the spelling against the `context` line of the unit you mean.
summary: `consumes` names a context that does not exist.

blurb: A call such as `pay.charge(…)` reaches a service of the consumed context, and `pay` has none by that name. Only a service's `on call` handler can be called across contexts, so check the spelling against the consumed context and that the service has an `on call` handler. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `bynk.consumes.service_arity`.
summary: Called a service the consumed context does not declare.

blurb: A `Container` is built from a Dockerfile: `@build("dir")` names the project-relative directory that holds it, and `bynk check` looks for `dir/Dockerfile`. A directory with no Dockerfile would fail only when `wrangler deploy` tried to build the image, so it is refused here. Create the Dockerfile, or correct the path. Bynk does not read or generate the Dockerfile, and the image must be built for `linux/amd64`.
example:
capability Renderer = Container @build("containers/renderer") @port(8080)    // ✗ containers/renderer/Dockerfile does not exist
capability Renderer = Container @build("containers/renderer") @port(8080)    // ✓ once containers/renderer/Dockerfile exists
summary: A `Container`'s `@build` directory holds no `Dockerfile`, so there is no image to build.

blurb: `@build` on a `Container` is a directory inside the project, written relative to the project root with `/` separators: `@build("containers/renderer")`. An empty path, an absolute path, a drive path, a path with `\` and a path that leaves the project with `..` are refused, so the build context can never reach outside the project and the emitted configuration stays a function of the source.
example:
capability Renderer = Container @build("../renderer") @port(8080)       // ✗ leaves the project
capability Renderer = Container @build("containers/renderer") @port(8080) // ✓
summary: A `Container`'s `@build` is not a directory inside the project: it is empty, absolute, uses `\`, or leaves the project with `..`.

blurb: A container's image is built by `wrangler deploy` from the Dockerfile that `@build` names. The generated `wrangler.toml` reaches it from the Worker's output directory, `<out>/workers/<worker>`, by a relative path back into the project, so the output directory has to be inside the project; the path is computed from the directory the build is written to. A build into a directory outside the project is refused, naming each container and both paths, because a path that climbs out and back in would break when the output is moved, and copying the build directory into the output would take `node_modules`, secrets and large files with it. Build into a directory inside the project: set `[build] out` or pass `--out` a path under the project root.
example:
# bynk.toml
[build]
out = "../dist"    # ✗ outside the project
out = "dist"       # ✓ inside it
summary: A build with a `Container` is written to an output directory outside the project, so `wrangler` cannot reach the container's Dockerfile from the Worker's output directory by a relative path inside the project.

blurb: Contexts may not form a circle of `consumes` clauses, whether directly or through others. `bynk deploy` takes the order in which to upload the Workers from the `consumes` clauses, because Cloudflare resolves a Service Binding when a Worker is uploaded and so the callee must already exist; a cycle has no such order. The error names the cycle and sits on one of its clauses. Remove one clause: usually the callee takes what it needs as an argument instead of calling back. Logic both contexts need can move into a `commons` that each `uses`.
summary: Contexts form a `consumes` dependency cycle.

blurb: A Worker's bindings share one `env`, so each name can be declared once. Bynk names the bindings after what the context declares: an agent, a consumed context, a derived capability, and the `Kv` namespace of `bynk.cloudflare`, whose binding is `KV`. Here the consumed context `kv` also becomes a Service Binding named `KV`, and the two would overwrite each other. Rename the declaration behind one of them. The error is on the one you can rename, not on the `bynk.cloudflare` clause. A bundle build has no bindings, so only the Workers target checks this.
summary: A Worker would declare two bindings with the same name, such as an agent `Kv` and the `bynk.cloudflare` KV namespace (both `KV`).

blurb: A context that `consumes` another may hold and pass on the other's types, but may not build one. A refined or opaque type can promise an invariant, a `Matches` pattern or a smart constructor, and that holds only if every value is made by the owner; `.of`, `.unsafe` and a variant constructor are refused from outside, as is the record syntax of an opaque type. Ask the owner for the value instead: a service that returns it, or takes the plain input and does the check. `bynk.context.opaque_inspection` is the other side, looking inside such a value.
summary: A context-owned type was constructed from outside that context.

blurb: Decoding creates a value, and a context may not create one of a type another context owns and exports opaque. A decoder would check no more than the base type, because the owner's predicate is the owner's secret. So a handler that takes such a type as its input (an HTTP, queue, event or WebSocket handler decodes it from bytes), and a `Json.decode`, `Json.decodeSql` or `Codable` witness of it, are refused. Take the plain form of the input and let the owner's service make the value. A reply from the owner's own service is fine: its decode is generated.
summary: A context decoded a type another context owns and exports opaque: through `Json.decode`, `Json.decodeSql` or a `Codable` witness, or as the input of an HTTP, queue, event or WebSocket handler. Decoding creates a value, which only the owning context may do; its codec would check no more than the base type.

blurb: A provider with no body (`provides Clock = SystemClock`) says its implementation comes from elsewhere, and only an `adapter` has a binding to supply it. In a context every provider is written in Bynk, so it needs a body implementing the capability's operations. Add one, or move the capability into an adapter if the code is TypeScript. The reverse mistake is `bynk.adapter.provider_has_body`.
summary: A bodiless (external) provider was declared outside an `adapter`.

blurb: A context that writes `exports opaque { T }` lets other contexts hold a `T`, pass it on and call its methods, but not look inside it: they cannot `match` on it, read a field, match a record pattern against it, or name one of its variants. Only the owning context sees the shape, so it can change the representation, or keep an invariant the type's constructors enforce, without breaking a consumer. Ask the owner for what you need instead: a service that returns the answer as a plain value, such as a `Bool`. If the shape is meant to be public, the owner exports it with `exports transparent { T }`.
summary: An opaquely-exported type was inspected from outside its context.

blurb: A context that `uses` a commons gets its sum types by name, but not their variant constructors, so `Circle(1.0)` is refused there: the context re-exports the type under its own name, without the constructors. Build the value in the commons, in a function that returns it, and call that function from the context.
summary: A variant of a `uses`-sourced commons sum type was constructed directly inside a context, where the emitter's per-context rebrand leaves its constructors out of scope.

blurb: Every `requires` and `ensures` clause has a name, and a failure report points at a clause by that name, so each name must be unique within one function, across both kinds. Rename the repeat; the error is on its name.
example:
fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  requires bigger: x > 0
  ensures bigger: result > x      // ✗ `bigger` is already taken

fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  requires positive: x > 0
  ensures bigger: result > x      // ✓
summary: A function declares two contract clauses (`requires`/`ensures`) with the same name.

blurb: A contract clause is checked on every call in the dev and test build, and by the runner on generated inputs, so its predicate must be a pure `Bool` over the parameters and `result`. Effects (`Effect.pure`, `?`) and test-only constructs (`expect`, `val`, observations, `faults`, `trace`) cannot appear in it. State the claim as a plain comparison, and keep assertions and effects in a `case`.
example:
fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  ensures bigger: expect result > x   // ✗ `expect` is a test statement

fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  ensures bigger: result > x          // ✓ a pure `Bool`
summary: A contract predicate uses an effectful or test-only construct; a contract clause must be pure.

blurb: A `requires` or `ensures` clause is a claim the function can meet or break, so its predicate must be a `Bool`. A value of another type, such as an `Int`, claims nothing that could fail. Write a comparison or another `Bool` expression over the parameters (and `result`, in an `ensures`).
example:
fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  ensures bigger: result + 1      // ✗ an `Int`, not a `Bool`

fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  ensures bigger: result > x      // ✓
summary: A contract predicate does not have type `Bool`.

blurb: A function's `ensures` is checked at every call, in production and in every test that reaches it. A test that calls the function and `expect`s the same predicate adds nothing and has to be kept in step with the contract. The compiler flags the repeat. The check is narrow: it fires only on a syntactic restatement over the same arguments. Delete the test, or keep a case only for a specific value a reader should see, such as `expect discount(100, 10) == 90`.
summary: A `case`/`property` merely restates a contract clause already declared at the function; the test is redundant.

blurb: A `requires` clause is checked on entry, before the function has returned anything, so `result` is not bound there. Only an `ensures` can read it. Either state the condition over the parameters, or, if it is a claim about the return value, make it an `ensures`. A parameter that is itself named `result` is read as that parameter.
example:
fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  requires small: result < 100    // ✗ nothing has been returned yet

fn inc(x: Int) -> Int
  ensures small: result < 100     // ✓ checked on exit
summary: A precondition (`requires`) references `result`; the return value is only in scope inside an `ensures`.

blurb: A scheduled trigger carries one thing, the time it fired, so an `on schedule` handler takes at most one parameter, and it must be an `Instant`: the time the schedule fired. Drop the parameter, or type it `Instant`. A parameter typed `Int` (the old spelling) is this error too: write `at: Instant`, and use `at.toEpochMillis()` where the body needs the number.
example:
on schedule("*/5 * * * *") (at: Int) -> Effect[Result[(), String]] { … }   // ✗ the time is an `Instant`

on schedule("*/5 * * * *") (at: Instant) -> Effect[Result[(), String]] { … }          // ✓
summary: A cron handler declares more than one parameter, or a non-`Int` one.

blurb: The context's `scheduled` entry point picks the handler by the schedule that fired, so each schedule may be declared once across all its `from cron` services. Two handlers with the same one would leave it with two to run. Merge them into one handler, or give one a different schedule.
summary: Two cron handlers declare the same schedule.

blurb: A cron schedule is a standard five-field expression: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week, separated by whitespace. Bynk checks the field count at compile time so a schedule the platform's cron trigger would reject is caught before deploy, not when it silently never runs. Only the count is checked at compile time. A bad parameter or return type on the handler is `bynk.cron.bad_params` or `bynk.cron.return_not_effect_result`.
example:
on schedule("every day") () -> Effect[Result[(), String]] { … }   // ✗ words, not five fields

on schedule("0 3 * * *") () -> Effect[Result[(), String]] { … }   // ✓ 03:00 every day
summary: A cron expression is not five whitespace-separated fields.

blurb: A cron run has no caller to hand a value to and no retry channel: `Ok(())` completes the run silently and `Err(e)` logs `e` and completes. So the handler must return `Effect[Result[(), E]]`, with `()` on the success side, for some error type `E`. Return `Ok(())` when the work is done and map a failure to `Err`. The queue counterpart is `bynk.queue.return_not_queue_result`.
example:
on schedule("*/5 * * * *") () -> Effect[Result[Int, String]] { … }   // ✗ a cron run has nowhere to put an `Int`

on schedule("*/5 * * * *") () -> Effect[Result[(), String]] { … }   // ✓ unit on success
summary: A cron handler does not return `Effect[Result[(), E]]`.
A `D1` migration does not apply to an empty in-memory SQLite, so the binding's literal SQL is not checked against its schema (warning).

blurb: A `D1` database's migrations are the SQL files in `migrations/<database>/`, applied in number order, each once. So a file's name must give its place in that order: `NNNN_<name>.sql`, four digits, an underscore, then letters, digits, `_` or `-`, directly in its database's directory. A file named any other way, one in a nested folder, or one whose number another migration of the same database already has could not be put in order, so the build refuses it rather than skip it. Rename the file, or give it the next free number.
example:
migrations/shop-orders/1_create_orders.sql      // ✗ not four digits
migrations/shop-orders/0002_add_note.sql
migrations/shop-orders/0002_add_total.sql     // ✗ `0002` is taken

migrations/shop-orders/0001_create_orders.sql   // ✓
migrations/shop-orders/0002_add_note.sql
migrations/shop-orders/0003_add_total.sql       // ✓ the next free number
summary: A file in the project's `migrations/` folder isn't `migrations/<database>/NNNN_<name>.sql`, or shares its number with another migration of the same database.
A `D1` migration in the project's `migrations/` folder can't be read, or isn't UTF-8 text.
A directory in the project's `migrations/` folder matches no `D1` instance's database name, so its migrations are never applied, usually because the capability was renamed (warning).

blurb: `select[T]` and `firstAs[T]` read each row into the record `T`, matching columns to fields by name, so every field needs a column of that name. `Json.decodeSql` reads a literal `all` or `first` the same way, for each required field. Rename the field, or alias the column in the SQL (`… AS price`) so the names agree.
summary: A record read from a literal D1 statement has a field with no column of that name. For a `select[T]` / `firstAs[T]` row type, the column list the compiler writes from `T` does not prepare against the schema the binding's migrations build; for a `Json.decodeSql[T]` of the rows of a literal `all` / `first`, a required (non-`Option`) field of `T` has no result column.

blurb: Bynk prepares each literal SQL statement of a `D1` capability against the schema your migrations build, applied to an empty in-memory SQLite, so a syntax error or an unknown table or column is a compile error, not a failure on the first request. Nothing runs. Correct the statement, or add the migration that creates what it names. A project whose schema is made elsewhere can turn the check off with `[check] d1_sql = false`.
example:
let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id, totl FROM orders", [])     // ✗ no such column: totl

let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id, total FROM orders", [])    // ✓
summary: A literal D1 statement does not prepare against the schema the binding's migrations build: a syntax error, or an unknown table or column.

blurb: D1 refuses a statement bound to a different number of values than it has parameters, so Bynk counts them at compile time by SQLite's rule: the highest `?N`, with a bare `?` taking the next number. It checks a list written out in place, or a name `let`-bound to one. Pass one `SqlValue` for each parameter, or change the SQL.
example:
let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = ?1 AND total > ?2", [Text(id)])                 // ✗ two parameters, one value

let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = ?1 AND total > ?2", [Text(id), Integer(100)])    // ✓
summary: A literal D1 statement uses a different number of bound parameters (`?N`) than the list literal passed with it holds.

blurb: Your own project's path dependencies can point anywhere, but a dependency's own path dependencies are honoured only when they stay inside the workspace: a path out of it names a directory that need not exist where the package is used. A fetched package's path dependencies are never honoured. Move the target into the workspace.
example:
# lib/bynk.toml, a dependency of the project
[dependencies]
core = { package = "acme/core", path = "../../outside" }   // ✗ outside the workspace

core = { package = "acme/core", path = "../core" }         // ✓ a workspace member
summary: A path dependency declared by a dependency resolves outside the workspace; a dependency's own path dependencies are honoured only between members of one workspace.

`bynk deploy` refused to put a context that hosts agents on a different Worker script than it was last deployed to (into or out of a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group, between groups, or after a group is renamed or re-keyed): an agent's state belongs to its script, so it would start empty and the old data would stay behind. Start it fresh deliberately with `--accept-fresh-agent <context>`, which a move out of a group that stays cannot use.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, and a Worker has one assets directory. So a fixed asset path (`at "/…"`) names one file across the whole group: two members serving different files at one path would leave the Worker unable to say which to send. A path that would be a folder of another member's file is refused for the same reason. Give one of the assets another path, or put the contexts in different groups.
summary: Two members of one `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group serve a fixed asset path (`at "/…"`) from different files, or one that would be a folder of the other; a group has one assets directory, so each fixed path names one file.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, and a Worker has one `wrangler.toml`, so its members share one set of binding names. Two members that declare a binding the same way share it. Two that declare different bindings under one name are refused, because one name cannot bind two things. An agent is the usual case: each agent class is a Durable Object binding named after the class, and a class belongs to the context that declares it, so two members cannot each declare an agent of the same name. Rename one, or put the contexts in different groups.
summary: Two members of one `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group declare different bindings under the same name; members share one `wrangler.toml`, so identical declarations share a binding and differing ones are refused.

blurb: Each `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group becomes one Worker, and a context is deployed in exactly one Worker: its routes, its services and its agents' state belong to one script. A context listed in two groups would be deployed twice, as two copies that share nothing. List it in one group. A context in no group stays its own Worker.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = ["shop.orders", "shop.billing"]

[deploy.workers.edge]
contexts = ["shop.orders"]     // ✗ already in `core`

contexts = ["shop.gateway"]    // ✓
summary: A context is listed in two `[deploy.workers.<key>]` groups; a context is deployed in one Worker only.

A worker was compiled against a contract its live dependencies no longer provide, or no longer provides the contract its live callers were compiled against, so `bynk deploy --context` refuses to ship it.

blurb: A route or custom domain sends the requests that match it to one Worker. If two `[deploy.workers.<key>]` groups claimed the same one, only one Worker could have it, and which would depend on the order they were deployed in. So each route and each custom domain is claimed once across all the groups. Hosts are compared without regard to case, and the same host with a different path is a different route. Remove the repeat, or give one group another route.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = ["shop.orders"]
routes = ["shop.example.com/*"]

[deploy.workers.edge]
contexts = ["shop.billing"]
routes = ["shop.example.com/*"]           // ✗ `core` claims it

routes = ["shop.example.com/billing/*"]   // ✓ another path, another route
summary: A route or custom domain is claimed twice across `[deploy.workers.<key>]` groups.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group is a Worker made of the contexts it lists. A group that lists none would be a Worker with nothing to run, and its key would still claim a Worker name and a deploy record. That is almost always a mistake: contexts left out, or a group that should have been deleted. List the group's contexts, or remove the table.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = []                                  // ✗ no context

contexts = ["shop.orders", "shop.billing"]   // ✓
summary: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group lists no context.
A build breaks the contract a declared foreign caller's client was generated at, as pinned in `bynk.foreign.toml`, so `bynk deploy` refuses to ship it.

blurb: Each Worker on Cloudflare is one script with one name. A group's Worker is named by its `name`, or by its key when it has none, and a context in no group is a Worker of its own, named after the context with each `.` as `-` (`shop.billing` is `shop-billing`). Two Workers with one name would overwrite each other on deploy. So a group's key or `name` may not be another group's Worker name, nor the Worker of a context in no group. Choose another key or `name`, or put that context in the group.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = ["shop.orders"]

[deploy.workers.edge]
contexts = ["shop.billing"]
name = "core"         // ✗ `core` is already a Worker's name

name = "shop-edge"    // ✓
summary: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group's key or script name is another group's, or is the Worker of a context in no group.

blurb: A WebSocket upgrade request names no service, and a `from websocket` service has no path of its own, so a Worker hands every upgrade to its one WebSocket service. A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, so at most one member may declare a `from websocket` service, and that one takes every upgrade, whatever its path. Put the contexts in different groups, or leave one in no group so that it is a Worker of its own. Within one context, a second WebSocket service is `bynk.service.websocket_multiple`.
summary: More than one member of a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group declares a `from websocket` service; an upgrade request names no path or service a group could route it by, so a group has at most one such member, which takes every upgrade request whatever the path.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group lists the contexts to deploy together as one Worker, and only a context is deployed. A `commons` is compiled into each context that uses it, and an adapter into each context that consumes it, so neither has a Worker of its own to share. Remove the entry: the contexts that use the commons carry it with them.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = ["shop.orders", "money"]   // ✗ `money` is a commons

contexts = ["shop.orders"]            // ✓
summary: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group lists a unit that is not a `context`; only contexts are deployed as Workers.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, which answers each HTTP method and path with one handler. Two members that declare the same method and path would give the Worker two handlers for one request, so the later one is refused. Change one of the routes, often by giving each context a path prefix of its own, or put the contexts in different groups. Within one context the same clash is `bynk.http.duplicate_route`.
summary: Two members of one `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group declare the same HTTP method and path; a Worker answers a route with one handler.

blurb: A service is called by its name alone: a call from another context goes to `/_bynk/call/<service>`, and the address names no context. A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, which answers all their services, so two members with a service of the same name would leave it unable to tell the calls apart. Rename one of the services, or put the contexts in different groups.
summary: Two members of one `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group declare a service of the same name; a Worker answers its members' services by name.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group names its members by their qualified context names, and each must be a context the project declares. A name that matches none is usually a typo, or a context that has since been renamed, and a group cannot deploy a context that does not exist. The note suggests the nearest name. Correct the entry, or remove it.
example:
[deploy.workers.core]
contexts = ["shop.ordres"]   // ✗ no such context

contexts = ["shop.orders"]   // ✓
summary: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group lists a context the project does not declare.

blurb: `bynk deploy` uploads each Worker after the Workers it binds to, since a Service Binding must name a script that already exists. So the Workers' bindings must run one way: a cycle has no order to deploy in. Contexts cannot consume each other in a cycle (that is `bynk.context.consumes_cycle`), but a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group folds its members into one Worker, and that can close a cycle among contexts that have none: if a member of `front` calls a member of `back`, and another member of `back` calls a member of `front`, the two Workers bind to each other. Move a context out of its group, or into the other, so the calls between Workers run one way. A publisher's Worker also binds to its subscribers, so a subscriber that calls its publisher can close a cycle too.
example:
// bynk.toml
[deploy.workers.front]
contexts = ["shop.web", "shop.prices"]

[deploy.workers.back]
contexts = ["shop.stock", "shop.reports"]

// shop/web.bynk
consumes shop.stock

// shop/reports.bynk
context shop.reports   // ✗ `back` binds to `front`, and `front` to `back`
consumes shop.prices

// bynk.toml
[deploy.workers.front]
contexts = ["shop.web"]                                    // ✓

[deploy.workers.back]
contexts = ["shop.stock", "shop.reports", "shop.prices"]   // ✓ calls run from `front` to `back` only
summary: Workers bind to each other in a cycle that involves a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group: a group folds its members into one Worker, which can close a cycle among contexts that are themselves acyclic. A Worker is uploaded after the Workers it binds to, so the cycle cannot be deployed.
`bynk.toml` declares `[deploy.workers]` groups, which only a `workers` build uses; this build is a `bundle`, which has every context in one program and ignores them (warning).

blurb: `detach` stops waiting for an effect and hands it to the execution context, so something must keep the effect alive after the handler returns. A service handler has an execution context that does. An agent handler runs inside the agent's own object, with no such context, and its effects are awaited so that they finish with the handler. So `detach` is refused there, and in a closure there. Await the effect instead, with `do` or `let _ <-`, or move the `detach` to the service handler that calls the agent. A `detach` of a store operation is `bynk.detach.store_op`.
summary: A `detach` was used in an agent handler, which has no execution context to keep a detached effect alive.

blurb: `detach` hands a running effect to the execution context, and only an effectful body has effects to run: a pure function never runs one. Change the enclosing function's return type to `Effect[…]`. The same rule holds for `bynk.within.in_pure_context` and `bynk.race.in_pure_context`.
summary: A `detach` was used in a pure (non-effectful) context.

blurb: In an agent handler, a store write is not work to detach: it is staged and committed atomically with the rest of the handler, so there is nothing to leave running. `detach` is refused there for any effect, and a store operation gets its own code to point at the fix. Drop the `.detach()` and write `do field.op(…)`; the write is committed with the handler. For a `detach` that is not of a store operation see `bynk.detach.in_agent_handler`.
summary: A `detach` targets an agent store operation, which is part of the handler's atomic commit and cannot be detached.
A `[Name]` doc link resolves to nothing in the unit's scope (editor hint only).

blurb: `5.minutes` is a `Duration`, which the compiler stores as a whole number of milliseconds, so it multiplies the count by the unit when it reads the literal. A count whose total does not fit in a 64-bit integer is refused rather than wrapped into a wrong or negative span. No real timeout or interval is that large: write a smaller count, or a smaller unit.
example:
fn forever() -> Duration { 9007199254740991.days }   // ✗ overflows the millisecond range

fn forever() -> Duration { 365.days }                // ✓
summary: A `Duration` literal (`<int>.<unit>`) exceeds the representable millisecond range.

blurb: `<-` waits for an effect, so it is only allowed in a body that is itself effectful, one whose return type is `Effect[T]`. A function that returns a plain `Int` promises that it waits for nothing and reaches nothing outside, and a `<-` inside it would break that promise for every caller. A `par` block awaits too, and is refused in the same place. Change the return type to `Effect[T]` and return `Effect.pure(…)`, or compute the value without an effect. Calling a function value that returns an `Effect` is `bynk.effect.fn_value_in_pure_context`.
summary: An `<-` bind was used in a pure (non-effectful) context.

blurb: `let x <- e` waits for `e` and binds its result, so `e` must be an `Effect[T]`. A plain value has nothing to wait for, and `<-` on one usually means the right-hand side is not the call you meant. Write `let x = …` for a pure binding. Where an effect is required and you hold a plain value, wrap it with `Effect.pure(…)`. A `<-` in a body that is not itself effectful is `bynk.effect.bind_in_pure_context`.
summary: An `<-` bind was applied to a non-`Effect` value.

blurb: Calling a capability operation is an effect, and effects are only allowed in a body that is itself effectful, one that returns `Effect[T]`, so that a type tells you whether a body reaches outside. A lambda checked against a plain function type such as `(Int) -> Int` is a pure body, so a capability call inside it is refused even when the handler around it is effectful. Make the call in the handler, bind it with `<-`, and pass the result in. A call the `given` clause does not cover is `bynk.given.undeclared_capability`.
summary: A capability was used in a pure context.

blurb: A call to a service in a consumed context is an effect, as a capability call is, so it is only allowed in a body that is itself effectful. A handler is effectful, but a lambda inside it is a body of its own, and a service call alone does not make it effectful. Make the call in the handler body, bind it with `<-`, and use the result in the lambda.
summary: A cross-context call was made in a pure context.

blurb: `do e` awaits an effect and discards what it returns, which is fine for a unit or an ordinary value but not for a `Result`: an `Err` dropped this way is lost without a trace. Bind it and handle the error with `let r <- e` and a `match` (or `?`). If dropping the outcome is really what you want, write `let _ <- e`, which is legal and keeps the discard visible in the source. `do` on a plain value is `bynk.effect.do_on_non_effect`.
summary: A `do` statement was applied to an `Effect[Result[_, _]]`, which would drop an `Err`; bind it, write `let _ <- e` to discard it deliberately, or `do e.detach()` to stop waiting and have a failure reported.

blurb: `do e` runs an effect as a statement, so like `<-` it belongs in a body that is itself effectful, one whose return type is `Effect[T]`. A function that returns a plain `Int` promises to wait for nothing and reach nothing outside, and a `do` inside it would break that promise for every caller. Change the return type to `Effect[T]` and end with `Effect.pure(…)`, or drop the `do`. The same mistake with `<-` is `bynk.effect.bind_in_pure_context`.
summary: A `do` statement was used in a pure (non-effectful) context.

blurb: `do e` performs an effect, so its operand must be an `Effect[T]`: a call to something effectful. A plain value has nothing to run, which usually means the operand is not the call you meant. Call the effectful function you intended. If you wanted the value, bind it with `let`. An effect whose result is a `Result` is `bynk.effect.do_discards_result`, and `<-` on a plain value is `bynk.effect.bind_on_non_effect`.
summary: A `do` statement was applied to a non-`Effect` value.

blurb: Calling a function value whose type returns `Effect[T]` is an effect, just as calling a capability is, and effects are only allowed in a body that is itself effectful, one whose return type is an `Effect`. Bynk makes effects explicit so that a function's signature tells you whether it can touch the outside world: a function that returns a plain `Int` is pure and can be reasoned about as such. A call through a parameter would hide an effect behind that signature, so it is refused. Either make the function return `Effect[T]` and bind the call with `<-`, or take a pure function instead. A capability call from a handler that has not declared it is a different mistake, `bynk.given.undeclared_capability`.
summary: An effectful function value was called in a pure context; like a capability call, it is legal only where the enclosing body is effectful.

blurb: Bynk starts an effectful call as soon as it is built, so an `Effect[T]` that is built and then dropped still runs, unawaited, racing every statement after it, and nothing in the program shows it. Effects are meant to happen in the order you wrote them, so in an effectful body an `Effect` value must be bound with `let x <- …`, run with `do …` (for an `Effect[()]`), or returned as the body's value. The error fires where an `Effect` is built in a value position that cannot await it: the right-hand side of a plain `let` (including `let _ = …`), a list element, and the payload of `Some`, `Ok`, `Err`, a variant or a record field. An argument to another call is left alone, because the parameter decides what happens to it. If you want the result, use `<-`; if only the effect, use `do`.
summary: An `Effect` value in an effectful body was built but not bound with `<-`, sequenced with `do` or returned — in a plain `let`, a list element or a constructor payload — so it runs eagerly and unawaited (#1658).

blurb: An email `on message` handler takes the message as one `InboundEmail` parameter: inbound email delivers one message per call, so the handler is `on message(mail: InboundEmail) -> Effect[EmailVerdict]`. A parameter of another type, or none, or more than one, is refused. Import `InboundEmail` and `EmailVerdict` from `bynk.cloudflare`.
summary: An email `on message` handler does not take exactly one `InboundEmail` parameter.

blurb: Inbound mail is dispatched to a service by its envelope recipient, so each address belongs to one service. Addresses compare without regard to case. A literal address and the catch-all `*@domain` for the same domain may both be claimed: the literal address wins, and the catch-all takes everything else. Merge the two handlers, or claim different addresses.
summary: Two `from email` services claim the same recipient address.

blurb: A `from email` service claims one address and decides each message it is given, so it has exactly one `on message` handler. To treat two addresses differently, declare two services, each with its own address.
summary: A `from email` service declares more than one `on message` handler; it has exactly one.

blurb: A `from email` service claims a bare address, `local@domain`, or a whole domain with `*@domain`. The domain is dotted labels of letters, digits and `-`. A display name (`Support <a@b.example>`), a list, a wildcard inside the local part, and an address with spaces or quotes are refused: Email Routing matches the bare address.
example:
service support from email("Support <support@shop.example>") { … }   // ✗ a display name

service support from email("support@shop.example") { … }            // ✓
summary: A `from email("…")` binding is not a recipient address a service can claim.

blurb: An email handler decides what happens to the message, and the decision is named: `Accept`, `Reject(reason)`, `Forward(to)` or `Reply(message)`, the `EmailVerdict` sum from `bynk.cloudflare`. It is not a `Result` or a `String`, because the decision is independent of success or failure. It is the agency rule that gives a queue handler `QueueResult`.
summary: An email `on message` handler does not return `Effect[EmailVerdict]`.

blurb: An embed becomes a `String` in the compiled code, so its file must be text. A file holding a NUL byte is binary, and a `String` made from it would be meaningless. Binary data belongs in `assets/`, where the platform serves it as a file. Text that is not valid UTF-8 is `bynk.embed.invalid_encoding`.
example:
embed logo = "embeds/logo.png"    // ✗ the file has a NUL byte

asset logo = "assets/logo.png"    // ✓ a binary file is served, not read
summary: An `embed` names a file with a NUL byte, so it is binary, not text.

blurb: An embed is a `String` constant used by its name, so a unit declares each name once: a second `embed shell` would leave `shell` meaning two files. Give each embed its own name. An embed whose name is an asset's, a function's or a type's is `bynk.resolve.name_conflict` instead.
example:
embed shell = "embeds/page.html"
embed shell = "embeds/other.html"     // ✗ `shell` is already declared

embed shell = "embeds/page.html"
embed footer = "embeds/other.html"    // ✓ one name each
summary: An `embed` name is declared more than once in the same unit.

blurb: An `embed` becomes a `String`, which is Unicode text, so the file must be valid UTF-8. A file saved in another encoding, such as Latin-1, holds bytes that are not UTF-8 and cannot be read as text. Re-save it as UTF-8. A file that holds a NUL byte is binary and is `bynk.embed.binary_content`; a binary file belongs in `assets/`, as an `asset`.
example:
embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✗ the file is Latin-1, not UTF-8
embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✓ once the file is saved as UTF-8
summary: An `embed` names a file that is not valid UTF-8.

blurb: An `embed` compiles a file's text into the program as a `String`, so the file must exist when the project is built, or there is nothing to compile in. The path is relative to the project root and must name a regular file under `embeds/`; a symbolic link is not followed. Create the file, or correct the path. A file that exists but cannot be read is `bynk.embed.unreadable_file`.
example:
embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✗ no such file in the project
embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✓ once embeds/page.html exists
summary: An `embed` names a file that is not in the project's `embeds/` folder.
A single-file build met an `embed` declaration, which needs a project's `embeds/` folder.

blurb: An `embed` is compiled into the Worker of each context that declares it, or that `uses` a commons that does. An adapter is the host boundary, not a Worker, so it has nowhere to carry the text, and an `embed` there is refused. Declare it in a context or a commons, and have the context use that. For a file the platform serves rather than compiles in, see `bynk.asset.outside_context_or_commons`.
example:
// app/host.bynk
adapter app.host

binding "./host.binding.ts"

embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✗ an adapter cannot embed

// app/page.bynk
commons app.page

embed shell = "embeds/page.html"        // ✓ in a commons
summary: An `embed` declaration appears outside a context or commons.

blurb: An embed is compiled into the deployed code, so it may come only from the project's `embeds/` folder. If any path were allowed, a declaration could pull `.env` or a source file into the bundle just by naming it. Move the file into `embeds/` and name it there. A path that is empty, absolute or contains `..` is `bynk.embed.unsafe_path` instead.
example:
embed shell = "templates/page.html"    // ✗ not in the embeds/ folder

embed shell = "embeds/page.html"       // ✓
summary: An `embed` names a file outside the project's `embeds/` folder.
An `embed` names a file over 256 KiB, or the project's embedded files total over 1 MiB.
An `embed` names a file in the project's `embeds/` folder that could not be read.

blurb: An embed's path is joined onto the project root to find the file, so it must stay inside the project: it may not be empty or absolute, and it may not contain a `..` segment, which could climb out of it. Write the path relative to the project root, inside `embeds/`. A relative path that is only outside `embeds/` is `bynk.embed.outside_embeds_dir`.
example:
embed shell = "embeds/../page.html"    // ✗ a `..` segment

embed shell = "embeds/page.html"       // ✓
summary: An `embed` path is empty, absolute, or contains a `..` segment.

blurb: An `on event` handler takes the event payload and, optionally, a second parameter of type `EventEnvelope`, which carries the emission's metadata: its event id, publisher, time and schema version. Any other count, or any other type in second place, has nothing to receive it. Remove the extra parameter or type it `EventEnvelope`. A wrong first parameter is `bynk.event.handler_param_type_mismatch`.
summary: An `on event` handler declared the wrong number of parameters, or a second parameter whose type is not `EventEnvelope` — it takes the event payload and, optionally, the runtime envelope.

blurb: `via schema(N)` filters a subscription by the envelope's `schemaVersion`. Versions count up from 1, so every bound must be a positive `Int` literal: `schema(0)` or `schema(0..3)` names a version no event has. Write a version, a range such as `schema(2..4)`, or `_` for every version. A range whose lower bound is above its upper one is `bynk.types.empty_range_pattern`.
summary: A `via schema(...)` dispatch clause's argument is malformed — it must be a positive `Int` literal, a range of positive `Int` literals, or `_`.

blurb: `@schema(N)` states the version an event is at, so that the number can be reviewed in the source and is checked against the version the registry computes. `N` must be one positive `Int` literal, given by position, and `@schema` may appear once on an event: `@schema(0)`, `@schema("2")`, `@schema(v: 2)` and a second `@schema` are all refused. Write `@schema(2)`, or drop the annotation, since the registry tracks the version anyway.
example:
event Paid @schema(0) = {    // ✗ versions start at 1
event Paid @schema(1) = {    // ✓
    id: String,
}

const Version: Int = 1
event Refunded @schema(Version) = {    // ✓ an `Int` constant bound to a literal
    id: String,
}
summary: An event's `@schema(N)` annotation is malformed — `N` must be a single, positive, positional `Int` literal, and `@schema` may appear at most once on an event.

blurb: A `from Events(E)` service has exactly one `on event` handler. To react to an event in two ways, declare two services, each subscribing to it: every subscriber is delivered to independently. So the second handler is refused here, and the fix is to move it into a service of its own.
summary: A `from Events` service declares more than one `on event` handler; it has exactly one.

blurb: `Events.emit[E]` takes an `event` type. A plain `type` declared in the same context is refused: nothing could subscribe to it, since a `from Events(…)` header names events, so the emission would silently go nowhere. Declare the type with `event` instead, or name the event you meant. A name that is not declared in this context at all is `bynk.event.emit_outside_owner`.
summary: `Events.emit[E]` named a type `E` that is declared in this context, but is not itself an `event` — only an `event` type may be emitted.

blurb: Only the context that declares an event may emit it. A consumer can see the event through `consumes`, to subscribe to it with `from Events(…)`, but being able to name a type does not make it yours to forge: other contexts then could not trust that an event came from its owner. Emit an event of your own, or call a service of the owning context and let it emit.
summary: `Events.emit[E]` named an event `E` not declared in the emitting context — only an event's declaring context may emit it.

blurb: An `on event` handler's first parameter is the event itself, so its type must be the one the `from Events(E)` header names. A subscription pattern is checked against that event, and the body reads `e` at that type. Make the parameter `E`, or change the header to the event you mean to handle. The optional second parameter is `EventEnvelope`; other mistakes there are `bynk.event.bad_params`.
summary: An `on event(e: T)` handler's declared parameter type does not match its `from Events(E)` header's event type.

An event's field shape changed in a way the schema registry cannot evolve additively — a field was removed, retyped, added without a default, or lost a default it previously had. Give the new shape a new event type name, or make the change additive.

blurb: An `event` is declared in a context, and only that context may emit it, so an event belongs to its owner. A `commons` is shared code that other units `uses`, with no owner to emit from, so one may not declare an event. Declare the event in the context that raises it. Other contexts subscribe by consuming that context.
example:
commons shop

event Paid = { id: String }   // ✗ a commons has no owner to emit it

context shop

event Paid = { id: String }   // ✓ declared where it is emitted
summary: An `event` was declared outside a context.

blurb: A subscription pattern narrows delivery by field: `from Events(Paid { region: Domestic, .. })` runs the handler only when `region` is `Domestic`. The listed fields combine with AND, so naming one twice would ask for two values at once, or say the same thing twice, and is refused rather than guessed at. List each field once. To accept several values, leave the field out of the pattern and `match` on it in the handler.
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern listed the same field more than once.

blurb: A subscription pattern compares a field with a literal or a variant, so the value must be of the field's type: an `Int` literal for an `Int` field, a `String` for a `String`, a variant of the field's own sum type. A value of any other type could never match an emission. Write one of the field's type.
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern field's matched value is not compatible with that field's declared type.

blurb: A subscription pattern filters on the event's own fields, so each name in it must be one the event declares. A name that matches none could never filter anything, and is usually a misspelling; the diagnostic lists the declared fields. Use one of them.
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern named a field that `E` does not declare.

blurb: A pattern that tests a sum-typed field names a variant of that type, and an emission can only carry the variants the type declares. A name it lacks, often a misspelling, could never match. Use a variant the type declares. A variant that carries a payload is refused too, as `bynk.event.pattern_variant_payload`.
example:
type Region =
    | Domestic
    | International
    | Refunded(reason: String)
event Paid = { id: String, region: Region }

service onPaid from Events(Paid { region: Region.Nowhere, .. }) {   // ✗ `Region` has no `Nowhere`

service onPaid from Events(Paid { region: Region.Domestic, .. }) {   // ✓
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern's variant value names a variant that does not exist on the field's declared sum type.

blurb: A pattern can test only which variant a field holds, not what it carries. For a variant with a payload that would admit emissions the pattern looks as if it excludes, so only payload-free variants are allowed. Subscribe to a payload-free variant, or drop the pattern and read the field in the handler's body.
example:
type Region =
    | Domestic
    | International
    | Refunded(reason: String)
event Paid = { id: String, region: Region }

service onPaid from Events(Paid { region: Region.Refunded, .. }) {   // ✗ `Refunded` carries a `reason`

service onPaid from Events(Paid { region: Region.Domestic, .. }) {   // ✓ no payload
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern's variant value names a variant that carries a payload — only nullary variants are admitted, since testing the tag alone would silently ignore the payload.

blurb: Emission is fire-and-forget: nothing receives a subscriber's result, so an `on event` handler returns `Effect[()]` and anything else is refused. Return `Effect.pure(())` once its work is done, and move a value it computes into an effect the handler performs, such as a write. A handler that does not return an `Effect` at all is `bynk.service.return_not_effect`.
summary: An `on event` handler returns an `Effect` of something other than `()`; emission is fire-and-forget, so it returns `Effect[()]`.
An event's `@schema(N)` annotation disagrees with the version the schema registry computes from the event's build history.

blurb: The only annotation an event accepts is `@schema(N)`, which asserts its schema version. Names like `@indexed` belong to agent state and mean nothing on an event, so a stray or misspelt one would be silently ignored if it were not refused. Remove the annotation, or use `@schema` with a positive integer.
example:
event Paid @indexed = { id: String }   // ✗ not an event annotation

event Paid @schema(1) = { id: String }   // ✓
summary: An `event` declaration carried an `@`-annotation other than `@schema` — event annotations are a closed set.

blurb: A `from Events(E)` header must name an event declared in this context or in a context it `consumes`. A name that matches neither would be a subscription that never receives anything, and nothing would say so; it is almost always a misspelling, or a `consumes` that is missing. Fix the name, or add `consumes` for the context whose `event` it is.
example:
context mailer

consumes orders

service onPaid from Events(Payd) {   // ✗ no event `Payd`

service onPaid from Events(Paid) {   // ✓ the event `orders` declares
summary: A `from Events(E)` subscription named `E`, which is not a declared event in this context or any consumed context.

blurb: A function that uses `detach`, `within` or `race` hands work to the execution context, which a service handler has. An agent handler, a WebSocket handler, a provider operation, a function that is not effectful and a `const`, `store` or predicate initialiser do not. Calling such a function from one of those, directly or through other functions, or naming it as a value, is refused. The note gives the chain of calls down to the construct. Make the call in a service handler, and pass what it returns on.
summary: A call to, or reference to, a function that hands work to the execution context (`detach`, `within` or `race`, directly or through the functions it calls) appears where no execution context exists: an agent handler, a WebSocket handler or a provider operation.

blurb: `expect <call> faults` claims that an effectful call throws, for instance because a `stub … fails`. Only a call can fault, so the subject must be the call itself, with type `Effect[_]`. A value already bound, or a pure method on one, has nothing left to throw. Write the call inside the claim, not a name bound from it. A fault that is not claimed fails the case.
example:
// tests/vault.test.bynk
let label = "sealed"
expect label.length() faults   // ✗ a pure method, not an effectful call
expect box.call() faults       // ✓ the call that faults
summary: A fault claim's subject (`expect <call> faults`) is not an effectful call: a value, or a call whose type is not `Effect[_]`.

blurb: An `expect` predicate is a pure claim: the same predicate surface as `invariant` and `ensures`. A capability or service call inside it, even one held in a list or returned by a lambda, would run when the claim is checked, and its call would be recorded as if the unit under test had made it. Run the call before the claim with `let x <- …`, then state the claim about `x`. A fault claim (`expect <call> faults`) is the one form that runs its call.
summary: An `expect` predicate contains an effectful call (a sub-expression of type `Effect[_]`); a predicate must be pure.

blurb: `expect` states a claim that is checked when the case runs, so its predicate must be a `Bool`: true, or the case fails. A count or a record is not a claim. Compare the value with what you expect (`==`, `<`, `is`), or use a method that returns `Bool`. It is the same predicate surface that `invariant` and `ensures` use.
summary: `expect` was given a non-`Bool` predicate.

blurb: `expect` is a test claim, checked when a `case` runs. Production code has no test runner to report a failure to, so an `expect` in a function, a handler or anywhere else outside a `case` body is refused. To check a condition in running code, return a `Bool` or a `Result`; to check it in a test, move the `expect` into a case. A `requires` or `ensures` contract is the always-on form.
summary: `expect` was used outside a `case` body.

blurb: `exports capability { Clock }` lets other contexts depend on `Clock` and have it built for them, so the exporting context must also say how: a `provides Clock = … { … }` declaration. Without one, a consumer would hold a capability that nothing in the project can instantiate. Add the provider. (A derived capability, `capability Name = Kind`, cannot be exported at all; that is `bynk.exports.derived_capability`.)
summary: An exported capability has no provider in its context.

blurb: A type is exported `opaque`, so consuming contexts can pass it around but not look inside it, or `transparent`, so they can. It cannot be both, and the compiler will not pick for you. Keep the clause you mean and delete the other. The same visibility twice is `bynk.exports.duplicate_export`.
example:
exports opaque { OrderId }
exports transparent { OrderId }    // ✗ already exported `opaque`

type OrderId = String where Matches("ORD-[0-9]+")

exports opaque { OrderId }         // ✓ one visibility
summary: A type is exported with conflicting visibilities.

blurb: A derived capability is an instance of a platform resource, such as a KV namespace, and its data belongs to the context that declares it. Exporting it would let another context read and write that data directly. Keep it out of `exports capability`; another context reaches the data through this context's services.
summary: `exports capability` names a derived capability, whose instance stays with its context.

blurb: A type or capability is exported once. Naming it again in a second `exports` clause with the same visibility adds nothing, and usually means a clause was pasted twice, or a name was meant for another one. Delete the repeat. Within a single clause the repeat is `bynk.exports.duplicate_in_clause`, and the same type under both `opaque` and `transparent` is `bynk.exports.conflicting_visibility`.
summary: The same name is exported more than once.

blurb: An `exports` clause lists each type once. Naming one twice is a typo or a pasted name, and the second may have been meant for another type. Delete the repeat, or correct the name. The same type in two separate clauses is `bynk.exports.duplicate_export`.
summary: A name appears twice in one `exports` clause.

blurb: `exports capability { Clock }` offers a capability of this context to the contexts that consume it, so the capability has to be declared in this context, and provided there too (`bynk.exports.capability_not_provided`). A name that is not declared is usually a misspelling. Correct it, or declare the capability here. A name in a type `exports` clause is `bynk.exports.undeclared_type`.
summary: `exports capability` names a capability that is not declared.

blurb: An `exports` clause lists types this context declares, to make them visible to the contexts that consume it. A name the context does not declare has nothing to export: it is usually a misspelling, or a type that is declared elsewhere. Correct the name, or declare the type in this context. A name in `exports capability` that is not declared is `bynk.exports.undeclared_capability`.
summary: `exports` names a type that is not declared.
A `todo(message)` placeholder: the code type-checks but faults when it runs. A non-failing warning, so `check --deny-warnings` refuses unfinished code in CI (warning).

blurb: A `fixture` becomes a `String` in the test code, so its file must be text. A file holding a NUL byte is binary, and a `String` made from it would be meaningless. Keep a text form of the data in the fixture, such as base64, and decode it in the case with `Bytes.fromBase64`. Text that is not valid UTF-8 is `bynk.fixture.invalid_encoding`.
example:
fixture blob = "fixtures/blob.bin"    // ✗ the file has a NUL byte

fixture blob = "fixtures/blob.b64"    // ✓ its base64 text
summary: A suite's `fixture` names a file that contains a NUL byte, so it is binary, not text.

blurb: A fixture is a `String` constant used by its name in the suite, so a suite declares each name once: a second `fixture note` would leave `note` meaning two files. Give each fixture its own name. A fixture whose name is a declaration already in scope is `bynk.resolve.name_conflict` instead.
example:
fixture note = "fixtures/a.txt"
fixture note = "fixtures/b.txt"      // ✗ `note` is already declared

fixture note = "fixtures/a.txt"
fixture other = "fixtures/b.txt"     // ✓ one name each
summary: A suite declares two `fixture`s of the same name.

blurb: A `fixture` becomes a `String`, which is Unicode text, so its file must be valid UTF-8. A file saved in another encoding, such as Latin-1, holds bytes that cannot be read as text. Re-save it as UTF-8. A file that holds a NUL byte is binary and is `bynk.fixture.binary_content`.
example:
fixture note = "fixtures/note.txt"    // ✗ the file is Latin-1, not UTF-8
fixture note = "fixtures/note.txt"    // ✓ once the file is saved as UTF-8
summary: A suite's `fixture` names a file that is not valid UTF-8.

blurb: A `fixture` reads a file into a `String` for the suite's cases, so the file must exist as a regular file in the project's `fixtures/` folder. A misspelt name, a file not yet added, or a symbolic link (which is not followed) leaves the suite without its input. Add the file or correct the path. A path outside that folder is `bynk.fixture.outside_fixtures_dir`; an empty, absolute or `..` path is `bynk.fixture.unsafe_path`.
summary: A suite's `fixture` names a file that is not in the project's `fixtures/` folder.

blurb: A fixture is test input, and it may come only from the project's `fixtures/` folder. If any path were allowed, a declaration could read `.env` or a source file just by naming it. Move the file into `fixtures/` and name it there. A path that is empty, absolute or contains `..` is `bynk.fixture.unsafe_path` instead.
example:
fixture note = "data/note.txt"        // ✗ not in the fixtures/ folder

fixture note = "fixtures/note.txt"    // ✓
summary: A suite's `fixture` names a file outside the project's `fixtures/` folder.
A suite's `fixture` names a file over the 4 MiB limit for one fixture file.
A suite's `fixture` names a listed file that could not be read.

blurb: A fixture's path is joined onto the project root to find the file, so it must stay inside the project: it may not be empty or absolute, and it may not contain a `..` segment, which could climb out of it. Write the path relative to the project root, inside `fixtures/`. A relative path that is only outside `fixtures/` is `bynk.fixture.outside_fixtures_dir`.
example:
fixture note = "fixtures/../note.txt"    // ✗ a `..` segment

fixture note = "fixtures/note.txt"       // ✓
summary: A suite's `fixture` path is empty, absolute or contains a `..` segment.
A suite declares a `fixture` that none of its cases, properties or helpers uses (warning).
The formatter would drop a comment, so it leaves the file unchanged.
A file mixes the retired `--` comment or `--|` doc spellings with a line that reads differently under the old and new comment rules (#2203), so the formatter leaves it unchanged.
The formatter's output does not re-parse to the same program, so it leaves the file unchanged.

blurb: A generic function with an `Ord` bound, named as a value, is instantiated where it stands, from the function type expected there. When that type is still open, because the receiving parameter's own type is not fixed yet, there is no `T` to choose, and a guess could order by the wrong type. Wrap the function in a lambda, which is checked after the other arguments, or annotate the expected function type.
summary: A generic function with an `Ord` bound is used as a value, and its type arguments cannot be determined from the type expected at that reference; annotate the expected type (constrained-generics slice 1).

blurb: A capability operation is carried out by its provider, written in TypeScript, so it has no Bynk body for a bound to serve; an `Ord` bound would also add a hidden comparator argument. Only `Key` and `Codable` are accepted, and both are handled at the call site. Remove the bound, and compare in the code that calls the operation.
summary: A generic capability operation's type parameter carries a bound other than `Key` or `Codable`; operations take only those two (constrained-generics slices 2 and 3).

blurb: A `Codable` parameter of a capability operation is encoded at the call site, so the provider receives plain JSON. Putting `T` in the return type asks the call site to decode the provider's reply back into `T`, and that is accepted only for the standard library's own operations, whose providers are reviewed with the runtime and which declare what a reply that does not decode means. A capability you declare returns plain data, such as a `String`, and you decode it where the call is made with `Json.decode`.
summary: A user-declared capability operation's `Codable` type parameter appears in its return type. A typed read, the call site decoding the provider's reply as the instantiated payload, is accepted only for the standard library's own operations (#3458, lifting ADR 0696 decision 5).

blurb: The type parameters of one declaration are told apart by name, and a repeat would collapse into a single parameter, so `Pair[T, T]` would force both fields to the same type with no sign of it. Give each parameter its own name. A method's own type parameter may not reuse a name from its receiver type either, as that would make the two ambiguous.
example:
type Pair[T, T] = { a: T, b: T }    // ✗ `T` declared twice

type Pair[A, B] = { a: A, b: B }    // ✓ one name for each
summary: A `type` or `fn` declares the same type-parameter name more than once (v0.157, ADR 0183).

blurb: Type parameters are for a type whose shape can mention them: a record, `{ value: T }`, or a sum whose variants carry payloads. A refined, opaque or alias type has a fixed base, so a parameter would have nowhere to go. Give the type a record or sum body that uses its parameters, or drop the parameters.
example:
type Wrapped[T] = Int            // ✗ `T` has nowhere to be used

type Wrapped[T] = { value: T }   // ✓ a record may be generic
summary: A `type` declaration carries type parameters on a refined, opaque or alias body; only a record (`type Name[T] = { … }`) or sum (`type Name[T] = | … | …`) body may be generic (v0.157/#593, ADRs 0183/0197).

blurb: `embeds E as V` lets `?` wrap an `E` error in the variant `V`, picking the variant by the error's type. In a generic sum that conversion would have to hold for every instantiation, which is not supported. Drop the `embeds` clause and wrap the error by hand where it is needed, with `.mapErr(Payment)`, or make the sum non-generic.
example:
type PayError = enum { Declined }

type Failure[T] =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    | Other(value: T)
    embeds PayError as Payment    // ✗ a generic sum cannot embed

type Failure[T] =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    | Other(value: T)             // ✓ no `embeds`; wrap with `.mapErr(Payment)`
summary: A generic sum type carries an `embeds` clause; embedding into a generic sum is not supported (#593).

blurb: A capability operation's reply policy, `@onUndecodable(miss)` or `@onUndecodable(fault)`, says what a reply that does not decode as the operation's payload type means. It belongs to the standard library's own operations, where the provider is reviewed with the runtime, so a capability you declare takes no annotation. Remove it.
summary: A capability operation carries an annotation outside the standard library, or a first-party operation's is not `@onUndecodable(miss)` or `@onUndecodable(fault)`: the reply policy of a typed read is internal to first-party operations (#3458).

blurb: A static method on a generic type (one with no `self`) is generic over the type's parameters, and a call has to be able to fix each of them: from its arguments, from the type the call is expected to have, or from explicit type arguments. If the method's parameter and return types never mention one of the type's parameters, nothing in a call can determine it, so the declaration is refused once, here, rather than every call being ambiguous. Mention the parameter in the signature, or make the method a free function. An instance method (with `self`) is not affected, since the receiver carries the type. A call that leaves a parameter open anyway is `bynk.generics.uninferable_type_arg`.
summary: A *static* method on a generic type never mentions one of the type's parameters in its parameter or return types, so no call could determine it from the arguments or the expected type. Mention the parameter in the signature, or make the method a free function (constrained-generics slice 4; instance methods are supported, #594).

blurb: `Json.encode` and `Json.decode` work only on types that cross the JSON boundary, and a type parameter might be a function, an `Effect` or another type that does not. So a type parameter that is encoded or decoded, or passed to a `Codable`-bounded parameter of another generic or of a capability operation, must be declared `T: Codable` (or `where A: Codable` for a receiver type's parameter), and a call must instantiate it with a type that is `Codable`. At run time the bound costs a hidden codec argument, so a refined type is still revalidated on decode. `Codable` does not imply `Eq`, so the diagnostic's fix writes `T: Eq + Codable` beside an existing `Eq`, and `bynk check --fix` applies it across a project. It is the `Json` counterpart of `bynk.generics.missing_eq_bound`, `bynk.generics.missing_ord_bound` and `bynk.generics.missing_key_bound`.
summary: A type parameter is encoded or decoded with `Json.encode`/`Json.decode`, or passed to a `Codable`-bounded parameter of another generic or of a capability operation, but is not declared `Codable` (`[T: Codable]`, or `where A: Codable` for a receiver type's parameter). The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix that declares `Codable`, beside an existing `Eq`, which `Codable` does not imply (constrained-generics slice 3).

blurb: `==` and `!=` work on a type parameter only if the function says so with an `Eq` bound. A type parameter stands for any type, and some types cannot be compared: a function, an `Effect`, a `Query`, a `Stream` or a held `Connection`. The bound puts that requirement in the signature, where a caller, hover and signature help can see it, instead of leaving it to fail inside the body. The same rule applies when a generic passes its own parameter to an `Eq`-bounded parameter of another generic, so a bound appears at every link of a chain of calls. Declare `T: Eq`; `T: Ord` and `T: Key` also allow `==`. The diagnostic's fix adds the bound, and `bynk check --fix` applies it across a project.
summary: A type parameter is compared with `==`/`!=`, or passed to an `Eq`-bounded parameter of another generic, but is not declared `Eq` (`[T: Eq]`, or `where A: Eq` for a receiver type's parameter). The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix (ADR 0430, amended by constrained-generics slice 0).

blurb: A `Map` key or a `Set` element must be a type that can be held under a canonical encoding, and a type parameter might be a function or another type that cannot. So a type parameter that reaches a `Map` key or a `Set` element, in a signature, a generic type's field, or a `distinct`, `groupBy` or join key, must be declared `K: Key`, and a call must instantiate it with a key type. `Key` implies `Eq`, so an existing `Eq` bound is replaced rather than joined (`K: Eq + Key` is a warning). The diagnostic's fix declares the bound, and `bynk check --fix` applies it across a project.
summary: A type parameter keys a `Map` or `Set` (a `Map` key, a `Set` element, a `distinct`/`groupBy`/join key), or is passed to a `Key`-bounded parameter of another generic, but is not declared `Key` (`[K: Key]`, or `where A: Key` for a receiver type's parameter; on the type for a generic type's own parameter). The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix that declares `Key`, replacing an existing `Eq`, which `Key` implies (constrained-generics slice 2).

blurb: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` work on a type parameter only if the function says so with an `Ord` bound. A type parameter stands for any type, and many types have no total order: a function, an `Effect`, a `Bool`, a record that does not `derives Ord`. The bound puts the requirement in the signature, where a caller, hover and signature help can see it, and a call must instantiate it with an orderable type. The same rule covers an ordering key and a parameter passed on to an `Ord`-bounded parameter of another generic, so the bound appears at every link of a chain of calls. Declare `T: Ord`; it implies `Eq`, so an existing `Eq` is replaced (`T: Eq + Ord` is only a warning). The diagnostic's fix adds the bound, and `bynk check --fix` applies it across a project.
summary: A type parameter is ordered (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, an ordering kernel key), or passed to an `Ord`-bounded parameter of another generic, but is not declared `Ord` (`[T: Ord]`, or `where A: Ord` for a receiver type's parameter). The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix that declares `Ord`, replacing an existing `Eq`, which `Ord` implies (constrained-generics slice 1).

blurb: A generic type may refer to itself only uniformly: the self-reference must pass the declaration's own type parameters through unchanged and in order, as `Weird[T]` inside `Weird[T]`. Anything else is polymorphic recursion, such as `Weird[List[T]]` inside `Weird[T]`, or `Pair[B, A]` inside `Pair[A, B]`, and it generates an unbounded set of instantiations, so it is refused at the declaration. The same holds for mutually recursive generics: a partner may be applied only to the declaration's own parameters or to types that mention none, never to a type that wraps one of them.
example:
type Weird[T] = { value: T, next: Option[Weird[List[T]]] }   // ✗ a different instantiation

type Weird[T] = { value: T, next: Option[Weird[T]] }         // ✓ parameters passed through
summary: A generic type refers to itself with arguments other than its own type parameters, in order (`Weird[List[T]]` inside `Weird[T]`, or `Pair[B, A]` inside `Pair[A, B]`), or to a mutually recursive partner with an argument that wraps one of its own parameters (`Inner[List[T]]` inside `Outer[T]`). Such polymorphic recursion generates an unbounded set of instantiations and is refused at the declaration; a self-reference that passes the parameters through unchanged, and a partner applied to the declaration's own parameters or to types that mention none (of any arity), are accepted (#3192).

blurb: A recursive generic type, a record or sum that contains itself, declares and works inside a context, but it has no codec yet. So it is refused wherever a codec is required: a service or agent handler signature, an agent `store` field or key, an event field, an actor identity type, a `Json.encode` or `Json.decode` target, or a `Codable` witness. The error fires once per use, and when the type is reached through another type, its note names the field path. To cross a boundary today, use a concrete recursive type, or keep the generic one inside the context.
summary: A recursive generic type (a record or sum that transitively contains itself, through any wrapper or generic argument) is used where a codec is required: a service or agent handler signature, an agent store field or key, an event field, an actor identity type, a `Json.encode`/`decode` target or a `Codable` witness. It declares and works inside a context, but has no codec yet, so it cannot cross a boundary; when it is reached through another type, the note names the field path (#3192, ADR 0197).

A type parameter is declared both `Eq` and `Ord` (or `Eq` and `Key`); `Ord` and `Key` imply `Eq`, so the `Eq` is redundant. The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix that removes it (constrained-generics slices 1 and 2, warning).

blurb: A generic type is applied to exactly as many type arguments as it declares parameters: `Box[T]` takes one. Too many, too few, arguments on a type that is not generic, and a generic type named with no arguments at all are all refused, since each argument fills one parameter. A type parameter such as `T` is not itself generic, so `T[Int]` is refused too. Give the arguments the declaration asks for.
summary: A user-declared generic type is applied to the wrong number of type arguments, or a generic type is named without its `[…]` arguments (v0.157, ADR 0183).

blurb: The type arguments of a generic call do not fit. The checker infers each type parameter from the arguments, and an argument that contradicts what an earlier one settled is refused: `pick(1, "one")` cannot make `T` both `Int` and `String`. The same code covers explicit type arguments of the wrong number (`pick[Int, Int](…)`), type arguments given to a function that is not generic, and a type parameter named like a declared type. Make the arguments agree, give the type argument explicitly where the inference is not what you meant, or rename the parameter.
summary: Inferred or explicit type arguments conflict, have the wrong arity, target a non-generic function, or a type parameter shadows a declared type.

blurb: A call to a generic function leaves a type parameter undetermined. Bynk fixes a type parameter from the arguments and, failing that, from the type the call is expected to have; it never guesses. `none()` has no argument that mentions `T`, and `let x = none()` gives it no expected type, so there is nothing to choose `T` from. The error also fires when a lambda's parameter types depend on a parameter that the other arguments leave open. Give the type argument explicitly with `none[Int]()`, or annotate the binding so the expected type supplies it: `let x: Option[Int] = none()`.
summary: A generic function's type parameter could not be inferred from the arguments and was not given explicitly (`name[T](…)`); a bare generic function also cannot be passed as a value.

blurb: A bound after a type parameter, `T: C`, must name one of the four constraints Bynk has: `Eq`, `Ord`, `Key` and `Codable`. There are no user-defined constraints or interfaces, so a name like `Hashable` or `Comparable` is refused rather than silently ignored; ignoring it would let a function compile that promised more than the compiler could check. The same code is reported for a `derives` clause that names anything but `Ord`; naming `Eq`, `Key` or `Codable` there is `bynk.types.derives_automatic`, because they hold automatically. Pick the constraint that matches what the body does: `Eq` for `==`, `Ord` for ordering, `Key` for a `Map` key or `Set` element, `Codable` for `Json`.
summary: A bound, or a `derives` entry, names something that is not a constraint; the constraints are `Eq`, `Ord`, `Key` and `Codable`.

blurb: A `where` clause bounds a type parameter, so it must name one: the function's own, or, for a method, its receiver type's. A name that is neither is usually a misspelling. Correct it, or declare the parameter in the brackets after the function's name. A bound that does not exist is `bynk.generics.unknown_constraint`.
example:
fn same[T](a: T) -> T where U: Eq { a }   // ✗ `U` is not a parameter here

fn same[T](a: T) -> T where T: Eq { a }   // ✓ bound a parameter that is declared
summary: A method's `where` clause bounds a name that is not a type parameter of the method or of its receiver type.

blurb: A context may only depend on a capability that the context providing it exports. `exports capability { … }` is the provider's decision about what it offers other contexts, and a capability it leaves out stays its own. So `consumes clock { Clock }`, or a qualified `given clock.Clock`, is refused when `clock` does not list `Clock`. Add the name to the provider's `exports capability` clause (it must declare and provide the capability), or correct the spelling here. A context that is not consumed at all is `bynk.resolve.unconsumed_context`.
summary: `given B.Cap` or `consumes B { Cap }` names a capability the consumed context does not export.

blurb: `given` lets a function use capabilities, and only a context declares which capabilities it consumes. A commons is shared by every context that uses it, and those may consume different capabilities, so a function in a commons or a suite cannot declare `given`. Take the operation as a parameter instead, and pass `(m) => Logger.error(m)` from the handler, or move the function into the context that consumes the capability. A method cannot declare `given` anywhere: that is `bynk.given.fn_unsupported`.
example:
fn warn(what: String) -> Effect[()] given Logger { … }   // ✗ a commons function has no `given`

fn warn(log: (String) -> Effect[()], what: String) -> Effect[()] { … }   // ✓ the caller passes the operation in
summary: A function in a commons (or a suite) declares `given`; only a context function can.

blurb: Only a free function in a context that returns `Effect[T]` may declare `given`. A capability operation is an effect, so a function that reaches one has to say so in its return type, and a method has no place to carry the capabilities. `Events` is refused too: `Events.emit` buffers until its handler commits, so emit in the handler, or pass the event back to the caller. Return `Effect[T]` and make it a free function, or take the operation as a function-value parameter. A `given` in a commons is `bynk.given.fn_outside_context`.
