A git dependency's store entry, or a freshly fetched commit, doesn't hash to the checksum `bynk.lock` records; `bynk` refuses to build it.

blurb: A package's units are resolved against the packages it depends on, so the package graph needs an order: no package may depend, directly or through others, on itself or on the project. A cycle usually means two packages each want something of the other. Move what both need into a third package that each of them depends on, or merge the two.
example:
# packages/money/bynk.toml
[dependencies]
tax = { package = "acme/tax", path = "../tax" }

# packages/tax/bynk.toml
[dependencies]
money = { package = "acme/money", path = "../money" }   // ✗ `acme/money` depends on `acme/tax`

core = { package = "acme/core", path = "../core" }      // ✓ what both need, in a package of its own
summary: The package graph has a cycle: a dependency depends, directly or not, on itself or on the project.

blurb: A path dependency points at a directory that is a package: it has its own `bynk.toml` with a `[package]` table. The path is read from the manifest that names it. The entry is refused when there is no readable `bynk.toml` there, when it is not valid, or when it has no `[package]`. Correct the path, or add the manifest to the package.
example:
[dependencies]
lib = { package = "acme/lib", path = "pkg/libs" }   // ✗ no `bynk.toml` at `pkg/libs`

lib = { package = "acme/lib", path = "pkg/lib" }    // ✓ the package's directory
summary: A path dependency's directory has no readable `bynk.toml`, its `bynk.toml` is invalid, or it has no `[package]`.

blurb: A `[dev-dependencies]` package is there for the project's suites, and a deployable build leaves suites out, so a package that only suites need is never compiled into it. A context or commons that reached one would break that build, so only a suite may. If the source needs the package, move its entry to `[dependencies]`; otherwise keep the use in a suite.
summary: A commons, context or adapter reaches a `[dev-dependencies]` alias, which only a suite may use.

blurb: A build holds one copy of each package, so every dependency on a package must reach it in the same directory. Two entries that name one package but point at different directories would give two copies, with two sets of types where there should be one. Point both at the same directory, or drop one. Two aliases onto one directory are fine.
example:
[dependencies]
lib = { package = "acme/lib", path = "pkg/lib" }
util = { package = "acme/lib", path = "vendor/lib" }   // ✗ `acme/lib` from a second directory

util = { package = "acme/lib", path = "pkg/lib" }      // ✓ the same directory
summary: One package is reached from two different directories; a build holds one copy of each package.
`git` couldn't clone, fetch or check out a git dependency, or the revision it names doesn't exist.
`bynk.lock` can't be read: it isn't valid TOML, has no `version`, is a version this toolchain doesn't read, or locks a package to something that isn't a commit.
`--locked` was given, and resolving the manifests would change `bynk.lock`.

blurb: A path dependency gives the package's name twice: `package = "acme/lib"` in your `[dependencies]`, and `name` under `[package]` in the manifest at that path. They must agree, so that what you asked for is what you get. A mismatch usually means the path is the wrong directory, or the package was renamed. Correct whichever is wrong.
example:
[dependencies]
money = { package = "acme/money", path = "pkg/lib" }   // ✗ `pkg/lib` is the package `acme/lib`

money = { package = "acme/lib", path = "pkg/lib" }     // ✓ the name it declares
summary: A path dependency's `package` names a different package than the directory's `[package] name`.
A git dependency has no `bynk.lock` entry, or its store entry is missing; `bynk fetch` fetches it (refused under `--offline`).

blurb: A package lists in `exports` the units it offers to its users, and keeps the rest free to change, as a library keeps its internals. A unit that exists but is not listed is refused, so a consumer cannot come to rely on it. Use one of the exported units, or ask the package to export it. Leaving `exports` out shares every commons and adapter. A name the package does not declare at all is `bynk.package.unknown_unit`.
example:
exports = ["notify"]      // in the package's `bynk.toml`

uses lib.internal     // ✗ not in `exports`

uses lib.notify       // ✓ an exported unit
summary: A `uses` or `consumes` reaches a unit its dependency declares but doesn't list in `[package] exports`.

blurb: A dependency is reached as `alias.unit`, where the unit is a commons or adapter the package declares. A name after the alias that matches none of them is refused, most often because it is misspelt. The diagnostic's note lists the units the package shares. A unit that exists but is not exported is `bynk.package.unit_not_exported`.
example:
commons notify          // in the package `acme/lib`

uses lib.notifiy      // ✗ the package declares no `notifiy`

uses lib.notify       // ✓
summary: A `uses` or `consumes` names, through a dependency alias, a unit the dependency doesn't declare.
A git dependency's URL or revision looks like a command-line option, or uses a transport other than `https`, `ssh` (or `file`, from the project's own manifests).

blurb: A dependency may not declare an `asset` or an `embed`, because the path would be resolved against the project that consumes it, whose `assets/` or `embeds/` folder is not the package's. Move the file into your own project, and have the package take its content as an argument.
example:
commons board                           // in the package `acme/lib`

asset style = "assets/board.css"        // ✗ a dependency cannot declare one
fn sheet() -> String { style.url }

commons board

fn sheet(url: String) -> String { url } // ✓ the project supplies the URL
summary: A dependency declares an `asset` or an `embed`, which would resolve against the consuming project's `assets/` or `embeds/`; a per-package namespace for either isn't designed yet.
One package is reached at two different git revisions (or from git and a path); a build, or a workspace, holds one copy of each package.

blurb: A `par { … }` block issues all its bindings together and waits for them, so it holds only `let x <- e` and `do e`. Anything else has no effect to overlap, nothing to join, or must stay in order: a plain `let`, `:=` or a `store` write, `expect`, `advance`, a nested `par`, a `let … else`, a bare expression (write `do e`) and an empty block. Store writes stay sequential; for `parTraverse` closures the rule is `bynk.par.store_write_in_closure`. Move the statement before or after the block; the names a block binds are in scope after its closing brace. See also `bynk.par.sibling_name` (a binding reading another binding of the same block) and the warning `bynk.par.single_binding`.
summary: A `par { … }` block holds a statement other than `let x <- e` or `do e`: a refutable `let … else`, a plain `let`, `:=` or a store write, `expect`, `advance`, a nested `par`, or anything that is not a statement.

blurb: The bindings of a `par` block are issued together and the block waits for all of them, so a `?` inside one has no single place to return from. Bind each effect's `Result` in the block and apply `?` after it, where the lines run in source order and the first `Err` propagates. A `?` on an argument can be computed before the block instead.
summary: A `?` appears inside a `par { … }` binding. `?` takes a `Result` value, not an effect, so a binding's own result is unwrapped after the block (`let user = userR?`), where the `?` lines run in source order; a `?` on an argument is computed before the block.

blurb: The bindings in a `par { … }` block run together, so none can read the result of another: there is no order in which one could be given the other's value. A binding that mentions a name a sibling binds is refused, even where an outer binding of that name exists, so a stale value is never picked up silently. Binding one name twice in a block is refused as well, since later code could not tell which result is meant. Move the dependent binding after the block, where every name is in scope, or rename.
summary: A `par { … }` binding mentions a name another binding in the same block binds, or binds a name twice. The bindings run together, so none can read a sibling's result; the rule holds even where the name would resolve to an outer binding.
A `par { … }` block has a single binding, which is a plain `let x <- e` with extra syntax (warning).

blurb: The closure given to `parForEach`, `parTraverse`, `parTraverseAll` or `parTraverseTry` runs once per element, all at once, so it may not write a `store` field, which is the rule a `par { … }` block already follows. Every `<-` is an await point, so a `get` then a `put` in the closure lets the other branches write in between, and their updates are lost. A single call such as `update` is atomic per key, but it is refused here too, so the two rules stay equal. Run the loop with `forEach` (or `traverseAll` / `traverseTry`), where each element finishes before the next starts, so a single-call `update` stays atomic. A store write reads the entry before it stages the write, so the sequential form reads one entry at a time; per-key atomicity is the reason for the rule. To keep the concurrent part, collect with `parTraverseAll` and write afterwards.
summary: A closure passed to `parForEach`, `parTraverse`, `parTraverseAll` or `parTraverseTry` writes a `store` field (`put`, `remove`, `update`, `upsert`, `add`, `append` or `:=`). Its branches run concurrently, and a `get` then a `put` across them loses updates, so store writes stay sequential, as they do in a `par { … }` block.

blurb: A block has no expression statements: each statement is a `let`, `do`, `expect`, `:=` and so on, and the last expression is the block's value. An expression written on its own line with more of the block after it would have its value thrown away, so the compiler asks you to say what happens to it. Bind it: `let _ = expr` when you only want to discard a value, or `let _ <- expr` when it is an effect to run and await (a call through a capability or an agent, or a cell's `.update`). The parser cannot see types, so it picks the `<-` form for a call that looks like an effect and the `=` form otherwise, and its note names the other. The fix is machine-applicable, so `bynk check --fix` applies it.
summary: An expression stands alone as a statement, followed by more of the block; a block has no expression statements, so its value would be discarded. Bind it with `let _ <-` (an effect) or `let _ =`.

blurb: A `stub` or `env` clause sets up the world a test case runs in, so it comes at the start of the case body, before any statement. One after a `let` or other statement is refused, so the setup reads in one place above the steps that depend on it. Move the clause above the first statement of the case.
summary: A `stub` or `env` clause came after a statement in a test case; they lead the case body.

blurb: A `const` always states its type: `const Limit: Int = 100`. A constant is part of its unit's interface, so a reader, or a unit that `uses` it, can see its type without inferring it from the initialiser. Write the type after the name, before the `=`.
example:
const Limit = 100          // ✗ no type annotation
const Limit: Int = 100     // ✓
summary: A `const` declaration has no type annotation; a constant's type is always written (`const Name: Type = …`).

blurb: In the fragment form of a `context` (the header with no braces), the `consumes` clauses come straight after the `uses` lines, before any `type` or `fn`, so a unit's dependencies are all stated at the top. Move the `consumes` line up. `uses` and `exports` follow the same rule, as `bynk.parse.uses_after_decls` and `bynk.parse.exports_after_decls`.
example:
context shop.orders
type Id = String
consumes shop.payment            // ✗ a declaration comes first

context shop.orders
consumes shop.payment            // ✓ clauses straight after the header
type Id = String
summary: `consumes` appears after other declarations.

blurb: A handler annotation, such as `@cache(maxAge: 5.minutes)`, applies to the handler after it, so it must sit directly above an `on`. Here something else, or the end of the service, follows it. Move the annotation to just above its handler.
summary: A handler-position annotation (e.g. `@cache`) is not followed by an `on` handler.

blurb: A line of three or more dashes opens or closes a documentation block, so two dash lines turn the code between them into documentation, and it is never compiled. Use a line comment for a divider. To show code in a documentation block, put it in a Markdown code fence.
summary: A documentation block's content (outside Markdown code fences) parses as declarations, so a pair of dash dividers has turned code into documentation.

blurb: A service has one CORS policy, and it applies to every route in it. Two `cors` blocks could grant different things, and the reader would not know which holds, so the second is refused. Merge them into one. `security` and `limits` follow the same rule (`bynk.parse.duplicate_security`, `bynk.parse.duplicate_limits`), as does `json` (`bynk.parse.duplicate_json`).
summary: A service declares more than one `cors { }` policy.

blurb: A service's `json` policy sets whether its response bodies use plain or tagged JSON, so there is one setting for the whole service. A second block would contradict the first, and is refused. Keep one. A single route can still differ with `@json` on its handler. The same rule holds for `cors`, `security` and `limits`, as `bynk.parse.duplicate_cors` shows.
summary: A service declares more than one `json { }` policy.

blurb: A service has one `limits` policy, and it sets the body-size cap for its body-taking routes. Two blocks could name different caps, and the reader would not know which holds, so the second is refused. Merge them into one, keeping the cap you mean. A single route can still differ with `@limit` on its handler. `cors`, `security` and `json` follow the same rule (`bynk.parse.duplicate_cors`, `bynk.parse.duplicate_security`, `bynk.parse.duplicate_json`).
summary: A service declares more than one `limits { }` policy.

blurb: A service has one `security` policy, and it sets the security headers (`hsts`, `nosniff`) stamped on every response. Two blocks could set them differently, and the reader would not know which holds, so the second is refused. Merge them into one. `cors`, `limits` and `json` follow the same rule (`bynk.parse.duplicate_cors`, `bynk.parse.duplicate_limits`, `bynk.parse.duplicate_json`).
summary: A service declares more than one `security { }` policy.

blurb: An agent is its storage and the `on call` handlers that read and change it. One with no handler can never be called, so it is refused, as is one with no `store` field (`bynk.parse.expected_agent_storage`). Add a handler.
summary: An `agent` body is empty.

blurb: A capability is a set of operations that a unit asks for with `given` and that a provider supplies. With no operations there is nothing to call or to provide, so an empty one is refused. Declare at least one operation, or remove the capability.
summary: A `capability` body is empty.

blurb: An interpolation hole, `\(…)`, holds one expression, whose value is written into the text. An empty `\()` has nothing to write. Put an expression in the hole. To write the characters `\(` themselves, escape the backslash: `\\(`.
summary: An interpolation hole `\(…)` contains no expression.

blurb: A `match`, or the `else match` of a `let … else`, must have at least one arm. Each arm gives the match a value, so one with no arms has none to give. Write an arm for each shape the value can take; a final `_ =>` arm takes whatever the others leave.
summary: A `match` has no arms.

blurb: A service is its handlers, so one with none can never be called or triggered, and is refused. (A service that subscribes to `Events` takes exactly one `on event`.) Add a handler, or remove the service.
summary: A `service` body is empty.

blurb: A pattern in `from Events(E { … })` narrows delivery to events whose fields match, so it must name at least one field to match on. An empty `E {}` filters nothing and only looks as if it does. For every event of the type, drop the braces: `from Events(E)`.
summary: A `from Events(E { ... })` subscription pattern listed no fields — use `from Events(E)` (no braces) for an unfiltered subscription.

blurb: An agent is addressed by its key, so the key is the first thing in its body: `key id: Type`. Anything else there, usually a `store` field written first, is refused, so that how an agent is found is the first thing a reader sees. Move the `key` line to the top.
summary: Expected a `key` declaration in an agent.

blurb: An agent exists to hold state, and its state is its `store` fields, so one with none is refused. Declare at least one. A `store` field has a kind such as `Cell`, `Map` or `Set`. An agent with storage but no handler is `bynk.parse.empty_agent`.
summary: An agent declares no storage — it has no `store` fields.

blurb: After `type Name =` the parser found something that is not a record `{ … }`, a sum starting with `|`, an `enum` or an `opaque` type, so it wanted a base type (`Int`, `String`, `Bool`, `Float`, `Duration`, `Instant`, `Bytes` or `Decimal`) to build on. The commonest cause is a sum written without its leading `|`. Another is naming an existing record or sum, as in `type Id = Order`, which a type declaration cannot do; for a distinct type, use `opaque` over a base type. The position is the first token after the `=`.
example:
type Shape = Circle | Square              // ✗ a sum starts with `|`
type Shape = | Circle | Square            // ✓
summary: Expected a base type.

blurb: A capability body is a list of operations, each a signature that starts with `fn`: the capability says what can be done, and a provider supplies how. The parser found something else where the next operation should begin. The commonest cause is leaving off the `fn`. An `on` handler, a `type` or a `let` does not belong in a capability either. The message names the token it found, and the position is where the operation should have started. A provider body has the same rule: `bynk.parse.expected_provider_op`.
summary: Expected a capability operation.

blurb: The parser needed an expression, a value, and found a token that cannot start one. The commonest cause is a record written without its type: `{ x: 0 }` is not an expression, so write `Point { x: 0 }`. Others are an operator with nothing after it (`a +`) and a trailing comma in a call (`f(a, )`). The message names the token it found, where the parser gave up. For an operator or a comma with nothing after it that is the token after the mistake, so read what comes before it.
summary: Expected an expression.

blurb: A service or agent body is its handlers, each starting with `on`, beside its own clauses (a service's policies, an agent's `key` and `store` fields). The parser found something else where a handler should begin. The commonest cause is a helper `fn`, or a `let`, written inside the body: declare a helper beside the service, in the context, and its handlers can call it. Another is a handler with its `on` left off (`GET("/a") …`, `call get() …`). The position is the first token of the item that is not a handler.
summary: Expected a handler.

blurb: A unit's body is a list of declarations, and the parser found something else where the next one should begin. The message lists what this kind of unit accepts (a commons, a context and a suite differ). The commonest cause is code at the top level, which holds declarations only: a `let` outside any function (a constant is `const Name: Type = …`) or a call. Others are a misspelt keyword (`function`, `pub fn`) and a stray `}` after a fragment-form unit's last declaration. The position is that token, so look just before it too.
example:
let limit = 100                           // ✗ code at the top level of a unit
const Limit: Int = 100                    // ✓ a named constant
summary: Expected a declaration.

blurb: After `where`, and after each `&&`, a refinement takes the name of a predicate from a fixed list (`NonNegative`, `InRange(0, 150)` and so on, which the note gives), not a comparison. The list is closed, so the compiler can check a literal against the refinement at compile time. The commonest cause is a comparison such as `where >= 0`; a name that is not on the list, as in `where n > 0`, is `bynk.parse.unknown_predicate`. The position is the token that is not a predicate name.
example:
type Age = Int where >= 0                 // ✗ a predicate is a name, not a comparison
type Age = Int where NonNegative          // ✓
summary: Expected a refinement predicate.

blurb: A provider body implements the operations its capability declares, each starting with `fn` and carrying a body. The parser found something else where the next operation should begin. The commonest cause is leaving off the `fn`; an `on` handler, a `type` or a `let` does not belong in a provider either. The message names the token it found, and the position is where the operation should have started. A capability body has the same rule: `bynk.parse.expected_capability_op`.
summary: Expected a provider operation.

blurb: The parser was part-way through a construct and the next token had to be one particular token: a `)` closing a list, a `,` between items, a `:`, `=`, `->` or `=>`, or a `}`. The message says which, and what it found instead. The commonest cause is a missing comma: in `fn add(a: Int b: Int)` it finds `b` where `)` was due. Others are `->` for `=>` in a match arm and `:` for `->` before a return type. A missing `)` or `}` is reported at the next token that cannot continue, often on the line below, so read the line above. If the file ended instead, it is `bynk.parse.unexpected_eof`.
example:
fn add(a: Int b: Int) -> Int { a + b }    // ✗ no `,` between the parameters
fn add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int { a + b }   // ✓
summary: Expected a specific token.

blurb: A type was expected here, and the next token cannot start one. The message says which position wanted it (`as the return type`, `as the parameter type`). The commonest cause is a type left out: a `->` with nothing before the `{`, or a `:` with nothing after it. A trailing comma in a type-argument list (`Map[String, ]`) and a value where a type belongs (`n: 5`) land here too. The position is the token after the gap, so look just before it.
summary: Expected a type.
Expected a `commons` or `context` header.

blurb: An `exports` clause says how consumers may use what it lists, so it needs a visibility: `exports opaque { … }` keeps a type's shape private to its context, `exports transparent { … }` shows it, and `exports capability { … }` offers a capability. A bare `exports { … }` is refused: the choice decides what other units can rely on, so it is written out. Pick one.
example:
exports { P }                           // ✗ no visibility

exports transparent { P }               // ✓
summary: Expected a visibility keyword.

blurb: In the fragment form of a `context` (the header with no braces), the `exports` clauses come after the `uses` and `consumes` lines and before any `type` or `fn`, so what a unit offers is stated at the top. Move the `exports` line up. `uses` and `consumes` follow the same rule, as `bynk.parse.uses_after_decls` and `bynk.parse.consumes_after_decls`.
example:
context shop.orders
type Id = String
exports transparent { Id }       // ✗ a declaration comes first

context shop.orders
exports transparent { Id }       // ✓ clauses straight after the header
type Id = String
summary: `exports` appears after other declarations.

blurb: A `.bynk` file holds one `commons` or `context`, and the parser found more after it ended. The commonest cause is a `}` too many: the unit closed early, or an extra brace sits at the end, and the first token after the close is reported, either the stray brace or the next declaration. Count the braces back from there. The other is a second `commons` or `context` in the same file; each goes in its own file. The position is the first token after the unit's end, not the brace that ended it. Inside a string, an interpolation `\(…)` holds a single expression, and a second token in it lands here too.
summary: Unexpected tokens after an otherwise complete construct.

blurb: `Result` takes two type arguments, the success type and the error type: `Result[T, E]`. `Map` takes two as well, `Map[K, V]`, and a type applied to an empty `[]` needs at least one. A `Result[Int]` leaves out the error a caller has to handle, so it is refused rather than guessed. Give every argument.
summary: Wrong number of generic type arguments.

blurb: An `agent` has only `on call` handlers. HTTP routes (`on GET`, `on POST`, …), schedules and queue messages belong on a `service`, which receives the request or event and calls the agent. Move the protocol handler to a service and give the agent an `on call` operation for it to call.
summary: A protocol handler (`on GET`/`schedule`/`message`) was declared in an agent.

blurb: An agent's declarations come in phases: `store` fields, then `invariant`s, then `on` handlers. An invariant after a handler is refused, so that every property the handlers must preserve sits together above them. Move the invariant above the first handler.
summary: An `invariant` was declared after a handler; invariants precede handlers.

blurb: A record pattern or construction may write a field by name alone (`{ total }`), which binds a variable of that name. A reserved word cannot be a variable, so `{ type, .. }` is refused, though `type` is allowed as a field label before a `:`. In a pattern, name the binding: `type: type_`; the compiler offers that fix. In a construction, give the value: `type: "Org"`.
summary: A reserved keyword was used as a field shorthand, which would bind a variable of that name.

blurb: A lambda parameter written as a record pattern already names its type, in `Item { … }`, and its names take their types from that record, so a `: Type` after the pattern is refused. Remove the annotation; the fix is machine-applicable, so `bynk check --fix` applies it.
example:
items.map((Item { qty, .. }: Item) => qty)    // ✗ the pattern names the type
items.map((Item { qty, .. }) => qty)          // ✓
summary: A lambda parameter with a record pattern carries a type annotation; the pattern's type name already gives the parameter's type.

blurb: A lambda parameter may be a pattern only when it is a record pattern that cannot fail, as in `(Item { qty, .. }) => qty`. A lambda is given a value and has no `else`, so a pattern that can miss, such as `Some(n)`, a list, a literal or a range, has no way to say what happens then. Take a name and `match` on it in the body.
example:
xs.map((Some(n)) => n)               // ✗ a lambda has no `else` for `None`

xs.map((o) => match o {              // ✓ the `match` covers both
    Some(n) => n
    None => 0
})
summary: A lambda parameter is a pattern other than a record pattern; only an irrefutable record pattern may stand in for a name.

blurb: A lambda parameter pattern must match every value of its type, because a lambda has no `else` for the rest. `Item { status: Paid, qty, .. }` matches only some items. Use bare names, `f: name` or `f: _`; the note names the first field that can fail. To handle the other cases, take a name and `match` on it in the body.
example:
items.map((Item { status: Paid, qty, .. }) => qty)   // ✗ not every item is `Paid`

items.map((i) => match i.status {                    // ✓ every status is handled
    Paid => i.qty
    Pending => 0
})
summary: A lambda parameter's record pattern can fail to match some value of its type, and a lambda has no `else` to fall back on.

blurb: `else` after a `let` says what the block does when the pattern does not match. A plain name matches every value, so this `else` could never run, and it is refused rather than ignored. To handle a failure, bind a pattern that can fail: `Ok(x)`, `Some(x)`, or a qualified variant such as `Status.Pending`. Otherwise drop the `else`.
summary: An `else` follows a plain `let name = …` binding, which matches every value, so the `else` could never run.

Nested `match`es on `Option`/`Result` that each carry on in one arm and give up in the other, which `let … else` writes flat. A hint with a machine-applicable rewrite; never fails a build and is hidden from the terminal (hint).

blurb: A `let` that takes a value apart with a pattern gives its names the types they have in the value, so it has no place for an annotation after the pattern. Remove the `: Type`. To pin the type of the value itself, annotate an ordinary `let` first and match on that.
summary: A `let` with a pattern carries a type annotation; the pattern's names take their types from the value.

blurb: A `let` that takes a value apart with a pattern must say what the block produces when the value does not match, so it needs an `else`. Only a record pattern that cannot fail (every field a bare name, `f: name` or `f: _`) may leave it out. Add `else { … }` after the value, or write a `match`. The note names the first field that can fail to match.
summary: A `let` binds a pattern but has no `else` saying what the block produces when the value does not match; only a record pattern that cannot fail may omit it.

blurb: In a list pattern the `..` (or `..rest`) stands for the elements the pattern does not name, and it must be the last element and appear once. A pattern that matches the end of a list, such as `[.., last]`, is not available, so match from the front. When only `_` patterns follow the `..`, the error offers a machine-applicable fix that moves it to the end.
summary: A `..` in a list pattern is not the final element; suffix forms such as `[.., last]` are not available.

blurb: A `Float` literal has a digit on each side of the point, as in `1.0` and `0.5`; `1.` and `.5` are refused. This keeps a method call on a number, such as `1.toFloat()` or `2.5.round()`, unambiguous. Write the missing digit; the note gives the corrected literal.
example:
const Half: Float = .5     // ✗ no digit before the point
const Half: Float = 0.5    // ✓
summary: A float literal is missing a digit on one side of the `.` (`1.`, `.5`).

blurb: A block has no expression statements, so a `match` is its final value and nothing can follow it; a second `match` straight after the first is refused. Bind the first with `let _ = match …`. If the steps are fallible and each depends on the one before, `let … else` flattens them without nesting.
summary: A `match` ends the block it is in, because a block has no expression statements; a second `match` straight after it cannot follow.

blurb: A `migrate` step carries a stored record from an older schema version to the agent's current shape, so it belongs with the agent's storage and invariants, above the handlers that read the migrated state. One written after a handler is refused. Move it above the first handler. `bynk.parse.invariant_after_handler` and `bynk.parse.transition_after_handler` are the same rule for invariants and transitions.
summary: A `migrate` step is declared after an agent handler; migration steps precede the handlers.

blurb: A `migrate` step carries a stored record from an older schema version to the agent's current shape, so its body is only a list of what happens to each field: `field := value` assigns a current field, `let x = value` binds a local for later lines, and `drop field` discards a stored field on purpose. A step is pure, so nothing else belongs in it. The commonest mistake is `=` where `:=` is meant; a bare expression lands here too. The position is the first token of the line that is none of the three.
summary: A `migrate` step's body holds something other than `field := value`, `let` or `drop field`.

blurb: A declaration or member has one doc. Two doc lines in a row are two docs, not one of two lines. For more than one line, write a doc block: a `---` line, the text, and another `---` line. When every doc is a one-line `--- text`, the fix that joins them into a block is machine-applicable, so `bynk check --fix` applies it.
example:
--- Doubles a number.
--- Used by the pricing code.          // ✗ a second doc
fn double(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }

---                                    // ✓ one doc block
Doubles a number.
Used by the pricing code.
---
fn double(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }
summary: A declaration or member has two docs directly above it; a target has one doc, so a doc of more than one line is a `---` block.
An expression or type nests deeper than the parser's fixed limit.

blurb: Bynk has no `%` operator. Remainder is a method with its sign spelled out: `a.rem(b)` takes the dividend's sign (the C, Java and JavaScript `%`), `a.mod(b)` takes the divisor's (Python's `%`; use it for a cyclic index). When both operands are plain names or integer literals the error offers a `.rem` fix, never applied automatically: check that the sign is the one you want.
summary: `%` is not an operator; use `Int.rem` (the dividend's sign) or `Int.mod` (the divisor's).

blurb: Comparisons (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and equality tests (`==`, `!=`) do not chain, so `a < b < c` is refused rather than given a reading you may not have meant. Split a chain of comparisons with `&&`; to test the result of an equality, parenthesise it: `(a == b) == c`.
summary: A non-associative operator was chained (e.g. `a == b == c`).
A documentation block is not attached to a declaration (warning).

blurb: A service's policies open its body, before any handler, in one fixed order: `cors`, `security`, `limits`, then `json`, each optional. One fixed layout means a reader always finds a service's cross-cutting rules at the top, and the formatter has a single form to write. A policy after a later one, or after a handler, is refused. Reorder them. A policy given twice is a separate error, such as `bynk.parse.duplicate_cors`.
summary: A service's `cors`/`security`/`limits` policy is out of order or follows a handler; they open the body in the order `cors`, `security`, `limits`, `json`.

blurb: After `is`, a record pattern is written in parentheses. Bare, the `{` that opens its fields could equally open the block of the `if`, and the reader could not tell which. Write `x is (Type { field, .. })`. The fix is machine-applicable, so `bynk check --fix` applies it. A `match` arm needs no parentheses.
summary: A record pattern after `is` is not parenthesised — write `x is (T { f, .. })`.

blurb: Every record pattern ends with `..`. Record patterns are always open: they name the fields they care about and ignore the rest, so adding a field to the record later never breaks a pattern that was already written. The `..` makes that openness visible at the pattern. The compiler offers the fix: it adds `..` after the last field.
summary: A record pattern does not end with `..`; every record pattern is open.

blurb: A `where` guard on a `match` arm is written on the wildcard, as `_ where InRange(0, 100)`. In this version no other pattern can carry one, a name included, so binding the matched value together with a guard is not yet supported. Write `_ where …`, and refer to the value by the name it already has.
summary: A refined pattern's inner form is something other than `_`.

blurb: `~>` was removed. It started an effect and carried on without waiting, which `e.detach()` now says as an ordinary effect statement: it works for any `Effect[T]`, inside a lambda, `forEach` or helper, and reports a fault or an `Err` instead of losing it. Write `do e.detach()` where you wrote `~> e`. For a unit effect that does not need to outlive the handler, plain `do e` is enough, since `Logger` calls finish before they return. On v0.603.x, `bynk check --fix` rewrites each `~> e` for you. See the Book's Upgrading page.
summary: The `~>` send was removed; write `do e.detach()`.

blurb: A hard keyword (`type`, `fn`, `match`, `Int` and so on) was written where a name is expected: a parameter, a `let` binding, an operation name. Hard keywords are reserved everywhere, so none can be a name. Rename it. A keyword is still allowed as a field label when a `:` follows it (`{ type: String }`); the shorthand without the `:` is `bynk.parse.keyword_field_shorthand`.
summary: A reserved keyword was used as an identifier.

blurb: `self` is the receiver of a method, and only the first parameter of a method declaration, written `fn Type.method(self, …)`, may be named `self`. A free function has no receiver. Either name the type the function belongs to, making it a method, or drop `self` and take the value as an ordinary parameter.
summary: `self` is the first parameter of a free function; only a method declaration, `fn Type.method(self, …)`, has a receiver.

blurb: An agent's body is ordered: its `key`, its storage fields (`state` and `store`), its invariants and migrations, then its handlers. Putting the fields first means the whole shape of the agent's persisted state is read before any code that uses it. A storage field declared after an invariant or a handler is refused. Move it up beside the other fields.
summary: Agent storage (`state` / `store`) is declared after the invariants or handlers.

blurb: A `transition` checks each committed step of an agent against the one before it, so it belongs with the agent's invariants, above the handlers whose steps it constrains. One written after a handler is refused. Move it above the first handler. `bynk.parse.invariant_after_handler` and `bynk.parse.migrate_after_handler` are the same rule for invariants and migrations.
summary: A `transition` is declared after an agent handler; step invariants precede the handlers.
An `adapter` appeared where it is not allowed.
A `context` appeared where it is not allowed.

blurb: The file ended while the parser still needed something: usually a closing `}`, `)` or `]`, or an expression after an operator or a `,`. The message says what it expected, and the position is the end of the file. The commonest cause is a `}` missing at the end of a braced unit or function. A missing brace with further declarations after it is reported as `bynk.parse.expected_token`, at the next `fn` or `type`, so it may be well above the end: check the nesting from the last declaration you edited.
summary: Unexpected end of input.
A `suite` appeared where it is not allowed.

blurb: `Effect.pure(value)` is the only operation spelled on `Effect` itself in an expression: it lifts a plain value into `Effect[T]`. An effect otherwise comes from calling a handler or a capability's operation. Use `Effect.pure`.
summary: An unknown method on `Effect`.

blurb: A handler is `on` and a kind the compiler knows: `call`, an HTTP method, `schedule`, `message` and the like. An HTTP method is written in capitals, `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, so `on get(…)` is not a handler. Spell the kind as one of these.
summary: An unknown handler form (expected `call`, an HTTP method, `schedule`, or `message`).

blurb: A refined type is a base type plus a rule from a fixed set of built-in predicates: `Matches`, `InRange`, `MinLength`, `MaxLength`, `Length`, `NonNegative`, `Positive`, `NonEmpty` and `IsoDate`. There are no user-defined predicates. Use one of these; for a numeric range that is `InRange(lo, hi)`, inclusive at both ends.
example:
type Age = Int where Between(0, 150)    // ✗ not a predicate
type Age = Int where InRange(0, 150)    // ✓
summary: An unknown refinement predicate.

blurb: A test case's tier says how much of the program it runs against, and there are three: `unit`, `integration` and `system`. Any other name after `as` is refused, usually a misspelling. Leave the clause out for `unit`, the default.
summary: A `case`/`suite` `as <tier>` clause names something other than `unit`, `integration`, or `system`.

blurb: In the fragment form of a `commons` or `context` (the header with no braces), the `uses` clauses come straight after the header, before any `type` or `fn`. Move the `uses` line up. `consumes` and `exports` clauses follow the same rule, as `bynk.parse.consumes_after_decls` and `bynk.parse.exports_after_decls`: `consumes` after the `uses` lines, `exports` after the `consumes` lines.
example:
commons demo
type Id = String
uses util              // ✗ a declaration comes first

commons demo
uses util              // ✓ clauses straight after the header
type Id = String
summary: `uses` appears after other declarations.

blurb: A variant of a sum type or enum is written like a constant: an uppercase letter, then letters, digits or `_` (`Active`, `NotFound`). A lowercase variant such as `suspended` is refused. Capitalise the name.
example:
type Status =
    | Active
    | suspended   // ✗ a variant starts with a capital

type Status =
    | Active
    | Suspended   // ✓
summary: A sum-type or enum variant name is not capitalised.

blurb: When the project has a `schema.sql` at its root, Bynk parses each literal SQL statement of a `Postgres` capability, so a syntax error shows up when you check, not on the first request. It also flags a statement of several commands, which a prepared statement does not accept: send each with its own call, or use `transaction`. The parser is a pure-Rust one with a Postgres dialect, not Postgres' own, so it can refuse valid SQL, a newer or rarer form; that is why this is a warning and never blocks a build. Nothing runs, and the statement is not checked against the schema, which Bynk does not own. Correct the statement, or delete `schema.sql` to turn the check off.
example:
let _ <- Main.all("SELEC id FROM orders", [])        // ✗ expected a statement, found SELEC

let _ <- Main.all("SELECT id FROM orders", [])      // ✓
summary: A literal `Postgres` statement does not parse with the Postgres dialect of a pure-Rust SQL parser, or is more than one command, in a project that has a `schema.sql` (warning: the parser is not Postgres' own, so it may refuse valid SQL).

blurb: When the project has a `schema.sql`, Bynk counts the parameters of each literal `Postgres` statement, by Postgres' rule: the highest `$n`, so `$2` alone still takes two values. It checks a list written out in place, or a name `let`-bound to one. A `$n` inside a string, a quoted name, a comment or a dollar-quoted body is text, not a parameter. Pass one `PgValue` for each, or change the SQL. A gap (`$2` with no `$1`) is counted as two parameters; Postgres refuses it at run time (it cannot type `$1`), which this check does not look for.
example:
let _ <- Main.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND qty > $2", [PgInteger(id)])                 // ✗ two parameters, one value

let _ <- Main.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND qty > $2", [PgInteger(id), PgInteger(5)])    // ✓
summary: A literal `Postgres` statement uses a different number of parameters (its highest `$n`) than the list literal passed with it holds, in a project that has a `schema.sql`.

`bynk.contracts.lock` (the older service contracts a callee still accepts) is missing its version field, empty, truncated, unparseable, or of an unsupported version — restore it from version control rather than deleting it, since a callee that forgets the contracts it accepts refuses its live callers.
`bynk.contracts.lock` has one service accepting more older contracts than the build keeps comfortably (warning).
`bynk.contracts.lock` lists an older contract the service no longer accepts, because it is unreadable or no longer compatible with the contract the service has now; the entry is ignored (warning).
`bynk.toml`'s `[workers] compatibility_flags` lists a flag twice, or one every Bynk Worker already has; the duplicate is dropped (warning).

blurb: A unit's module doc is one piece of prose. When a unit is split across files, at most one of them may open with it: with two, the tools would have to join them in some file order and the result would read oddly. The error names every file that carries one. Keep the doc in the file that best introduces the unit, and remove the others.
example:
// text/case.bynk
---
Text helpers.
---
commons text

// text/trim.bynk
---
Trimming.
---
commons text       // ✗ a second module doc

commons text       // ✓ the doc stays in case.bynk
summary: More than one file of a multi-file unit carries a module doc.

blurb: A package's `exports` list names the commons and adapters it shares. A context is a deployment unit, owned by the project that deploys it, so a package never shares one, and listing one is refused. Remove it, or move what other projects need into a commons and list that. A name that is no unit of the package at all is `bynk.project.export_unknown`.
example:
[package]
name = "acme/shop"
exports = ["shop.checkout"]     // ✗ a context

exports = ["money"]             // ✓ a commons
summary: `bynk.toml`'s `[package] exports` lists a context: a package shares commons and adapters, never a context, which belongs to the project that deploys it.

blurb: A package's `[package] exports` lists the units it shares, by their qualified names, and each must be a `commons` or an adapter the package declares. A name that matches none is usually a typo, or a unit that has since been renamed or moved, and a consumer's `uses` of it would fail far from the cause. Correct the name, or remove the entry. Listing a context is `bynk.project.export_context`.
example:
[package]
name = "acme/shop"
exports = ["mony"]    // ✗ no unit `mony`

exports = ["money"]   // ✓ the package's `commons money`
summary: `bynk.toml`'s `[package] exports` lists a name that isn't a commons or adapter the project declares.

blurb: A unit's name comes from its path: `commons money` lives in `money.bynk`, or in the files of a directory `money/`. With both, the path no longer says where `money` lives, or which unit the directory's files belong to, so the project is refused. Keep one: move the file into the directory, or fold the directory into the file.
example:
src/money.bynk           // ✗ `money/` is a directory too
src/money/rates.bynk

src/money/core.bynk      // ✓ one directory, both files `commons money`
src/money/rates.bynk
summary: A unit exists as both a file and a directory.

blurb: A source file's path is its unit's identity: `context commerce.orders` lives at `commerce/orders.bynk`, or in a file under `commerce/orders/`, relative to an include root. A reader can then find a unit from its name alone. Rename the file or directory to match the declared name, or change the name. Test suites are exempt.
summary: A source file's path does not match its declared name.

blurb: A name belongs to one unit, so every file declaring it must agree on its kind. One file saying `commons shop` and another `context shop` would make the name both a library and a deployable unit. Give the files different names, or make them the same kind. A context is the deployable unit, and a commons is the shared code it uses.
summary: A name is declared as both a commons and a context.
No project root could be determined.

blurb: A project compiles the `.bynk` files under its include roots: `src/` (and `tests/`) by default, or the trees that `[paths] include` names. Finding none means there is nothing to build, which almost always means the sources are somewhere the project does not look, or the command was pointed at the wrong directory. Hidden directories, `out/` and `node_modules/` are never searched. Point `[paths] include` at the sources, or run the command from the project's root.
example:
# the sources are in lib/, and src/ is empty
[project]
name = "shop"           // ✗ nothing under src/

[paths]
include = ["lib"]       // ✓
summary: The project contains no source files.
A source file could not be read.

`bynk.schema.lock` (the schema registry for events and agent state) is missing its version field, empty, truncated, or otherwise unparseable — restore it from version control rather than deleting it, since deleting it would silently re-baseline every event's and agent's history.
`bynk.toml`'s `[unstable] allow` lists an item that nothing experimental lies in or under: it is stable now, so the entry can go (warning).

blurb: `[unstable] allow` opts in to experimental standard-library items by path: a unit (`bynk.cloudflare`), an item it exports (`bynk.cloudflare.RateLimit`) or a capability operation (`bynk.cloudflare.Kv.list`). An entry that names nothing in the standard library allows nothing, and is usually a typo, which would leave the `bynk.stability.experimental` error it was meant to clear. Correct the path, or remove the entry. An entry for a real item that is no longer experimental is only a warning.
example:
[unstable]
allow = ["bynk.cloudflare.RateLimt"]    // ✗ no such item

allow = ["bynk.cloudflare.RateLimit"]   // ✓
summary: `bynk.toml`'s `[unstable] allow` lists a path that names no standard-library unit, exported item or operation.

blurb: A `for all q: Quantity` property draws only valid values of `Quantity`, so a body that just asserts the type's refinement, `expect q > 0` over `Int where Positive`, cannot fail and proves nothing about your code. The compiler flags it. The check is narrow: it fires only when the body is that one `expect`, restating `Positive` or `NonNegative` over the bound value, so a near-copy may pass. Assert something about what your code does with the value, or delete the property.
summary: A `property` merely re-checks a refinement its type already guarantees.

blurb: A `where` clause on `for all` discards each generated input that fails it, so it must be a `Bool`. A filter of another type, such as an `Int`, cannot say whether to keep an input. Write a comparison over the bound variables.
example:
for all n: Int where n + 1 {   // ✗ an `Int`, not a `Bool`

for all n: Int where n > 0 {   // ✓
summary: A `for all ... where` filter does not type to `Bool`.

blurb: A provider calls an agent handler, and the handler needs a capability the provider's `given` does not list. A handler's `given` is widened to cover the agent handlers it calls, but a provider's is not. The provider is constructed with exactly the capabilities in its `given`, and those are all it can hand on to the agent. So the provider must list everything the agent handler needs: the handler's own `given`, and the `given` of any agent handler it calls in turn.
summary: A provider calls an agent handler that needs a capability the provider's `given` does not list.

blurb: A provider's `given` lists the capabilities it is built from, and the context builds providers in dependency order. A capability that depends on itself, directly or through other providers, has no order to be built in, so every provider on the cycle is reported. Break the cycle: remove a `given` one side does not really need, move the part both need into a third capability that each depends on, or merge the two if they are one thing. Dependencies on other contexts follow `consumes`, which has its own check, `bynk.context.consumes_cycle`.
summary: Providers form a capability dependency cycle through `given`.

blurb: A `provides` block offers the capability's operations and no others. Callers reach a provider only through the capability, so an operation it does not declare could never be called, and it usually means a misspelt name or an operation added to the wrong capability. Remove it, or declare it on the capability. A capability operation the provider omits is `bynk.provider.missing_operation`.
summary: A `provides` block implements an operation not in the capability.

blurb: A capability operation with its own type parameter, `fn dedup[T](…)`, can only be implemented by an external provider: a class written in TypeScript in an adapter's binding file. A provider with a Bynk body has no `T` to work with, so it could only return a value it was already given. Declare the capability in an `adapter` and give `provides` no body. An external provider inside a context is refused, as `bynk.context.external_provider`.
summary: A Bynk-bodied `provides` implements a capability operation that declares its own type parameter — only an external (bodiless) provider can.

blurb: A `provides` block implements a capability, so it must supply every operation the capability declares: callers are checked against the capability, and an operation the provider lacks would have nothing to run. The error is on the `provides` line and names the missing operation. Add it, with the signature the capability declares. An operation the capability does not declare is `bynk.provider.extra_operation`.
summary: A `provides` block is missing a capability operation.

blurb: A `provides` block says how a context's own capability is implemented, so it belongs in the context that declares the capability. A commons holds only pure declarations, with no effects to provide. Move the provider into the context. A `capability` in a commons is refused for the same reason, as `bynk.capability.outside_context`.
summary: `provides` was declared outside a context.

blurb: A provider operation must have the signature its capability declares: the same number of parameters, the same parameter types and the same return type. Callers are checked against the capability, so a provider that returns something else would hand them a value of the wrong type. The error points at the parameter or return type that differs, or at the operation when the counts differ. Change the provider to match, or change the capability, and with it every provider of it.
summary: A `provides` operation's signature does not match the capability.

blurb: A `provides` block implements a capability that the same context declares, and none of that name is declared here, so there is nothing to check the operations against. This is usually a misspelt name, or a capability that lives in another context: a provider cannot implement one from elsewhere. Declare the capability next to its provider, or correct the name.
summary: `provides` names a capability that does not exist.

blurb: `joinOn` and `leftJoin` pair up rows whose two keys are equal, and equality is only meaningful between values of one type. A `String` key on one side and an `Int` on the other can never match, so the join is refused. Change one key function so that both return the same type. A join on a condition rather than equal keys is `join`.
summary: A `joinOn`/`leftJoin` left and right key function return different types.

blurb: `sum` and `average` add the values the key function returns, so the key must be numeric: `Int`, `Float` or `Duration`, or a refined type over one of them. A `String` or a record cannot be added. Return a numeric field. `sum` also adds a `Decimal` key, exactly, on a `List` and on a `Query`. `average` does not take one: a mean is a division, and a `Decimal` division needs a scale and a rounding mode, so sum the key, then `div(Decimal.fromInt(n), scale, mode)` by the count. To pick by an ordering rather than add, `min`, `max` and `sortBy` accept any orderable key.
summary: A `sum`/`average` key function does not return a numeric type (`Int`, `Float`, or `Duration`; `sum` also takes a `Decimal`, `average` does not).

blurb: A queue consumer is invoked once per message, so `on message` takes exactly one parameter: the message, of any type that can be decoded from the queue body. Two parameters leave the second with nothing to supply it, and none leaves the handler without the message. Put what you need into the message type itself: a record with those fields is one parameter. Name the parameter `message` by convention.
summary: An `on message` handler does not take exactly one `message` parameter.

blurb: The context's `queue` entry point picks the handler by the queue's name. Two `on message` handlers for the same name would leave it with two to run. Merge them into one handler, or move one to a `from queue` service for another queue. The rule holds across the project too: Cloudflare accepts one consumer Worker per queue, so two contexts consuming one queue, in a `[deploy.workers]` group or not, could never both deploy. Move the queue to one context; any number of contexts may still send to it.
summary: Two `on message` handlers, in one context or in two, consume the same queue.

blurb: `from queue("…")` names a Cloudflare queue, so the name must be one Cloudflare accepts: 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits or `-`, starting and ending with a letter or digit. An empty name, capitals or `_` are refused here, rather than failing at deploy. Rename it, for example `order-events`.
summary: A `from queue("…")` binding has an empty queue name, or one Cloudflare refuses.

blurb: A queue consumer answers the queue, not a caller, and the only answers it understands are `Ack` (the message is handled) and `Retry(reason)` (deliver it again). The handler's return type is therefore fixed at `Effect[QueueResult]`, so a `Result` or a value cannot be mistaken for a verdict. Return `Ack` on success and `Retry` with a reason when the message should come back. The cron counterpart is `bynk.cron.return_not_effect_result`.
example:
on message(message: String) -> Effect[Result[Int, String]] { … }   // ✗ the queue needs a verdict

on message(message: String) -> Effect[QueueResult] { … }   // ✓ `Ack` or `Retry(…)`
summary: An `on message` handler does not return `Effect[QueueResult]`.

blurb: `race` hands the side that loses to the execution context, and an agent handler has none. Call it from the service handler that calls the agent, so the race is run from outside. The same rule holds for `bynk.within.in_agent_handler`.
summary: `a.race(b)` was used in an agent handler, which has no execution context to hand the losing effect to.

blurb: `race` starts two effects and hands the loser to the execution context, and only an effectful body has one: a pure function never runs an effect at all. Change the enclosing function's return type to `Effect[…]` so its body can run it. The same rule holds for `bynk.within.in_pure_context`.
summary: `a.race(b)` was used in a pure (non-effectful) context.

blurb: `race` hands the side that loses to the execution context, which only a service handler's body, or a function's it calls, has. A WebSocket handler, a provider operation and a test `case` have none. Move the `race` into a service handler or a function, and have the case call that, stubbing a slow side with `stub … after`. In an agent handler the rule is `bynk.race.in_agent_handler`.
summary: `a.race(b)` was used outside a service handler's body and outside a function (in a provider operation, a WebSocket handler or a test `case` body), where no execution context exists.

blurb: An override in a record spread must have the type its field declares. The spread produces a value of the record's type, and a field of another type would break that type, so the mismatch is refused at the override instead of surfacing later. Give the field a value of its declared type, converting explicitly where needed: nothing converts implicitly.
summary: A record-spread override has the wrong type for the field.

blurb: The base of a spread supplies the fields that are not overridden, so it has to be a value of a record type. An `Int`, a `List` or a sum value has no fields to copy. Spread a record, or build the record with every field written out. A base of a different record is `bynk.record_spread.type_mismatch`.
summary: The base of a record spread is not a record.

blurb: A spread, `T { ...base, x: 1 }`, copies the fields of `base` that you do not name, so the result has the base's own type. It cannot convert one record type to another, even one with the same fields, and a `T` that names a different type from the base's is refused. Write the base's type, or, to build a different record, give every field: `Point { x: s.x, y: s.y }`. A base that is not a record is `bynk.record_spread.non_record_base`.
summary: A record spread's base is a different record type.

blurb: A record spread, `T { ...base, field: value }`, copies every field of `base` and replaces the ones you list. Each listed field has to be one the record declares: a misspelt or invented name would otherwise be dropped silently, or build a value that is not a `T`. Check the field name against the type's declaration. To add a field, declare it on the type first.
summary: A record spread overrides a field the record does not have.

blurb: A literal written where a refined type is expected is checked at compile time, and this one does not satisfy the type's predicate. A refined type is a base type plus a rule (`InRange`, `NonEmpty`, …), and a literal that breaks the rule can never be a valid value, so the compiler rejects it instead of admitting it. Use a value that satisfies the predicate, or loosen the type. A value known only at run time goes through `.of`, which returns a `Result`.
summary: A literal does not satisfy the refined type's predicate.

`bynk login`, `bynk logout` or a `bynk org` command didn't go through: you aren't signed in or your session expired, the registry has no account API (or is read through a mirror), the sign-in was declined or its code expired, or the registry refused the request (a taken or reserved name, not the owner, an unknown member or token).
A registry archive is malformed or hostile: not a `bynk-tree-v1` stream, a path that is absolute or climbs out of the package, an out-of-order or repeated file, or past the size limits.
An index line isn't signed by a key the trusted key's rotation chain reaches, or its signed registry `id` or package `name` isn't the one asked for (a forged or replayed line).
A registry couldn't be read: unreachable, an error status, a refused or missing token, a redirect from https to http, too many redirects, or a response past the size limit.
A registry's keys don't lead from the key trusted for it (pinned in `[registries]`, or recorded in `bynk.lock`), or it now declares a different `id`.

`bynk registry conformance` found a registry breaking the protocol: a check failed (a wrong status, an unsigned or mis-signed line, a checksum that isn't the tree sent, a refusal without its JSON body, …); each failure names the check and the protocol section it holds the registry to.

`bynk publish` or `bynk yank` didn't go through: the project isn't a versioned package, it has a path or git dependency, its registry has no publish API (or is read through a mirror), or the registry refused the request (no or wrong token, an existing version, an invalid upload).
`bynk.lock` locks a package to one registry, but its organisation now routes to another; a misrouted organisation fails rather than resolving a same-named package elsewhere.

No registry serves a package: its organisation isn't listed by any `[registries]` entry (the first-party registry isn't live yet), the registry has no `config.json`, or it has no such package or archive.

blurb: Your `bynk.lock` locks a version that its registry has withdrawn. A withdrawal is a takedown — for a legal request or confirmed malware — so unlike a yank, which keeps a version for locked builds, the registry has deleted its archive and there is nothing to fetch. The message quotes the registry's reason. A machine that already has the tree in its store keeps building; elsewhere, move off the version with `bynk update` and the dependency's alias. The reason is unsigned, so when it was read through a mirror the message says the origin wasn't consulted.
example:
error[bynk.registry.withdrawn]: `acme/money` 1.4.2 was withdrawn by registry `acme-internal`: "removed at the copyright holder's request"
  = note: `bynk.lock` locks this version; choose another with `bynk update money`

$ bynk update money     # resolves to the newest version not withdrawn
summary: `bynk.lock` locks a registry version that its registry withdrew (a takedown: yanked, and its archive deleted), and its tree isn't in the store.

blurb: A project installs one version of each npm package, so every adapter that `requires` a package must give the same range for it. Two adapters that ask for `jose` at `^4` and `^5` leave the build with no version that satisfies both, so the second is refused and names the first. Ranges are compared as written, so `^5` and `^5.0.0` conflict too. The same code reports one adapter that lists a package twice at different ranges. Give both the same range. A package the toolchain itself pins, such as the one its own bindings use, must be required at that exact version.
summary: Two adapter `binding … requires { … }` entries give different version ranges for one npm package.

blurb: An adapter in a git or registry dependency requires an npm package your project hasn't approved. A dependency's adapters bring their npm packages into your build's `package.json`, and the next `npm install` runs whatever those packages run; so an npm package from someone else's code enters only after you approve it once. The approval is one package at one range, recorded in `bynk.lock` (`approved = true`), so a changed range asks again. Review the package (the note names the dependencies that brought it in), run `bynk approve jose`, and commit `bynk.lock`. Your own adapters and path dependencies need no approval.
example:
# bynk.lock, as a fetch wrote it — the build fails until approved
[[npm]]
package = "jose"
range = "^5.2.0"
required-by = ["acme/money:tokens"]

# after `bynk approve jose` — the build passes
[[npm]]
package = "jose"
range = "^5.2.0"
required-by = ["acme/money:tokens"]
approved = true
summary: A reached adapter of a git or registry dependency requires an npm package, at a range, that the project hasn't approved in `bynk.lock`; review it and run `bynk approve <package>`.

blurb: An adapter's `requires` states the npm versions its binding is written against, and the build installs exactly what it says. `*`, `x`, `latest` and a range with no digit in it accept whatever version is newest on the day, so two builds of the same source can differ. Name a range that has a version in it, such as `^5.2.0`.
example:
binding "./tokens.binding.ts" requires { "jose": "*" }        // ✗ any version at all

binding "./tokens.binding.ts" requires { "jose": "^5.2.0" }   // ✓ a pinned range
summary: An adapter `binding … requires { … }` entry has an unpinned version range.

blurb: A bare variant name such as `Failed("down")` builds a value of the sum that declares it. When two sums in scope declare the name (two of your own, or two that a consumed unit exports, like an adapter's error enums), the compiler reads the expected type: an annotated `let`, a parameter, a return type, or a `stub`'s operation. It builds the sum that type names. With nothing expecting either sum it cannot know which you meant, and it never picks one, so the name is refused. Qualify it as `TypeName.Variant`, or give the value a type. A `match` arm needs neither, because it reads its scrutinee's sum.
example:
type DbError = | Constraint(message: String) | Failed(message: String)
type MailError = | RateLimited | Failed(message: String)

let e = Failed("down")       // ✗ `DbError` or `MailError`?

fn mail() -> Result[Int, MailError] {
    Err(Failed("down"))          // ✓ the return type picks `MailError`
}

DbError.Failed("down")       // ✓ qualified
summary: A bare variant name is declared by several sum types in scope, and no expected type picks one.

blurb: A call to a declared `fn` must pass exactly as many arguments as it has parameters. Bynk has no optional or variadic parameters and fills nothing in, so a missing or extra argument is always a mistake, and the compiler cannot tell which one was meant. Add or remove the argument, or change the declaration. The error points at the call and labels the declaration. A call through a function value or a built-in operation is `bynk.types.call_arity`, and a method is `bynk.types.method_arity`.
summary: A function was called with the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: A constant's value is fixed when its module loads, so its initialiser must be static: a literal, a `Duration` literal, a record, list or variant built from static values, `Some`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`, `T.unsafe(lit)`, an empty `List`/`Map`/`Set`, or another constant. A function call (even a pure one), an operator, an interpolated string, a field access, a lambda, `if` and `match` are not. The code is also reported when a static value is not of the declared type. Write the value out, or make it a `fn` and call it where it is used.
summary: A `const` initialiser is not a static value of the declared type: only literals, constructors over static values, `T.unsafe(lit)`, `List.empty()`/`Map.empty()`/`Set.empty()`, `Duration` literals and references to other constants are allowed.

blurb: Constants may refer to each other in any order, across files and through `uses`, but a value cannot depend on itself: in a cycle no member has anything to start from. The error lists the cycle (`First` → `Second` → `First`) and is reported once, at the member declared first. Break the cycle by giving one member a literal or other static value. A reference such as `Second` is itself a static initialiser, so this is the only rule that limits constants naming each other; `bynk.resolve.bad_const_initialiser` covers initialisers that are not static at all.
example:
const First: Int = Second   // ✗ `First` → `Second` → `First`
const Second: Int = First

const Second: Int = 10   // ✓ end the chain at a literal
summary: Constants refer to each other in a cycle, so none of them has a value.

blurb: A constant is named in upper-camel case, a capital letter and then letters, digits or `_`, like a variant, so that a constant reads differently from a binding wherever it is used. The grammar accepts any identifier here and leaves the case to the checker, so a lower-case name is reported with a suggested spelling instead of failing to parse. Rename it, and every use of it: `MaxRetries`, not `maxRetries`.
example:
const maxRetries: Int = 3   // ✗ a constant's name starts with a capital

const MaxRetries: Int = 3   // ✓
summary: A constant's name is not upper-camel case (`MaxRetries`, not `maxRetries`).

blurb: An adapter is the program's boundary with the host: it declares capabilities and the providers a binding supplies, not values for the program to share, so a `const` is refused there. Declare the constant in a commons, which a unit reads by `uses`, or in the context that needs it, and move it out of the adapter.
summary: A `const` declaration appears outside a context or commons.

blurb: An actor is named by the `by` clause of a handler, and its name is one of the unit's top-level names, so two actors of one name leave a `by` with nothing to choose between. Rename one, or delete the repeat. The same holds for the other named declarations: `bynk.resolve.duplicate_service`, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_agent` and `bynk.resolve.duplicate_capability`.
summary: Two actors share a name.

blurb: An agent is addressed by its name, and the name is one of the unit's top-level names, so two agents of one name leave a call with nothing to choose between. Rename one, or delete the repeat. The same holds for the other named declarations: `bynk.resolve.duplicate_service`, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_actor` and `bynk.resolve.duplicate_capability`.
summary: Two agents share a name.

blurb: A capability is named by the `given` clauses that ask for it and by the calls made through it, and its name is one of the unit's top-level names, so two capabilities of one name leave those with nothing to choose between. Rename one, or delete the repeat. The same holds for the other named declarations: `bynk.resolve.duplicate_service`, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_agent` and `bynk.resolve.duplicate_actor`. A capability provided twice is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_provider`.
summary: Two capabilities share a name.

blurb: A constant is a value that every use of its name reads, so a name is declared once in a unit. With two `Limit`s, a use would have two values to read. Rename one, or delete the repeat. A constant whose name is a function's, a type's or another declaration's in the unit is `bynk.resolve.name_conflict`.
example:
const Limit: Int = 1
const Limit: Int = 2   // ✗ `Limit` is already declared

const Cap: Int = 2     // ✓ a different name
summary: Two constants share a name.

blurb: A record is built and read by field name, so each name may appear once in its declaration, and the same holds for the payload fields of one sum variant. A repeat usually means two different fields were intended: rename one, or remove it. A field set twice in a literal is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_field_init`.
example:
type Order = { id: Int, id: String }      // ✗ `id` declared twice

type Order = { id: Int, label: String }  // ✓ distinct names
summary: A record, or one variant's payload, declares a field twice.

blurb: A record literal gives each field one value. A field set twice leaves it unclear which value is meant, and is nearly always a pasted line or a misspelt name for the field that was meant. Remove the repeat, or correct the name. A field declared twice in the type is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_field`; a field left out of the literal is `bynk.resolve.missing_field`.
summary: A record construction initialises a field twice.

blurb: A function is called by its name, and Bynk has no overloading: two functions of one name in a unit, even with different parameters, would leave a call unable to say which it means. So a unit declares each function name once. Rename one of them. A suite's helpers repeat as `bynk.suite.duplicate_fn`, and a type's methods as `bynk.resolve.duplicate_method`.
summary: Two functions share a name.

blurb: A message code is the key `render` looks a template up by, so one block can give it only one text. A second entry under the same code leaves two templates for one key, and the second is refused. Delete the repeat, or give it a code of its own. The same code in different locale blocks is how a translation is written, and is not an error. A locale declared twice is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_message_locale`.
summary: A message bundle declares the same code twice in one block.

blurb: A `messages` block holds the templates for one locale, and `render(tag, msg)` picks the block by its tag. Two blocks for one tag leave it two sets of templates to choose from, so the second is refused. Merge them into one block, or correct the tag of the one meant for another language. A code repeated inside a block is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_message_code`.
summary: Two `messages` blocks in one bundle declare the same locale tag.

blurb: A method is looked up by its type and name, so `p.norm()` has to mean one body. A second `fn Point.norm` would leave the call with nothing to choose between. Delete the repeat, or give it a different name if it does something else.
summary: Two methods share a name.

blurb: A function's parameters are read by name in its body, and a call passes them in order, so each name may appear once in the list. A repeat is usually two different parameters meant, and the body could see only one of them. Rename one of the two, or remove it.
example:
fn area(w: Int, w: Int) -> Int { w * w }   // ✗ `w` declared twice

fn area(w: Int, h: Int) -> Int { w * h }   // ✓ distinct names
summary: A parameter name is repeated.

blurb: `provides Clock = …` is the one implementation a context supplies for `Clock`, and a handler that is `given Clock` is given that one. Two providers for the same capability leave it nothing to choose between, so the second is refused. Delete the one you do not want, or merge them into one provider. Declaring the capability itself twice is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_capability`.
summary: A capability is provided more than once.

blurb: A service is called by its name, and the name is one of the unit's top-level names, so two services of one name leave a call with nothing to choose between. Rename one, or delete the repeat. The same holds for the other named declarations: `bynk.resolve.duplicate_agent`, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_actor`, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_capability` and `bynk.resolve.duplicate_provider`, and for the entries of a message bundle, `bynk.resolve.duplicate_message_code` and `bynk.resolve.duplicate_message_locale`.
summary: Two services share a name.

blurb: A unit declares two types, or a type and an event, with the same name. A unit's top-level declarations share one scope in the emitted module, so a name can mean only one thing, and a type name appears in signatures and constructors with no way to say which declaration is meant. Rename one of them, or remove the repeated declaration. The check spans all of the unit's files, so the second declaration can be in a different file.
example:
type Money = Int
type Money = String          // ✗ `Money` is already declared

type Money = Int
type Label = String          // ✓ distinct names
summary: Two types share a name.

blurb: A sum value is identified by its variant name: in a `match` pattern, in a constructor, and as the `kind` of its JSON form. So each variant appears once in a type. A repeat is usually two different variants meant, or a line pasted twice. Rename one of them, or delete the repeat. A payload field repeated within one variant is `bynk.resolve.duplicate_field`.
example:
type Colour = | Red | Red     // ✗ `Red` declared twice

type Colour = | Red | Green   // ✓ distinct variants
summary: A sum type declares a variant twice.

blurb: A function's name on its own is the function, not its result. It is a value only where a function type is expected, such as an argument to `map`; anywhere else it is nearly always a forgotten call. Call it with its arguments, or pass it where a function is wanted.
summary: A function was referenced without being called.

blurb: A `let` may not reuse the name of a function declared in the unit. The name would mean the function in one place and the binding in another, and a reader could not tell which `total` is meant. Choose a different name for the binding. Reusing a type's name is `bynk.resolve.let_shadows_type`.
summary: A `let` binding shadows a function.

blurb: A `let` may not take the name of a declared type. The same name would then mean a type in one position and a value in another within one body, which is hard to read and easy to get wrong. Choose a different name for the binding, conventionally in lower case. Reusing a function's name is `bynk.resolve.let_shadows_fn`.
summary: A `let` binding shadows a type.

blurb: A method is declared on a type, as in `fn Order.total(self)`, and the type has to be declared in the same unit, so that every value of it can reach the method. A misspelt or missing type is the usual cause. Correct the name, or declare the type next to the method.
summary: A method is defined on an unknown type.

blurb: A record must be constructed with every field that has no default. There is no partial construction: a value of a record type is only valid once all its fields are present, so a downstream reader never has to wonder whether a field was set. Omitting a required field is therefore an error, not a fill-in-later. A field may be left out only when its declaration gives it a default, `field: T = expr`.
summary: A record construction omits a required field.

blurb: Two declarations of different kinds share a name. A unit's functions, assets, embeds, constants, types and events, services, agents and providers with a body (by their implementation name) all live in one namespace, across all of the unit's files, because they are one scope in the emitted module.
