Capabilities and actors each keep their own. Two types, or a type and an event, are `bynk.resolve.duplicate_type`, and two constants `bynk.resolve.duplicate_const`. Rename one of the two.
summary: Two declarations share a name.

blurb: `Name { field: value }` builds a record, so `Name` has to be a record type. A sum is built by naming one of its variants, and a refined type with `Name.of(value)`, which checks the value. A type that is opaque is its own error, `bynk.resolve.opaque_record_construction`.
example:
type Shape = | Circle | Square

fn make() -> Shape { Shape { side: 1 } }   // ✗ `Shape` is a sum, not a record

fn make() -> Shape { Circle }              // ✓ name a variant
summary: Record syntax was used on a non-record type.

blurb: An opaque type hides its representation so that nothing outside its own checks can produce a value of it, and a record literal `T { value: … }` would go round them. Build one with `T.of(value)`, which validates and returns a `Result`, or, inside the commons that defines the type, with `T.unsafe(value)`.
summary: An opaque type was constructed with record syntax.

blurb: Only a value of function type can be called. `n(5)` applies `n`, but `n` is an `Int`, so there is nothing to run. It is usually a missing operator or a parameter that was meant to be a function. Give the parameter a function type, such as `f: Int -> Int`, or drop the call. The check covers any local value, not only parameters.
summary: A value (such as a parameter) was called as a function.

blurb: A record cannot contain itself through record fields alone, whether directly (`next: Node` in `Node`) or round a cycle (`A` has a `B`, which has an `A`). A value of such a type could never be built, since making one needs one already, and the compiler could not synthesise the default value it needs for one. A cycle through an `Option`, `List`, `Map` or a sum type is fine, because that position can hold a value that ends the chain. Wrap one field in the cycle in `Option[…]`.
example:
type Node = { value: Int, next: Node }   // ✗ a `Node` would need a `Node`

type Node = { value: Int, next: Option[Node] }   // ✓ `None` ends the chain
summary: A record directly contains a field of its own type.

blurb: The compiler knows a few type names itself, and the type parser reads each one as the built-in wherever it appears in a type. A `type` declaration that reused one would be shadowed at every use, or fail confusingly there, so the declaration is refused. The names are `Asset`, `BoundaryRejection`, `Connection`, `History`, `HttpResult`, `List`, `Map`, `Query`, `QueueResult`, `RequestHeaders`, `RequestQuery`, `Set`, `Stream` and `TokenClaims`. Rename the type. They are reserved in type position only, so a value may still use the word. A constant with such a name is `bynk.resolve.name_conflict` instead, and the base types and words such as `Result` are keywords that the parser refuses earlier.
example:
type Set = { items: List[Int] }   // ✗ `Set` is the built-in set type

type IntSet = { items: List[Int] }   // ✓
summary: A type declaration reuses a compiler-known built-in type name.

blurb: The generated TypeScript reaches the host's built-in objects as `globalThis.<name>`, so a top-level declaration called `globalThis` (a type, function, agent, provider and so on) would hide all of them in its module. Rename the declaration. Parameters and local bindings may use the name: the compiler renames those itself.
example:
type globalThis = { n: Int }   // ✗ the name is reserved

type Counter = { n: Int }      // ✓ any other name
summary: A declaration is named `globalThis`, which the generated TypeScript uses to reach host globals.

blurb: A sum value is encoded as a flat JSON object whose `kind` field holds the variant's name, so a payload field called `kind` would collide with that tag. Rename the field, for instance to `category`.
example:
type Shape = | Circle(kind: String, r: Int) | Square(side: Int)   // ✗ `kind` is the variant tag

type Shape = | Circle(category: String, r: Int) | Square(side: Int)   // ✓ any other name
summary: A sum variant declares a payload field named `kind`, the variant's wire discriminant.

blurb: `self` is the value a method was called on, so it exists only in the body of a method, declared as `fn Type.name(self, …)`. A plain function has no receiver. Make the function a method of the type, or take the value as an ordinary parameter.
summary: `self` referenced outside a method or handler.

blurb: A type's name is not a function. A refined type is built with `.of(value)`, which checks the value and returns a `Result`, and a record with a literal such as `Order { … }`, so `Amount(5)` has no meaning to fall back on. A sum variant with a payload is the one exception: `Placed(at, total)` constructs it. A name that is not a type at all is `bynk.resolve.unknown_function`.
summary: A type name was called as if it were a function.

blurb: A type's name stands for a set of values, not for one, so it cannot be used where a value is expected. This is usually a missing constructor. Build a value in the type's own way: `Type { … }` for a record, a variant name for a sum, `Type.of(value)` for a refined type. A type used as a call, `Type(…)`, is `bynk.resolve.type_as_function`.
example:
type Metres = Int where NonNegative

fn grow(x: Int) -> Int { x + Metres }   // ✗ `Metres` is a type, not a value

fn grow(x: Int) -> Result[Metres, ValidationError] { Metres.of(x + 1) }   // ✓ build a `Metres`
summary: A type name was used where a value is expected.

blurb: A call such as `platform.pay.charge(1)` reaches into another context, and a context may only do that to one it has declared with `consumes`. The declaration is what makes a dependency between contexts visible and checked, instead of a name that happens to resolve. The same code is reported for a `given platform.pay.Cap` whose context is not consumed. Add `consumes platform.pay` (with an alias, if you want to call it by another name) at the top of the calling context. A consumed context that does not export a capability is `bynk.given.cross_context_unknown_capability`.
summary: A context's service was called, or its capability named in `given`, without a `consumes` declaration.

blurb: A record construction names a field the record type does not declare. A record's fields are fixed by its type declaration, and a literal may set only those. This is usually a typo in the field name, or a field meant for a different type. Reading a field a value does not have is the sibling code `bynk.types.unknown_field`.
summary: A record construction names a field the record type does not declare.

blurb: A call names a function that is not in scope. Only functions declared in the same unit, or brought in through `uses`, can be called; a capitalised name, which would construct an agent, needs an agent of that name in scope. This is most often a typo or a missing `uses`. A lambda cannot call itself through its own `let` name either, because the name is not bound until the lambda is built. A type used as a function, as in `Money(5)`, is the separate `bynk.resolve.type_as_function`.
summary: Called a function that does not exist.

blurb: A name was referenced that is not in scope. Every name in Bynk must be introduced before use — as a `let` binding, a parameter, a `fn`, a type, or a member brought in through `uses`/`consumes`. An unknown name is typically a typo, a missing declaration, or a reference to something defined in a module that has not been brought into scope.
example:
let greeting = "hi"
greetng          // ✗ no name `greetng` in scope
greeting         // ✓ the bound name
summary: Referenced a name that is not in scope.

blurb: A type was named with a `.` and a member it does not have. `T.name` refers to a variant of the sum type `T` or to a static method declared on it, and a misspelt variant has no such member. Some built-in types have a closed set: `HttpResult`, `ErrorStatus` and `RoundingMode` only their variants, `Float` only `parse`, `pi` and `e`, and `Decimal` only `parse` and `fromInt`. Check the spelling against the declaration, or declare the missing static method.
example:
type Colour =
    | Red
    | Green

Colour.Gren          // ✗ `Colour` has no variant `Gren`

Colour.Green         // ✓ the declared variant
summary: Referenced an unknown static member (e.g. `T.x`).

blurb: A type name was referenced that does not exist. Types must be declared (with `type`), be one of Bynk's built-in types, or be brought into scope from another module before they can be named. An unknown type is usually a typo or a missing declaration/import.
example:
fn greet(u: Usr) -> String { … }   // ✗ no type `Usr`
fn greet(u: User) -> String { … }  // ✓ the declared type
summary: Referenced a type that does not exist.

blurb: Agent state is stamped with the schema version of the build that wrote it, and older code faults with `NewerSchema` on records written by newer code. `bynk revert` therefore refuses to go back to a build with an older schema version while stored instances exist, while they are not known to be absent, or when the target is below the class's schema floor. The listing of stored objects lags a write by minutes, so within 30 minutes of the live deploy an empty listing counts as unknown. Deploy a fix forward instead.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  agent     Cart         refused: the target writes schema v1, the live version v2, and stored instances exist

bynk deploy   # fix forward
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the target writes an older agent schema version than the live one while stored instances exist, are not known to be absent, or the target is below the class's floor, so the older code would fault on newer records.

blurb: Cloudflare applies Durable Object class additions, removals and renames as migrations, and it cannot roll back across one. If the set of classes differs between the live version and the target, `bynk revert` refuses. Redeploy forward, with the class set you want, instead.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  classes   shop-orders  refused: the Durable Object classes differ between the two versions

bynk deploy   # redeploy forward
summary: `bynk revert` refused because a Durable Object class was added, removed or renamed between the live version and the target, and Cloudflare cannot roll back across a class migration.

blurb: Contexts call each other under contract hashes. Reverting one Worker can leave it expecting, or providing, a contract that another live Worker does not, and the runtime would refuse the calls. The check judges the result as if every selected Worker were reverted together, using the post-revert lock. Revert the whole project, or redeploy forward. See `bynk.deploy.contract_skew` for the same skew at deploy time.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run --context shop.orders
  contracts shop-orders  refused: the target no longer matches shop-payment

bynk revert   # the whole project, so the contexts revert together
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the target's contracts would no longer match another live Worker, judged as if every selected Worker were reverted together.

blurb: D1 migrations only move forward. If the live version applied a migration the target was not built against, the older code would meet a schema it was never written for. Bynk cannot judge a migration's SQL, so it refuses. If every such migration is additive, assert it per database with `--accept-schema-ahead <binding>`; otherwise deploy a fix forward. The same refusal is given when the applied migrations could not be read, because an unread list is never taken to be empty.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  d1        DB           refused: the live version applied 0003_add_index.sql after the target was built

bynk revert --accept-schema-ahead DB   # only if each such migration is additive
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the live version applied D1 migrations the target was not built against, or the applied migrations could not be read; migrations only move forward, so the older code may not run on the newer schema.

blurb: `bynk revert` reads the deploy facts that every `bynk deploy` records on the Worker version it pushes. Without them on both the live version and the target it cannot tell what changed in between, and every unknown is a refusal. A version deployed before facts were recorded, or one pushed outside Bynk, has none. Redeploy the version you want from its tag with `git checkout <tag> && bynk deploy`.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  facts     shop-orders  refused: the target version records no deploy facts

git checkout v1.4.0 && bynk deploy   # redeploy the previous tag instead
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the live version or the target version carries no deploy facts (`BYNK_DEPLOY_FACTS`), or the facts could not be read, so nothing can be checked against them.

blurb: `bynk revert` finds the target in the Worker's deployment history: by default the deployment before the live code's own upload, or the version named by `--to`. It refuses that Worker when it cannot place the live version or the target: a Worker first added in the bad release has nothing before it, the live upload is out of the listed history, a gradual deployment is in progress, or the history could not be read. A version made live outside Bynk has no upload deployment to step back from; name the version to go back to with `--to`. The plan still judges the other Workers.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run --context shop.orders
  history   shop-orders  refused: the live version is a gradual deployment

bynk revert --context shop.orders --to <version>
summary: `bynk revert` refused for one Worker because its deployment history cannot be placed: it has no earlier deployment, the live upload is outside the listed history, a gradual deployment is in progress, or the history could not be read.

blurb: The target version binds resources (KV namespaces, databases, limiters, Hyperdrive configs) by id. If the deploy lock no longer records the same id for a binding, the resource was re-provisioned or replaced since, and the older code would bind one that is no longer yours, or one `--prune` has deleted. `bynk revert` refuses. Redeploy forward.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  ids       shop-orders  refused: the target would bind a resource that has since been replaced

bynk deploy   # redeploy forward
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the target binds a KV namespace, database, limiter or Hyperdrive config that the deploy lock no longer records, usually because the resource was re-provisioned or replaced since.

blurb: A layout is how an agent's state is placed in storage, and each version's deploy facts record which one it writes. Code that writes an older layout than the live version cannot read records in the newer one: a build with the layout check faults them as `NewerLayout`, and one without it would orphan their entries. `bynk revert` refuses while stored instances exist or are not known to be absent. Deploy a fix forward.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  layout    Cart         refused: the target writes layout 1, the live version writes layout 2, and stored instances exist

bynk deploy   # fix forward
summary: `bynk revert` refused because the target writes an older agent storage layout than the live one while stored instances exist or are not known to be absent, so the older code could not read the newer records.

blurb: A `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group is one Worker script, so `bynk revert` puts every member back together. It refuses to go back to a version that held other contexts than the live one: a context that has moved into or out of the group since, or a version deployed before groups. Rolling back would take a member's code out from under its traffic. Redeploy forward instead.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run --worker core
  members   core  refused: the live version holds [shop.a, shop.b] and the target holds [shop.a]

bynk deploy   # redeploy forward
summary: `bynk revert` refused because a `[deploy.workers.<key>]` group's target version held other contexts than the live one (a context moved into or out of the group since, or the version predates groups), so a rollback would take a member's code out of the Worker.

blurb: A rollback can restore the old value of a secret that was rotated after the target was live, and its peers no longer accept that value. `bynk revert` counts the secret changes between the target and now and refuses if there are any. After a `bynk migrate sweep`, whose two changes touch only its own temporary key, pass `--accept-secret-changes`. A secret rotated before the release you are leaving is kept and does not count.
example:
bynk revert --dry-run
  secrets   shop-orders  refused: 2 secret change(s) since the target

bynk revert --accept-secret-changes   # only after a `bynk migrate sweep`
summary: `bynk revert` refused because a secret changed after the target was live, so the rollback could restore an old secret value that its peers no longer accept.
A `bynk.Secrets` read names its secret with a computed expression rather than a literal, so `bynk deploy` cannot plan it (warning).

blurb: A service with no `from` clause is called by its name, `svc.call(…)`, so it has one entry: exactly one `on call` handler. A second would never run, since only one of the two can answer the call. To offer a second operation, declare a second service.
summary: A service declares more than one `on call` handler; it has exactly one.

blurb: A service with no `from` clause is a call service, and admits only `on call` handlers; the protocol in the header is what says how a handler is invoked. A handler of another form needs its protocol named: `from http` for a route, `from cron`, `from queue("…")`, `from websocket(…)` or `from Events(E)`. The error suggests the one that fits the handler. If the service really is a mix, split it (see `bynk.service.mixed_protocols`).
summary: A `from`-less service has a handler other than `on call`.

blurb: A service is one protocol adapter: with `from http`, `from cron`, `from queue(…)`, `from websocket(…)` or `from Events(E)` it admits only handlers of that form, and one that does not match is refused. Declare a service per protocol. A handler in a service with no `from` at all is `bynk.service.missing_from`.
summary: A service mixes handler forms that do not match its `from <protocol>`.

blurb: A `service` is a context's entry point: a call, a route, a schedule, a queue consumer, a socket. A `commons` holds only shared types and pure functions, and has no context to serve from. Move the service into a context. Logic it shares can stay in the commons, which the context then `uses`.
example:
commons shop

service probe { … }   // ✗ a commons holds no entry points

context shop

service probe { … }   // ✓
summary: A `service` was declared outside a context.

blurb: Every service handler returns an `Effect[T]`, whatever its protocol. A handler runs as the context answers a call, route, schedule, message or frame, and its effects and `given` capabilities are the runtime's to run, so a bare `Int` is refused. Wrap the result: `Effect.pure(x)` for a value you already hold. An `on event` handler that returns an `Effect` of anything but `()` is `bynk.event.return_not_effect_unit`.
summary: A service handler's return type is not an `Effect`.

blurb: The protocol after `from` is one of a closed set: `http`, `cron`, `queue`, `websocket` or `Events`. Kafka and MQTT are transports, not protocols: use `from queue("…")` and bind the broker at the platform layer. A service with no `from` takes `on call` handlers.
example:
service worker from kafka {                // ✗ not a protocol

service worker from queue("jobs") {        // ✓ the queue protocol
summary: A `from <protocol>` names an unknown protocol (e.g. a transport like Kafka).

blurb: A `via` clause narrows which events an `Events` subscriber receives, and the only form is `via schema(N)`, which selects by the event's schema version. The set of `via` clauses is closed, so any other word after `via` is refused. Use `via schema(N)` or drop the clause. A malformed argument to `schema` itself is `bynk.event.bad_schema_dispatch`.
summary: A `via <name>(...)` clause on a `from Events(...)` header named something other than `schema` — `via` clauses are a closed set, and only `via schema(...)` exists today.

blurb: A WebSocket service names its two frame types in the header, `from websocket(in: ClientFrame, out: ServerFrame)`: `in` is what the server decodes from the client and `out` is what it sends back. The labels are fixed and in that order, so the compiler can tell the two apart without guessing from the handlers. Spell them `in:` then `out:`.
summary: The `from websocket` header is malformed — it binds frame types as `websocket(in: <type>, out: <type>)` (real-time track slice 3).

blurb: A WebSocket upgrade reaches the context by its `Upgrade: websocket` header alone, with no path to tell two endpoints apart, so a context can host only one `from websocket` service. The compiler reports every one but the first by name. Keep one, or move the other into a context of its own.
summary: A context holds more than one `from websocket` service — at v1 the Workers upgrade routes by the `Upgrade: websocket` header alone, so one WebSocket service per context (real-time track slice 3b).

blurb: A WebSocket service has exactly one `on open`, the handler that accepts the upgrade and receives the connection, and at most one `on message` and one `on close`. A service with no `on open` could never accept a client, and a second of any handler would leave it unclear which one runs. Add the missing `on open`, or remove the duplicate.
summary: A `from websocket` service must hold exactly one `on open` handler (the edge upgrade), and at most one `on message` (inbound) and one `on close` (real-time track slice 3/3b-iii).

blurb: An `on open` parameter is read from the upgrade request's query string, so it arrives as text, and the compiler builds it with the type's constructor from a `String`. A type that cannot be built from a string, such as `Int`, has no safe way in: a stray `?room=05` would name a different value from `5`. Declare the parameter as a `String`, a refined `String` or an opaque type over `String`, and parse any number in the body. HTTP path parameters follow the same rule, as `bynk.http.path_param_not_stringy`.
summary: A `from websocket` service's `on open` parameter has a type not constructible from `String`; it arrives as a query-string value (#1657).
A `bynk.set` free function is deprecated in favour of the `Set` method form (warning; auto-fixable).

blurb: Some standard-library items are experimental: they may change or disappear in any release, and the compatibility promise does not cover them. Using one is an error until the project opts in, so that relying on it is a choice someone made and can find. Add the item's path, as the error gives it, to `allow` under `[unstable]` in `bynk.toml`, or avoid the item. An entry that names no standard-library item is `bynk.project.unstable_unknown_item`.
summary: An experimental standard-library item is used without an `[unstable] allow` entry in `bynk.toml` covering it.

blurb: Each storage annotation is for one kind of store: `@ttl` for a `Cache`, `@retain` for a `Log` and `@indexed` for a `Map`. On any other kind it has nothing to act on: a `Map` has no expiry, for one. Move the annotation to a field of the kind it belongs to, or change the field's kind if that is what you meant.
example:
store sessions: Map[String, Int] @ttl(30.minutes)     // ✗ `@ttl` is for a `Cache`

store sessions: Cache[String, Int] @ttl(30.minutes)   // ✓
summary: A storage annotation is used on a kind it does not apply to (e.g. `@ttl` on a `Map`).

blurb: A storage annotation has a fixed set of kinds it applies to and a meaning that arrives in stages. `@bounded` is recognised on `Queue` and `Log`, but nothing acts on it yet, so it is refused rather than accepted and ignored. Leave it off. To limit a `Log`, use `@retain`, which drops entries older than a period. A known annotation on the wrong kind is `bynk.store.annotation_kind_mismatch`.
example:
store trail: Log[Event] @bounded(100)     // ✗ `@bounded` is recognised but has no effect yet

store trail: Log[Event] @retain(30.days)   // ✓ keep 30 days of entries
summary: A known storage annotation that nothing acts on yet (`@bounded`) is used; the others (`@ttl`, `@retain`, `@indexed`) are functional.

blurb: A `Cache` entry expires, and every operation on it but `remove` reads the clock to decide whether an entry is still live. So a handler that uses a `Cache` must declare `given Clock`, the same way one that reads the time itself would; the dependency is explicit even though the body never names the clock. Add `given Clock` to the handler's signature.
summary: A handler performs a `Cache` operation (TTL expiry reads the clock) without declaring `given Clock`.

blurb: A `Cache` is a keyed store whose entries expire, so it needs `@ttl(<duration>)`, how long an entry lives. Without an expiry it would only be a `Map`. The argument must be a `Duration` literal such as `5.minutes`; a bare number (`@ttl(5)`) or a computed value is refused too, because the lifetime has to be known when the program compiles. Add the annotation, or declare a `Map` if entries should be kept until removed.
example:
store live: Cache[String, Int]   // ✗ no lifetime for the entries

store live: Cache[String, Int] @ttl(5.minutes)   // ✓

const Life: Duration = 5.minutes
store quick: Cache[String, Int] @ttl(Life)   // ✓ a `Duration` constant bound to a literal
summary: A `Cache` field is missing its required `@ttl(<duration>)` annotation (a keyed store with no expiry is a `Map`).

blurb: Each storage kind takes a fixed number of type arguments: `Cell[T]`, `Set[T]` and `Log[T]` take one, and `Map[K, V]` and `Cache[K, V]` take two. The checker reads the arguments by position, so a wrong count cannot be guessed at and is refused where the field is declared. Give the kind the arguments it takes. To keep a key with a value use `Map`, and to hold a single value use `Cell[T]`.
example:
store total: Cell[String, Int]   // ✗ a `Cell` takes one type argument

store total: Cell[Int]   // ✓ one
summary: A storage kind was applied to the wrong number of type arguments (e.g. `Cell[A, B]`).

blurb: `Queue` is a recognised storage kind but is not yet implemented. The working kinds are `Cell`, `Map`, `Set`, `Log` and `Cache`, so a `store` of any other known kind is refused. Use one of them: an append-only `Log` is the closest to a queue. A name that is no storage kind at all is `bynk.store.unknown_kind`.
example:
store pending: Queue[Event]                 // ✗ not yet supported

store pending: Log[Event] @retain(30.days)   // ✓ an append-only sequence
summary: A known storage kind (`Queue`) is used before the slice that supports it.

blurb: `Log.append` stamps each entry with the time it was written, so it reads the clock and the handler has to declare `given Clock`. The window reads (`since`, `before`, `between`) take explicit `Instant`s and need no clock. Add `given Clock` to the handler that appends.
summary: A handler calls `Log.append` (which stamps the current time) without declaring `given Clock`.

blurb: A store `Map` or `Cache` key, or a store `Set` element, must be `String`, `Int` or a refined or opaque type over them. A store collection is saved as a JSON object keyed by the key's string form, and a record has no stable string form, so it cannot be a key (a composite key is not supported yet). Key by one of the record's id fields, or by an enum's name as a `String`. A value `Map` or `Set` follows a wider rule, `bynk.types.not_keyable`.
summary: A store `Set` element or `Map`/`Cache` key is not value-keyable — it must be `String`, `Int`, or a refined/opaque type over them (#1680).

blurb: A `store` field takes one of four annotations: `@indexed`, `@ttl`, `@retain` and `@bounded`. The set is closed, so a name outside it, usually a misspelling or one borrowed from another system, is refused rather than ignored. Use the annotation that says what you mean: `@retain` for how long a `Log` keeps entries, `@ttl` for a `Cache`. A known one on the wrong kind is `bynk.store.annotation_kind_mismatch`.
example:
store audit: Log[String] @keep(7.days)     // ✗ not a storage annotation

store audit: Log[String] @retain(7.days)   // ✓ how long a `Log` keeps entries
summary: A `store` field carries an annotation outside the closed `@indexed`/`@ttl`/`@retain`/`@bounded` set.

blurb: The type of a `store` field names a storage kind, which says how the state is persisted and which operations it has; it is not an ordinary type. The kinds are `Cell`, `Map`, `Set`, `Log` and `Cache`; `Queue` is reserved but not yet supported (`bynk.store.kind_unsupported`). A `List` or a record is not one, because nothing would say how to read or update it atomically. Pick the kind that matches how you use the data: `Set` for membership, `Map` for lookup by key, `Log` to append, `Cell` for one value.
example:
store tags: List[String]   // ✗ `List` is not a storage kind

store tags: Set[String]   // ✓ a storage kind
summary: A `store` field's type is not a known storage kind.

blurb: A `store Map` field is read as a lazy query through exactly three accessors: `.entries` (each a `MapEntry` with `.key` and `.value`), `.keys` and `.values`. Any other name after the field is refused. Its effectful operations, such as `put` and `get`, are method calls, not accessors. Use one of the three, or call an operation. A wrong method name on a store is `bynk.store.unknown_op`.
example:
store items: Map[String, Item]

items.names.collect()   // ✗ a `Map` has no `.names`

items.keys.collect()   // ✓ the keys, as a query
summary: A `store Map` field access is not one of its query accessors (`entries`/`keys`/`values`).

blurb: A `store` field's methods are its storage operations, which are effectful (await with `<-`), and each kind has a fixed set. `Map` and `Cache` take `put`, `get`, `update`, `upsert`, `remove`, `contains` and `size` (a `Map` also takes query operations); `Set` takes `add`, `remove`, `contains` and `size`; a `Cell` takes only `update`, being read by name and written with `:=`; a `Log` takes `append` and lazy query reads. Any other name is refused, even one the same type has as a plain value. For a read-modify-write use `update`, or `upsert` when the key may be absent. A wrong key query (`.entries`, `.keys`, `.values`) is `bynk.store.unknown_map_accessor`.
example:
let _ <- counts.increment("k")   // ✗ a `Map` store has no `increment`

let _ <- counts.upsert("k", 1, (v) => v + 1)   // ✓ add one, starting from 1
summary: A method called on a `store` field (`Map`, `Cache`, `Set`, `Cell` or `Log`) is not one of that kind's storage operations.

blurb: `stub … returns <value> after <delay>` makes the stubbed call complete only once the harness clock has advanced by that delay, so the delay must be a `Duration`, such as `3.seconds`. A bare number has no unit, so it is refused rather than guessed at as milliseconds or seconds.
summary: A test `stub … returns <value> after <d>` latency is not a `Duration`.

blurb: At the `system` tier each context runs as the Worker it deploys as, and that Worker builds its own capability providers, so there is no seam for a `stub` to override. A `stub` there would be accepted and then ignored, so it is refused. Move the case to a suite below `system`, where a `stub` replaces the seam, or remove the stub and test the real provider.
summary: A test `stub` is in a `system`-tier case, or at the scope of a `suite … as system` (or a suite whose cases run `as system`); each context runs as the Worker it deploys as, which builds its own capability providers, so there is no seam to override.

blurb: `returns each […]` gives one outcome per call, in order, and the last outcome repeats once the list runs out. An empty list has no outcome to repeat, so the first call would have nothing to return. List at least one. To return an empty list as a single value, write `returns []`, without `each`.
summary: A `stub … returns each […]` sequence is malformed (e.g. empty).

blurb: A `stub` gives an operation a fixed answer, but an operation with its own type parameter, `fn dedup[T](…)`, answers in whatever type the caller names, and a fixed value cannot be that. Such an operation cannot be stubbed. Test through the capability's real provider, and stub the other, non-generic operations of the capability if you need to.
summary: A test `stub` targets a capability operation that declares its own type parameter — not supported at v1.

blurb: A `stub` substitutes one of the capabilities the unit under test depends on: one the context declares, or reaches through a `consumes`. Any other name, including a misspelt one, leaves nothing to substitute. A commons has no capabilities, so it cannot be stubbed at all. Name a capability of the target, or add the `consumes` it needs. See `bynk.stub.unknown_op` for a wrong operation.
summary: A test `stub` overrides a capability the unit under test does not consume.

blurb: A `stub … returns <value>` stands in for a real provider, so the value must have the type the operation declares, as the real result would. `Meter.read` yields an `Int`, so it returns `7`, not a string; the `Effect` is supplied for you. Change the value, or stub the operation you meant. To inject a failure, write `fails` instead of a value.
summary: A test `stub … returns <value>` right-hand side does not match the operation's return type.

blurb: `stub Cap.op(…)` overrides one operation of a capability, so `op` must be declared by that capability. A misspelt or renamed operation matches nothing, so the stub is refused instead of leaving the default provider in place unannounced. Use the operation name the capability declares. See `bynk.stub.not_a_seam` when the capability itself is the wrong one.
summary: A test `stub` names an operation the capability does not declare.

blurb: A suite's cases see the target's own declarations and those of the commons it `uses`, and the suite's constants are used by bare name beside them. A suite constant with one of those names, or with that of a sum variant in scope, would silently change which value a mention reaches, so it is refused instead of shadowing. Rename it. A type clashing is `bynk.suite.type_name_clash`.
summary: A suite `const` has the name of a declaration or sum variant already in scope in the suite's cases.

blurb: A case is identified by its description in the runner's output and in failure reports, so each description must be unique across the suites that test one unit. Two cases with the same description cannot be told apart. Rename one; the error is on the repeat, with a label at the first.
summary: Two `case`s share a description.

blurb: A suite's constants are used by bare name in its cases, so a suite declares each name once: a second `const Limit` would leave `Limit` meaning two values. A `const` named like one of the suite's `type`s counts as a repeat too. Rename one. The same holds for a suite's types, as `bynk.suite.duplicate_type`, and for helper functions, as `bynk.suite.duplicate_fn`.
example:
const Limit: Int = 5
const Limit: Int = 9    // ✗ `Limit` again
const Cap: Int = 9      // ✓ a name each
summary: A suite declares two `const`s of the same name, or a `const` with the name of one of its `type`s.

blurb: An `env` clause gives a variable one value in its scope, so naming it twice in the same suite or the same case leaves two values and no way to choose. Keep one. A case's own `env` may still override a name its suite gives; only a repeat within one scope is refused.
summary: An `env { … }` clause gives the same name twice at one scope (a suite's `env` clauses, or one case's); a case's `env` may override a suite's name, but not repeat its own.

blurb: A case calls a suite helper by its bare name, so two helpers of one suite with one name would leave the call ambiguous. Give each a distinct name; the error is on the repeat. The same holds for a suite's types and constants: see `bynk.suite.duplicate_type` and `bynk.suite.duplicate_const`.
summary: A suite declares two helper `fn`s of the same name.

blurb: A suite's types are used by their bare names in its cases, so a suite declares each name once: a second `type Counted` would leave `Counted` meaning two shapes. Rename one. The same holds for a suite's constants, as `bynk.suite.duplicate_const`, and for helper functions, as `bynk.suite.duplicate_fn`.
summary: A suite declares two `type`s of the same name.

blurb: A `system` suite runs the participants as Workers, and an `env` entry is put on each Worker's `env`, beside the bindings that Worker already has: a Service Binding, a KV namespace, a Durable Object namespace, and the keys the test harness sets itself, such as a call edge's key or a foreign caller's secret. An entry with one of those names would replace the binding, so the compiler refuses it. Rename the variable. In this example `shop.ledger` consumes `Kv`, so its Worker already has a binding named `KV`.
summary: A `system`-tier suite's or case's `env` names a binding a participant's Worker already declares (a Service Binding, KV namespace, or Durable Object namespace), or a key the test harness sets on it (a call-edge key, a `Foreign` caller's secret), so the entry would clash with it on the Worker's `env`.

blurb: A Worker's variables and secrets are strings, so an `env` entry's value must be a `String` literal, `NAME = "value"`, or the name of a `fixture` the same suite declares. A number, a call or any other expression is refused, since the value is fixed when the suite is compiled. Write it as a string, and parse a number in the code that reads it.
summary: An `env { … }` entry's value is neither a `String` literal nor a `fixture` the same suite declares; a Worker's variables and secrets are strings, given verbatim.

blurb: A suite helper is a pure function that builds a value for a case: a request, a fixture, an expected result. Returning an `Effect` would hide a step of the test inside a helper. Build the value in the helper and run the effect in the `case`, where each step is visible with `<-`.
example:
// tests/desk.test.bynk
fn bump(n: Int) -> Effect[Int] { local.call(n) }   // ✗ returns an `Effect`
fn start() -> Int { 1 }                            // ✓ build the value
let n <- local.call(start())                       // ✓ run it in the case
summary: A suite helper `fn` returns an `Effect`; suite helpers are pure.

blurb: A suite helper is a plain function its cases call by name, so it is a free `fn`, not a method (`fn Type.name`). A method belongs to its type: declare it in the target or in a commons. In a suite, take the value as an ordinary parameter.
summary: A suite helper `fn` is a method (`fn Type.name`); suite helpers are free functions.

blurb: A suite helper is called by bare name from the suite's cases, which also see the target's declarations (services and agents included) and those of the commons it `uses`. A helper with one of those names would silently change which function a call reaches, so it is refused instead of shadowing. A fixture of the suite counts too, and `deps` and names beginning `__` are reserved for the runner. Rename the helper. A type or constant clashing is `bynk.suite.type_name_clash` or `bynk.suite.const_name_clash`.
summary: A suite helper `fn` has the name of a declaration already in scope in the suite's cases.

blurb: A suite's `type` is a plain shape that only its tests care about, such as a row to read back with `select[T]`, so it takes no type parameters. If you need a generic type, declare it in the target or in a commons, where the suite can use it. Otherwise write the concrete type.
summary: A suite declares a generic `type`; a suite type is a plain, non-generic shape.

blurb: A suite's cases see the target's own declarations and those of the commons it `uses`, and the suite's types are used by bare name beside them. A suite type with one of those names would silently change which type a mention reaches, so it is refused instead of shadowing. The same goes for a variant of a suite's own sum type. Rename it. A constant clashing is `bynk.suite.const_name_clash`.
summary: A suite `type`, or a variant of one, has the name of a declaration or sum variant already in scope in the suite's cases, or of another suite item.

blurb: A `suite` names the commons or context it tests, by its full dotted name, and that unit must be declared in the project. A name that matches none, usually a typo or a unit not written yet, would leave the suite testing nothing. Correct the name, or declare the unit.
summary: A `suite` targets a unit that does not exist.

blurb: The `browser` platform builds a module that runs in a web page: one in-process bundle, with nothing to deploy. The `workers` target lays a project out as one Cloudflare Worker per context, joined by Service Bindings, which a browser cannot run. So the two do not combine. Build for the browser with the `bundle` target, which is the default, or build Workers for the `cloudflare` platform.
example:
bynk build --target workers --platform browser   // ✗ Workers are not a browser build

bynk build --target bundle --platform browser    // ✓
summary: The `browser` platform builds only the in-process `Bundle` topology; `--target workers` is not a browser build.
One deployment unit's in-process closure uses platform-native capabilities from two mutually-exclusive platforms.
A deployment unit uses a platform-native capability but the build selects another `--platform`.

blurb: An actor that declares an `identity` stands for one particular caller, and the handler reads that identity. A case that acts as the actor must therefore say which caller, as in `by User("bob")`; a bare `by User` leaves the handler nothing to read. A handler that binds its caller (`by c: Caller`) wants the calling context's name the same way. Add the identity. The reverse mistake is `bynk.test.actor_no_identity`.
summary: A test omits the identity an identity-carrying actor requires: a bare call-site `by <Actor>`, or no `by` at all on a handler that binds its `Caller`.

blurb: A case supplies an identity only when the actor has one to give. An actor that declares no `identity`, and the failure principals `Nobody`, `Forged`, `Stale` and `Expired`, which present a missing or bad credential and so no verified caller, take no argument. Write `by Nobody`, not `by Nobody("bob")`. For an actor that does declare an identity and is given none, see `bynk.test.actor_identity_required`.
summary: A call-site `by <Actor>(x)` supplies an identity to an actor that takes none — a unit-identity actor (e.g. `Visitor`) or `Nobody`.

blurb: `advance` moves the harness clock, the single time source a test owns, so it names `Clock` and nothing else. No other capability has virtual time to move. To shape what another capability returns, use a `stub`. The clock only moves forward.
summary: An `advance` statement names a capability other than `Clock`; the test harness owns one time source, the first-party `Clock`.

blurb: `advance Clock by <amount>` moves the harness clock forward by a `Duration`. A bare number does not say what unit it counts, so it is refused. Write a duration literal such as `5.minutes`. See `bynk.test.advance_not_clock` for naming a capability other than `Clock`.
summary: An `advance Clock by` statement's amount is not a `Duration`.

blurb: `advance Clock by …` moves the harness clock, which only a `case` owns. A `property` runs its body once per generated input and has no clock of its own, and non-test code reads real time. Put the time-dependent step in a `case`. `bynk.test.advance_not_clock` and `bynk.test.advance_not_duration` cover the other ways to get `advance` wrong.
summary: An `advance Clock by` statement appears outside a test `case` body; only the test harness has a clock to move.

blurb: An asset is served by the platform before the Worker runs, and only to `GET`: it answers every other method with `405`. A case fetches one with `api.GET(asset)`, and a different method is refused, since the answer would be the platform's `405` and nothing your code decides. Use `GET`, and pass the asset alone. A `by` clause on the fetch is `bynk.test.principal_on_asset`.
summary: A suite fetches an asset with a method other than `GET`; the platform serves assets to `GET` and answers other methods with 405.

blurb: A service with an `on call` handler is internal to a deployment: it has no public route, and a `system` case can only send requests through the Worker's front door. So `svc.call(…)` is refused in one. Call it at `unit` or `integration`, or drive an http route that reaches it. For the event equivalent, see `bynk.test.event_needs_in_process`.
summary: A `system`-tier case calls an `on call` service with `svc.call(…)`; an `on call` service is internal to a deployment and has no public route for a `system` case to drive, so the case drives an `http` route that reaches it, or calls it at `unit` or `integration`.
A case drives `by Nobody` (the no-credential principal, which tests the auth seam's 401) outside a `system`-tier case, where there is no real seam to reject it.

blurb: `svc.event(e)` hands an event straight to a subscriber. At `system`, an event reaches a subscriber only through its publisher's fan-out across the deployed Workers, so there is no direct delivery to make. Drive the handler that publishes the event, or deliver the event at `unit` or `integration`. For the `on call` equivalent, see `bynk.test.call_needs_in_process`.
summary: A `system`-tier case delivers an event with `svc.event(e)`; at `system` an event reaches a subscriber only through its publisher's fan-out, so the case drives the emitting handler instead, or delivers the event at `unit` or `integration`.

blurb: `svc.event(e)` delivers an event through the handler the service subscribes with, so it takes the one event named in the service's `from Events(E)` header. Delivering a different event would test a path the service does not have. Pass the subscribed event, or test the service that does subscribe to the one you meant.
summary: A test body's `svc.event(e)` delivers an event the `from Events(E)` service does not subscribe to.

blurb: `svc.event(e)` delivers an event in a default envelope, whose `publisherId` is the context that publishes the event to the target: its own, or the one context it consumes that declares it. When two consumed contexts both declare the event there is no single publisher to name, so the case must build the envelope itself. Pass `svc.event(e, env)`, with an `EventEnvelope` whose `publisherId` names the one you mean; the target must consume `EventEnvelope` from `bynk`.
summary: A test body's `svc.event(e)` omits the envelope, but the event's publisher, which the default envelope names, is not one context the target declares or consumes.

blurb: `by Expired` sends an expired token, so it needs a route whose seam checks one: a `Bearer` or `Oidc` actor. A public route, or one guarded by a `Signature` actor, has no token to expire; for a `Signature` route `by Stale` sends a stale signature. Drive a route guarded by a `Bearer` or `Oidc` actor. See `bynk.test.nobody_needs_secured_route` for the same limit on `Nobody`.
summary: A case drives `by Expired` at an address that is not an http route with a `Bearer` actor (alone, or as a member of an actor sum) or an `Oidc` actor; it sends a correctly signed token whose `exp` has passed, so only a `Bearer` or `Oidc` seam can refuse it.

blurb: A case sends a credential only through its `by` clause: the driver builds the `Authorization` header (or the signature headers) from the actor it acts as. Sending an `Authorization` header as an extra request header, in `RequestHeaders.of`, would give the request two competing credentials, so it is refused. Choose the actor with `by`, and keep `RequestHeaders` for other headers.
summary: A `system` case sends `Authorization` as an extra request header to a route that declares no `headers:` parameter; the case's `by <Actor>` owns the credential the driver sends.

blurb: `expect <call> faults` claims that a handler throws. At `system` a fault reaches the case as an error response from the deployed Worker, not a throw, so claim it at `unit` or `integration`, or assert the response. A claim driven `by Nobody`, `Forged` or `Stale` fails at every tier: only a `system` case reaches the auth seam that refuses the request. Assert `Rejected(Unauthorized)` in a `system` case instead.
summary: A `system`-tier case claims a fault with `expect <call> faults`, or a fault claim at any tier is driven `by Nobody`, `by Forged`, `by Stale`, `by Expired`, `by WrongIssuer`, `by WrongAudience`, `by WrongAlgorithm` or `by NoSubject`; at `system` a fault reaches the case as an error response from the deployed Worker, never a throw, so the claim belongs at `unit` or `integration`.

blurb: `by Forged` and `by Stale` send a bad credential to a real auth seam, so the route must have a seam that can refuse it. `Forged` needs a `Signature`, `Bearer` or `Oidc` actor. `Stale` needs a `Signature` actor, since only a signature carries a timestamp to age. On any other route there is nothing to refuse and the case would test nothing, so it is refused. Drive a route with the right seam. See `bynk.test.stale_needs_timestamp` for a `Signature` actor with no timestamp.
summary: A case drives `by Forged` at an address that is not an http route with a `Signature`, `Bearer` or `Oidc` actor, or `by Stale` at one with no `Signature` actor (alone, or as a member of an actor sum); they send a bad credential, so only a `Signature`, `Bearer` or `Oidc` seam can refuse them.

blurb: `by Forged`, `by Stale` and the other bad-credential principals send a forged or out-of-date credential to the real auth seam, which only a `system` case reaches. In process the seam is skipped and the identity is simply given, so there is nothing to refuse. Move the case to `system` with `as system`.
summary: A case drives `by Forged`, `by Stale`, `by Expired`, `by WrongIssuer`, `by WrongAudience`, `by WrongAlgorithm` or `by NoSubject` outside a `system`-tier case; only the `system` driver signs a request or mints a token, so only there does the real `Signature`, `Bearer` or `Oidc` seam see the bad credential.

blurb: `by NoSubject` sends two correctly signed, unexpired tokens whose `sub` the seam must refuse: one empty, one missing. Only an `Oidc` actor's seam is driven with these tokens, so on any other route, a `Bearer` or `Signature` one or a public one, the case is refused. Drive a route guarded by an `Oidc` actor. The same holds for `bynk.test.wrong_issuer_needs_oidc_route`, `bynk.test.wrong_audience_needs_oidc_route` and `bynk.test.wrong_algorithm_needs_oidc_route`.
summary: A case drives `by NoSubject` at an address that is not an http route with an `Oidc` actor; it sends correctly signed tokens whose `sub` is empty and whose `sub` is missing, so only an `Oidc` seam can refuse them.

blurb: `by Nobody` sends no credential so that a route's auth seam answers `401`. A public route, guarded by `Visitor`, has no seam that refuses anyone, so the case would test nothing and is refused. Use `by Nobody` on a route guarded by a `Bearer`, `Oidc` or `Signature` actor, and act as `Visitor` on a public one. For the other failure principals, see `bynk.test.expired_needs_bearer_route`.
summary: A case drives `by Nobody` at a route with no Bearer, `Oidc` or Signature actor (alone, or as a member of an actor sum) (e.g. a public `Visitor` route) — there is no auth seam to reject the missing credential.

blurb: `D1.peek` reads a D1 database, so it names a capability derived from `D1` (`capability Orders = D1`). A capability on another binding, such as `Kv`, has no database for it to read.
summary: `D1.peek` names a capability that is not derived from `D1`; only a D1 binding has a test database to read.

blurb: `D1.peek(<participant>.<Capability>)` stands as the value of a `let`, and the case reads through the handle that binds. A `D1.peek` anywhere else, as an argument or the receiver of a call, has no handle to keep.
summary: `D1.peek` is used anywhere but as the value of a `let`; the handle is what a case reads through.

blurb: `D1.peek(<participant>.<Capability>)` gives an `integration` or `system` case a read-only handle on a participant's test database. Only those tiers stand one up, so the handle is refused in a `unit` case, a `property`, and in the app's own code. A `unit` case reads the capability it stubs.
summary: `D1.peek` is used outside an `integration` or `system` case; only those tiers stand up a participant's test database.

blurb: `D1.peek` names a capability as `<participant>.<Capability>`, where the participant is one of the suite's and declares the capability. The participant or the capability is not one.
summary: `D1.peek` names a participant or a capability that the suite does not have.

blurb: A `D1.peek` handle is read-only: it offers `all`, `first`, `select[T]` and `firstAs[T]`, and a statement that would write (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, a schema change) is refused, as is `run` or `batch`. A case makes the app write by driving the app.
summary: A `D1.peek` handle is asked to write, by a write operation (`run`, `batch`) or by a statement that would write; the handle is read-only.

blurb: `TokenClaims.of([…])` supplies the claims an `Oidc` actor's token carries, which the handler reads and the actor's rules check. A `Bearer` actor's token holds an identity and nothing else, so there is no claim set to fill, and the argument is refused. Drop the claims, or test a route guarded by an `Oidc` actor. See `bynk.test.actor_no_identity` for the other extra argument.
summary: A call-site principal passes token claims for an actor that isn't `Oidc`.

blurb: A handler guarded by an actor runs as that actor, so a case must act as it, with the identity type it declares. `by Visitor` carries no identity, so it cannot stand in for `User`, and an actor outside the handler's `by` sum is no member of it. Act as the actor the handler names. To exercise an unauthenticated request instead, use `by Nobody` in a `system` case.
summary: A call-site `by <Actor>` acts as an actor whose identity is incompatible with the addressed handler's actor, or names no member of the handler's actor sum.

blurb: An asset is public: the platform serves it before the Worker runs, so no actor's seam ever sees the request. A `by` clause on an asset fetch would name a principal that nothing checks, so it is refused. Drop the `by`. To test who may reach something, drive a route, not an asset. A method other than `GET` is `bynk.test.asset_address_method`.
summary: A suite's asset fetch carries a `by` clause; an asset is public and served before the Worker runs.

blurb: A wrong-method test, such as `DELETE` on a path declared only for `GET`, expects the `405` the router returns before any handler is chosen. No handler runs, so there is no actor to act as, and a `by` clause would suggest otherwise. Drop the `by` clause. To test who may call a route, address a method it does declare.
example:
// tests/api.test.bynk
let r <- api.DELETE("/a") by User("bob")   // ✗ no handler runs
let r <- api.DELETE("/a")                  // ✓
expect r is Rejected(MethodNotAllowed)
summary: A wrong-method `405` test carries a `by <Actor>` clause; it reaches no handler, so a principal is meaningless.

blurb: A handler declared `by u: User` runs as a verified actor, and a `case` has no real caller, so it must say who is calling with a call-site `by`. The same applies to a handler guarded by an actor sum: name one of its members. Append `by <Actor>(<identity>)` to the call.
summary: A test drives an identity-carrying handler, or one guarded by an actor sum, with no call-site `by <Actor>`.

Under `bynk test --against`, a `system` case's `expect` compares an `Instant` that isn't derived from the run (a constant such as `Instant.fromEpochMillis(0)`); in process the clock starts at the epoch, but a real runtime's Workers read wall-clock time.
A `system` case moves the harness clock with `advance Clock`, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: the deployed Workers read wall-clock time.
A `system` case fetches an asset with `svc.GET(asset)`, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: the fetch is answered in process.
A `system` case addresses an `on call` service, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: the service is internal, and each call is signed for one caller.

A `system` case's `env` disagrees with the named target it would run against (`bynk test --against`): it sets a secret, sets a name the target doesn't declare under `vars` or declares with another value, or leaves unset a name the target declares.
A `system` case reads a participant's test database with `D1.peek`, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: a deployment has no in-process database.
A `system` case delivers a queue message with `q.message(m)`, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: no public wire reaches a queue consumer.
A `system` case runs a cron handler with `svc.schedule(…)`, which a run against a real runtime (`bynk test --against`) can't honour: no public wire reaches a cron handler.

blurb: A test addresses an http route by method and route pattern, as in `api.POST("/items", body)`. The first argument must be that pattern as a string literal, so a number or a variable is refused. The same code covers other addresses used the wrong way, such as fetching an asset through a service that is not `from http`.
summary: A test body addresses a service the wrong way for its protocol (e.g. an http route without a leading path string).

blurb: `svc.call(…)` in a test runs the service's `on call` handler, so it takes that handler's parameters, and the number of arguments is checked as for any call. Add or remove arguments to match the handler. The asset address, `svc.GET(asset)`, takes the asset alone, and this code covers extra arguments there too.
summary: A test body's `svc.call(...)` passes the wrong number of arguments for the service's `on call` handler.

blurb: A case reaches a service through the address its protocol has. `svc.call(…)` runs an `on call` handler, so it needs one; a `from http` service is driven by route (`api.POST("/items", body)`), a `from cron` service by its schedule, a `from queue` service by message. Use the address the service has. The Book's table of addresses lists each.
summary: A test body invokes `svc.call(...)` on a service with no `on call` handler (a `from http`/`cron`/`queue` service).

blurb: A case addresses an http route by the pattern its handler declares, `"/items"`, not a concrete URL, and a cron or queue service by its own address. A path that no route in the service declares, for any method, is refused. To test the `405` for a wrong method, use a declared path with a method it lacks.
summary: A test body addresses an http route / cron schedule / queue message the service does not declare.
A smoke case (`bynk test --smoke`) gets a non-5xx answer whose status is not among those its route's handler declares; the case still passes (warning).

blurb: A snapshot is stored under its case and its name, so each `matches snapshot` in one case needs a name of its own. Two with the same name would compare against, and update, the same stored value. Give the repeat a distinct name.
example:
expect read("a") matches snapshot "delivery"
expect read("b") matches snapshot "delivery"   // ✗ name already taken
expect read("b") matches snapshot "second"     // ✓
summary: A case takes two snapshots (`expect v matches snapshot "name"`) under one name; a snapshot is keyed by its case and name.

blurb: A snapshot is keyed by its case and name, so it holds one value. A `property` runs its body once for each generated input, so there is no single value to store. Snapshot a fixed value in a `case`, and let the property assert what holds for every input.
summary: A `property` takes a snapshot; its body runs once per generated input, so the snapshot belongs in a `case` over a fixed value.

blurb: A snapshot is stored under its name, so the name must be a string literal: the compiler then knows every snapshot a suite takes. A variable or other expression is refused. Write the name as a literal.
example:
expect read("a") matches snapshot name        // ✗ not a string literal
expect read("a") matches snapshot "first"     // ✓
summary: `matches snapshot` is not followed by a string literal; a snapshot is named by a literal so the compiler knows every snapshot a suite takes.

blurb: A snapshot is stored in a file beside its unit suite and compared by the unit harness, so `matches snapshot` works only in a unit-tier `case` of a suite that tests a unit. A `system` case, or an integration or system suite, has no store to compare against. Take the snapshot in a unit case. See `bynk.test.snapshot_in_property` for the other place it is refused.
summary: A snapshot is taken in a `system`-tier case or in an integration or system suite; snapshots are stored per unit suite file and compared in the unit harness.

blurb: A snapshot stores the value as the JSON text `Json.encode` produces, so the value must be `Codable`: base types, named types and the built-in containers over them. A `Stream`, a function, an `Effect` or `()` has no such text. Snapshot a `Codable` value instead, such as a list.
example:
expect Stream.of([1, 2]) matches snapshot "items"   // ✗ a `Stream`
expect [1, 2] matches snapshot "items"              // ✓ a `List[Int]`
summary: The value of an `expect … matches snapshot` is not `Codable`: a snapshot stores the value's `Json.encode` text, so it must be in the domain `Json.encode` accepts.

blurb: A `Signature` actor refuses a stale request by reading a timestamp header and comparing it with a `tolerance`. `by Stale` signs a request in the past, so it means something only when the actor declares both; without them the seam has no window to refuse it by, and the case would test nothing. Add `timestamp = "<Header>"` and `tolerance = <seconds>` to the actor, or test the signature itself with `by Forged`. On a route with no `Signature` actor, see `bynk.test.forged_needs_signature_route`.
summary: A case drives `by Stale` at a `Signature` route whose actor declares no `timestamp` header and `tolerance`, so there is no replay window for the seam to refuse a stale signature by.

blurb: At `system` the driver mints an `Oidc` actor's token itself, writing its claims from the `"name: value"` lines of the `TokenClaims.of([…])` in the `by` clause. A `TokenClaims` held in a variable is opaque: it can be read with `get` and `has`, but its lines cannot be recovered, so the driver has nothing to mint from and the case is refused rather than sent with no claims. Write `TokenClaims.of([…])` in the principal, or move the case to `integration`, where the handler is given the value as it is.
summary: A `system`-tier case passes token claims to a call-site principal other than as a literal `TokenClaims.of([…])`; the driver mints the `Oidc` token's claims from those lines, which a `TokenClaims` value does not expose.

blurb: A call-site `by <Actor>` makes the case act as that actor, so it must name an `actor` the target context declares, or one of the prelude actors such as `Visitor` and `Caller`. Any other name, often a misspelling, has no identity to supply. Correct the name or declare the actor.
summary: A call-site `by <Actor>` names an actor the target context does not declare and that is not a prelude actor.

blurb: `Wire(…)` delivers raw text to an http body or path segment. A queue message, a cron tick, an `on call` or an event has no raw text form: it is a typed value, and `Wire` would hand it to a typed decoder as a string and fail confusingly at run time. Pass the typed value. To drive an http route with raw text, see `bynk.test.wire_needs_system`.
summary: A `Wire(...)` raw argument is passed to a queue, cron, `on call` or event address; `Wire` drives an http body or path segment only, so a queue message, cron tick or event is passed as a typed value.

blurb: `Wire(…)` hands raw text to the real boundary, before any decoding, so that a case can check what the boundary refuses. Only a `system` case has a real boundary: below it the handler is called directly, and the text would go in unchecked. Promote the case with `as system`, or pass a typed value instead. For other addresses, see `bynk.test.wire_http_only`.
summary: A `Wire(...)` raw argument is used outside a `system`-tier service address; `Wire` hands pre-validation input to the boundary and is meaningless at `unit` or in any other position.

blurb: `by WrongAlgorithm` sends two otherwise valid tokens under an algorithm the seam must refuse: one with `alg: none`, and one `HS256`-signed with the JWKS public key as the secret. Only an `Oidc` actor's seam is driven with these tokens, so on any other route, a `Bearer` or `Signature` one or a public one, the case is refused. Drive a route guarded by an `Oidc` actor. The same holds for `bynk.test.wrong_issuer_needs_oidc_route`, `bynk.test.wrong_audience_needs_oidc_route` and `bynk.test.no_subject_needs_oidc_route`.
summary: A case drives `by WrongAlgorithm` at an address that is not an http route with an `Oidc` actor; it sends a token with `alg: none` and an `HS256` token keyed with the JWKS public key, so only an `Oidc` seam can refuse them.

blurb: `by WrongAudience` sends a correctly signed, unexpired token whose `aud` is not the actor's audience. Only an `Oidc` actor has an audience to check: a `Bearer` token has none, and a `Signature` or public route has no token. On any other route the case is refused. Drive a route guarded by an `Oidc` actor. The same holds for `bynk.test.wrong_issuer_needs_oidc_route`, `bynk.test.wrong_algorithm_needs_oidc_route` and `bynk.test.no_subject_needs_oidc_route`.
summary: A case drives `by WrongAudience` at an address that is not an http route with an `Oidc` actor; it sends a correctly signed token whose `aud` is not the actor's, so only an `Oidc` seam can refuse it.

blurb: `by WrongIssuer` sends a correctly signed, unexpired token whose `iss` is not the actor's issuer. Only an `Oidc` actor has an issuer to check: a `Bearer` token has none, and a `Signature` or public route has no token. On any other route the case is refused. Drive a route guarded by an `Oidc` actor. The same holds for `bynk.test.wrong_audience_needs_oidc_route`, `bynk.test.wrong_algorithm_needs_oidc_route` and `bynk.test.no_subject_needs_oidc_route`.
summary: A case drives `by WrongIssuer` at an address that is not an http route with an `Oidc` actor; it sends a correctly signed token whose `iss` is not the actor's, so only an `Oidc` seam can refuse it.

blurb: A WebSocket connection's principal is given once, at `open`, and the connection carries it from there, as the platform recovers it from the socket. So `message` and `close` take no `by`: a case that named one could present a principal production never sees. Drop the `by`. To act as another principal, open a new `TestConnection`.
summary: A case's `svc.message(tc, frame)` or `svc.close(tc)` on a `from websocket` service carries a `by` clause; the connection's principal is given once, at `open`, and carried from there.

blurb: `svc.open(tc, …)`, `svc.message` and `svc.close` drive a `from websocket` service in process, against a `TestConnection`. A deployed WebSocket is a real upgrade through the Worker and a Durable Object, which a `system` case does not drive, so the address has nothing to run. Drive the service in a case at `unit` or `integration` instead.
summary: A `system`-tier case drives a `from websocket` service by address (`svc.open(tc, …)`, `svc.message(tc, frame)`, `svc.close(tc)`); a deployed WebSocket is a real upgrade through the Worker and a Durable Object, which a `system` case does not drive, so the case runs at `unit` or `integration`.

blurb: Below `system` a case runs in one process. No other context is stood up, so a `unit` or `integration` case, or a `property`, that reaches another context's service, directly or through a service or agent handler, has nothing to call unless the service is stubbed: `stub Pay.authorise(_) returns …` substitutes it, and only the services left unstubbed are reported. Stub each service the case reaches, promote the case to a `system` suite, which wires the contexts, or test the unit that does not cross.
summary: A `unit` or `integration` case, or a `property`, reaches another context's service, directly or through a target service or agent handler that calls one; below `system` no other context is stood up to call, so the flow belongs in a `suite … as system`.

blurb: A `system` case runs against deployed Workers and addresses services by their context path, which no `unit` or `integration` case can. So a suite holds either `system` cases only or none: a case of another tier in a `system` suite, or a `system` case among others, is refused. Move it into a suite of its own.
summary: A suite mixes `system` cases with `unit` or `integration` ones; a `system` case runs against deployed Workers and addresses services by context path, so it needs a `suite … as system` of its own.

blurb: A `system` case exists to cross a real serialise, JSON, deserialise boundary. A target has one if it consumes another context, or exposes an `http`, `queue` or `email` service. One with neither has nothing to cross, so a `system` suite adds nothing over `unit`. Run the suite at `unit` or `integration`, or give the target a service that has a boundary.
summary: An `as system` suite whose target has no serialisation edge: it consumes no other context and exposes no `http`, `queue` or `email` service, so there is no wire for a `system` case to cross.

blurb: A transition is checked inside one agent's commit, between that agent's own old and new states. Reading another agent would mean a call out to it, whose value could change before the commit lands, so the claim could not be held. A property that spans agents belongs in a saga or a scenario. Keep the transition to this agent's `old` and `new`. The mirror rule for states is `bynk.invariant.cross_agent_reference`.
example:
transition within_total: new.count <= Total("all").get()   // ✗ reads another agent

transition grows: new.count >= old.count                   // ✓ this agent's own step
summary: A transition predicate references another agent; step invariants are per-agent.

blurb: Transitions are named so that a violation can say which step rule was broken. Two with the same name in one agent would make that report ambiguous. Rename one, or merge the two predicates if they are one claim. The same rule for states is `bynk.invariant.duplicate_name`.
example:
transition grows: new.count >= old.count
transition grows: new.count < 100    // ✗ `grows` is already declared

transition capped: new.count < 100   // ✓ a distinct name
summary: An agent declares two transitions with the same name.

blurb: A transition is checked at each commit, over the old and new states, so it may only read: `old`, `new`, operators and pure value methods. `Effect.pure`, `?`, `expect`, `Val` and the other test-only forms are refused, as is anything that performs an effect. Rewrite the predicate as a plain `Bool` expression. The mirror rule for states is `bynk.invariant.impure_predicate`.
example:
transition grows: Effect.pure(new.count >= old.count)   // ✗ an effect, not a pure predicate

transition grows: new.count >= old.count                // ✓ a plain `Bool` expression
summary: A transition predicate uses an effectful or test-only construct; a step invariant must be pure.

A handler can make a move that an agent's `transition` refuses, from a state the agent can be in after a commit; at run time that call faults with `InvariantViolation` (warning). Resolve it in code: refuse the move first, with a `match` arm or an `is` test on the state field that the path can't get past.

blurb: A transition constrains a step, so it has to compare the state before the commit (`old`) with the state after (`new`). One that mentions neither is a claim about a single state, which an `invariant` states more plainly and checks the same way. Use `old` and `new`, or write it as an `invariant`.
example:
transition grows: count >= 0               // ✗ names neither `old` nor `new`

transition grows: new.count >= old.count   // ✓ compares the two states
summary: A transition references neither `old` nor `new`; it constrains one state, so it is an `invariant`, not a step.

blurb: A `transition` is a claim about a step, from `old` to `new`, that is either kept or broken, so its predicate must be a `Bool`. A bare `new.count` is a value, not a claim. Compare it with the old state: `new.count >= old.count`. An `invariant` is held to the same rule (`bynk.invariant.not_bool`).
example:
transition grows: new.count                // ✗ an `Int`, not a `Bool`

transition grows: new.count >= old.count   // ✓ a claim about the step
summary: A transition predicate does not have type `Bool`.

blurb: An argument has a different type from the parameter it is passed to. Bynk compares types exactly and converts nothing implicitly, so a `String` is never read as an `Int`, and a call that passes the wrong type is refused at the call, not left to fail later. The same code covers the arguments of methods, capability operations and constructors. Pass a value of the parameter's type, or convert it first with an explicit conversion such as `Int.parse` (which returns an `Option`, because the text may not be a number).
summary: A call, method, capability, or constructor argument has the wrong type.

blurb: An `Asset` names a file the platform serves; it is not data to keep or send. So an `Asset` cannot be a record field, a sum payload, an event field, an agent key or store field, or part of a service or agent handler signature. What crosses is its `.url`, a `String`: hold that instead. Other types refused there include `bynk.types.function_at_boundary` and `bynk.types.held_at_boundary`.
summary: An `Asset` type appears in a record field, boundary or store position; pass its `.url` instead.

blurb: A field default, `field: T = expr`, is filled in whenever a literal leaves the field out and whenever a decoded body omits its key, so it has to be a fixed value that has a wire form. The compiler accepts a literal, a variant, `Some`, `None`, `Ok` or `Err`, a record or list literal, `Map.empty()`, `Set.empty()`, and `T.unsafe(lit)` for an opaque type. A call to your own function, or a read of a binding, is refused: a default has to be a value known when the program compiles, not something computed at every construction and decode. In a generic record, a field whose type is the type parameter itself cannot have a default at all, since one value cannot suit every instantiation. Write the value out as a literal, or drop the default and require the field.
summary: A record or event field's default expression (`field: T = expr`) is not a static, wire-representable value of the field's declared type — a literal (including one admitted to a refined type), a sum variant of a type this context may construct (not a `uses`-sourced commons sum, which is `bynk.context.rebrand_construction`), `Some`/`None`/`Ok`/`Err`, a record, a list literal, `Map.empty()`/`Set.empty()`, or `T.unsafe(lit)` for an opaque type whose literal also satisfies the refinement. A field whose type is a generic record's type parameter has no default, and a default may not hold for one instantiation only: for a record field that applies a user generic (`Page[String]`, or `Page[T]` inside a generic record; an event or old-state field may not) it is a closed-form value at the instantiated type, writing nothing of the enclosing record's own type parameters. (Earlier versions reported this as `bynk.event.bad_field_default`.)

blurb: A function value was called with a different number of arguments from the number its type declares. A parameter or local of type `(Int, Int) -> Int` takes exactly two, and the call is checked against that type, so the mismatch is reported where it is made. The same code covers the built-in operations of `Map`, `Set`, `Cell`, `Cache` and `Log`, and `unreachable` and `todo`, which each take one message. Pass exactly the declared number. A declared `fn` called with the wrong number of arguments is the separate code `bynk.resolve.arity_mismatch`, and a method is `bynk.types.method_arity`.
summary: A function value, a built-in `Map`/`Set`/`Cell`/`Cache`/`Log` operation, or `unreachable`/`todo` was called with the wrong number of arguments (a declared `fn` is `bynk.resolve.arity_mismatch`).

blurb: `None` carries no value, so its `Option[T]` takes `T` from where it is used: an annotation, a parameter, or the function's return type. A `let` of a bare `None` has none, and the compiler will not guess, because `T` becomes part of everything the binding touches. Annotate it, as in `let missing: Option[Int] = None`, or use `None` where an `Option` is expected.
summary: The value type of `None` could not be inferred.

blurb: `Ok(v)` fixes only the success type and `Err(e)` only the error type, so the rest of the `Result` has to come from context: an annotation, a parameter type, or the enclosing function's return type. A bare `let r = Ok(1)` has neither, and the compiler will not guess. Annotate the binding, as in `let r: Result[Int, String] = Ok(1)`.
summary: The type parameters of a `Result` could not be inferred.

blurb: A `Matches` pattern, and the pattern of a regex method such as `matchesRegex` or `replaceRegex`, is analysed when the program compiles. Patterns run with JavaScript's backtracking `RegExp`, and one in which a repetition can split the same text several ways takes exponential time on a crafted near miss, so a few dozen characters of input could stall a handler. Nested or ambiguous repetition, such as `(a+)+` or `(a|aa)+`, is refused, bounded or not, as is a backreference under an unbounded quantifier, an unbounded quantifier over a body that can match the empty string, and a pattern too large or complex to analyse. Rewrite it so each repetition has one way to match: `a+` for `(a+)+`, or a separator the repeated part cannot match, as in `[a-z]+(-[a-z]+)*`. Two adjacent repetitions that compete, as in `\d*\d*`, are the milder `bynk.types.polynomial_regex`.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("(a+)+$")    // ✗ nested unbounded repetition

type Code = String where Matches("a+$")       // ✓ one way to match
summary: A `Matches` pattern, or a regex method's pattern, can match the same text in exponentially many ways (nested or ambiguous repetition, bounded or not), or cannot be analysed, risking catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS).

blurb: An `Oidc` actor's binder carries the verified token's claims (`who.claims`) for the handler that received the token. They are read there and never kept: a `TokenClaims` can't be a field, or cross a call, a message or an agent. Read the claim you need and keep that `String`.
example:
type Seen = { claims: TokenClaims }                 // ✗

let repo = w.claims.get("repository")            // ✓ keep the String
summary: `TokenClaims` appears where a value is stored or sent: a field of a type, or a boundary such as a call, a message or an agent.
