blurb: The function given to a combinator must return the shape the combinator chains on. `Option.andThen` wants an `Option` back and `Result.andThen` a `Result` whose error type matches the receiver's, so that the result is flattened, not nested. `List.flatMap` wants a `List` and `Query.flatMap` a `Query`. The effectful iterators and `flatMapOk` and `flatMapErr` want an `Effect[Result[…]]`, and `Option.orElse` wants the receiver's own `Option` type. If your function returns a plain value, you want `map`, which wraps it for you. Otherwise wrap the value yourself, as `Some(n + 1)`, or fix the function's result. A callback of the wrong type for the combinator's own signature is `bynk.types.argument_mismatch`.
summary: A callback passed to a combinator (`map`/`andThen`/`flatMap`/`traverseAll`/…) returns the wrong type.

blurb: `T.of(value)` takes exactly one argument, the base value to check, and so does `T.unsafe(value)` on an opaque type: a refined or opaque type wraps a single value. None gives it nothing to check, and two have no meaning. Pass the one value. Building a sum variant with the wrong number of arguments is `bynk.types.variant_arity`.
summary: `T.of` (or `T.unsafe`) on a refined or opaque type got the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: `Reps.of(x)` checks a value of the type's base against its predicates, so `x` must already be that base: an `Int` for `Reps`. The constructor validates; it does not convert, so a `String` is refused before any predicate runs. Turn the value into the base first, such as with `Int.parse`, or take it as the base type. `Reps.unsafe` on an opaque type has the same rule.
summary: A `.of` constructor was given an argument of the wrong base type.

blurb: `Decimal` is exact, and a quotient often has no exact decimal answer (one third), so `/` is not defined on it. `div` says what `/` leaves out: how many decimal places to keep and how to round. `+`, `-` and `*` stay exact. Write `a.div(b, 2, RoundingMode.HalfEven)`, with the scale and mode you need.
summary: `/` was used on `Decimal` operands. A quotient has no exact decimal answer, so division states its scale and rounding mode: `a.div(b, 2, RoundingMode.HalfEven)` (#2622).
A negated decimal literal would have more than 1000 characters of canonical text once its sign is counted, the most any `Decimal` may have (#2622).
`JsonError` is the deprecated spelling of `DecodeError` (warning; auto-fixable).

blurb: `derives` opts a type into a capability it does not have by default, and `Ord` is the only one: it needs every field to be orderable, so you ask for it. `Eq`, `Key` and `Codable` hold for a type without being asked, so naming one does nothing, and the compiler refuses it rather than leave a clause that suggests it matters. Remove the name, which the compiler's fix does. Any other name is `bynk.generics.unknown_constraint`.
example:
type Point = { x: Int, y: Int } derives Eq    // ✗ `Eq` holds already

type Point = { x: Int, y: Int }               // ✓
summary: A `derives` clause names `Eq`, `Key` or `Codable`, which hold for a type automatically; only `Ord` is opted into. The diagnostic carries a machine-applicable fix that removes the name (constrained-generics slice 1).

blurb: `derives Ord` orders a type field by field, in declaration order, so every field or payload must itself have an order. A `Bool`, a `Map`, a `Set`, a function, and a named type that does not derive `Ord` itself have none. Change the field to an orderable type, such as an `Int` rank, or give the field's own type `derives Ord`, or drop `derives Ord` and sort by a key with `sortBy`.
example:
type Task = { title: String, done: Bool } derives Ord        // ✗ a `Bool` has no order

type Task = { title: String, priority: Int } derives Ord      // ✓
summary: A type declares `derives Ord`, but one of its fields or payloads is not `Ord` (for example a `Map`, a `Set`, a `Bool`, a function, or a record that does not itself derive `Ord`); every part must be orderable for the declaration order to be a total order (constrained-generics slice 1).

blurb: `@example` gives `Val` the one value to use for a `Matches` or `IsoDate` refinement, which it cannot invent. A second `@example` would leave two candidates and no rule for choosing, so a refinement takes at most one. Keep the one you want. An example that does not satisfy the refinement is `bynk.types.example_violates`.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC") @example("XYZ")    // ✗ a second example

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC")                       // ✓
summary: A refinement carries more than one `@example`.

blurb: A `match` takes the first arm whose pattern fits, so a literal that an earlier unguarded arm already has can never reach a second arm. Bynk refuses the dead arm rather than let it hide a mistake, usually a mistyped value. Change the literal or delete the arm. An or-pattern is checked alternative by alternative, so `1 | 2` followed by `2` is caught as well. The same for a variant is `bynk.types.duplicate_variant_arm`.
summary: A `match` has two arms for the same literal value.

blurb: A record pattern lists the fields it reads, and each may be named once. Naming a field twice would bind or test the same value twice, which is almost always a slip for a different field. Keep one mention, and give it the name you want to use, as in `total: t`. The `..` at the end covers every field you leave out.
summary: A record pattern lists the same field twice.

blurb: A `match` runs the first arm that fits, so a second unguarded arm for a variant that an earlier arm already covers can never run. Bynk refuses the dead arm rather than let it hide a slip, usually a copied arm whose pattern was never changed. Delete it, or change it to the variant you meant. Arms are compared by shape, so `Err(A)` and `Err(B)` are not duplicates. The same mistake with a literal is `bynk.types.duplicate_literal_arm`.
summary: A `match` has two arms for the same variant.

blurb: `embeds E as V` lets `?` wrap an `E` error in the variant `V`. It picks the variant by the error's type, so a type may be embedded once: with two variants wrapping `PayError`, `?` could not tell which one an error belongs to. Embed the type in one variant, and build the other by hand where you want it.
example:
type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    | Refund(reason: PayError)
    embeds PayError as Payment, PayError as Refund    // ✗ `PayError` twice

type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    | Refund(reason: PayError)
    embeds PayError as Payment    // ✓ once
summary: A type is embedded by more than one variant of a sum, so `?`'s conversion would be ambiguous.

blurb: `embeds E as V` lets `?` wrap an `E` error in the variant `V` of the same sum, so `V` must be one of that sum's variants. Here it names none, usually a misspelling. Correct the name, or add the variant it should wrap into.
example:
type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    embeds PayError as Pay        // ✗ no variant `Pay`

type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    embeds PayError as Payment    // ✓
summary: An `embeds … as V` clause names a variant the sum does not declare.

blurb: `embeds E as V` has `?` wrap an `E` error into `V`, so `V` must take exactly that: one payload field, of type `E`. A variant with a payload of another type, or with more or fewer fields, has nowhere to put the error. Give `V` a single field of type `E`, or embed a different variant.
example:
type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: String)
    embeds PayError as Payment    // ✗ the payload is a `String`

type OrderError =
    | Payment(reason: PayError)
    embeds PayError as Payment    // ✓
summary: An `embeds E as V` target variant must have exactly one payload field, of type `E`.

blurb: A range pattern `lo..hi` matches every `Int` from `lo` to `hi`, both inclusive, so the low bound comes first. With `lo > hi` no value can match, so the arm is dead and almost certainly a typo, and the same goes for a range in a `via schema(...)` clause. Swap the bounds. A refinement written `InRange(150, 0)` is the separate `bynk.types.inverted_range`.
summary: A range pattern or `via schema(...)` range has its bounds inverted (`lo > hi`), so it can never match.

blurb: A refinement is a base type plus predicates, and a value must satisfy all of them. When the predicates contradict each other, nothing can satisfy them: the type has no values, and every `.of` and every boundary check would fail. The compiler works out the combined range of `Positive`, `NonNegative` and `InRange`, and the combined length of the length predicates, and refuses one that is empty. Drop or correct the predicate that conflicts, and read the note, which gives the empty range it found.
example:
type Debt = Int where Positive && InRange(-10, -1)    // ✗ positive, yet at most -1

type Debt = Int where Positive && InRange(1, 10)      // ✓
summary: A refinement admits no values (contradictory predicates).

blurb: `Err(e)` takes its error type from the surrounding `Result[T, E]`, the annotation or the function's return type, so `Err(404)` where `E` is `String` is refused at the value, with no conversion. Pass an `E`, or change the declared error type. The success half is `bynk.types.ok_value_mismatch`; with nothing to fix the `Result`, it is `bynk.types.cannot_infer_result_type_params`.
summary: An `Err` payload has the wrong type.

blurb: `@example` takes exactly one literal of the refinement's base type. It is read where the type is declared, not evaluated, so a call such as `Code.of("ABC")`, a name or a literal of another type is refused. Write the value itself, as a string for a `String` base.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example(Code.of("ABC"))    // ✗ a call, not a literal

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC")            // ✓

const Sample: String = "ABC"
type Tag = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example(Sample)   // ✓ a `String` constant bound to a literal
summary: An `@example` is not exactly one literal of the base type.

blurb: On a record field, `@example` pins the field's own value, which exists only where the field has a base type. A field of a named type takes its value from that type, so an example on the field would have no effect and is refused. Put the `@example` on the named type's declaration, where `Val` reads it.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}")
type Ticket = { code: Code where Matches("[A-Z]+") @example("ABC") }    // ✗ `Code` is a named type

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC")    // ✓ pin it on the type
type Ticket = { code: Code }
summary: An `@example` on a field whose type is a named type (it belongs on the named type).

blurb: `Val` cannot invent a string that matches a pattern, so a `Matches` or `IsoDate` refinement takes an `@example` for it to use. Every other refinement already has a value `Val` makes, so there is nothing for the example to do and it is refused. Remove the annotation.
example:
type Sku = String where NonEmpty @example("a")    // ✗ `Val` already makes one

type Sku = String where NonEmpty                  // ✓
summary: An `@example` on a refinement `Val` can already generate (only `Matches` and `IsoDate` take one).

blurb: `@example` is the value `Val` uses for a type it cannot fabricate, so it must be a valid one. The compiler checks it where the type is declared, against every predicate of the refinement, whether or not a test uses it; an example that fails one would give tests a value the type refuses. Write an example that satisfies the whole refinement.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("abc")    // ✗ lower case

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC")    // ✓
summary: An `@example` does not satisfy its refinement's predicates.

blurb: Some standard-library enums, among them `FetchError` and `Method`, are extensible: a minor release may add a variant. A `match` that names every variant they have today would then stop covering them, so the compiler asks for a wildcard arm now, and the `match` keeps compiling when a variant arrives. Listing every current variant is not enough. Add `_`, or `Err(_)` where the enum is wrapped, and put there whatever should happen for a variant you did not name. An enum of your own with the same name is not extensible; the rule follows the first-party enum. For an ordinary enum, a missing arm is `bynk.types.non_exhaustive_match`.
summary: A `match` covers an extensible standard-library enum (`FetchError`, `Method`) without a wildcard; it may gain variants in a minor release.

blurb: `.name` reads a field, and only a record has fields. A `String`, an `Int` or a `List` has methods instead, called with parentheses, so `name.length` is not a field read but `name.length()` is a call. A refined type is already its base type, so there is nothing to unwrap. To get at a sum type's payload, use `match`. A field a record lacks is `bynk.types.unknown_field`.
summary: Field access on a value that is not a record.

blurb: `@name("…")` is the only annotation a record field takes: it gives the field the key it has on an HTTP request where that key is not an identifier. Any other annotation is refused rather than ignored, so a misspelt one cannot silently do nothing. Write `@name`, or drop the annotation.
summary: A record field carries an annotation other than `@name("…")`.

blurb: Only a record's fields take defaults. A variant is built like a call, with every payload field given, so a default on a payload field would be an optional argument by another name. Remove it and give the field wherever the variant is built, or hold the optional values in a record, which can have defaults, and make that record the payload.
example:
type Retry =
    | Never
    | Times(n: Int = 3)    // ✗ a variant's field has no default

type Backoff = { n: Int = 3 }

type Retry =
    | Never
    | Times(opts: Backoff)    // ✓ the record carries the default
summary: A sum variant's payload field declares a default (`field: T = expr`). Only a record's fields may; a variant is built like a call, with every payload field given.

blurb: `@name` renames a field's key on an HTTP request, and the compiler reads that key at compile time, so it takes exactly one string literal, or a `String` constant bound to one: not a number, a computed value, a second argument or none. A constant must be declared exactly `String` (not a refined type) and bound to a string literal or to another such constant. Write the key as a literal, as in `@name("__Host-sid")`, or name it once with a constant.
summary: A field's `@name` does not take exactly one string literal, or a `String` constant bound to one.

blurb: A `cookies` or `query` record is read by name, and names that differ only in case are easily confused: a client that sends `page` would not match `Page`, yet both look like the same parameter. So two fields of such a record may not have wire names that differ only in case. Rename one. Two fields with exactly the same wire name are `bynk.types.field_name_duplicate`.
summary: Two fields of a `cookies` or `query` record have wire names that differ only in case.

blurb: A field's wire name is the key a request reader looks it up by, so two fields of one record cannot share one: both would read the same value. A field's wire name is its `@name`, or its own name when it has none. A field may also carry only one `@name`. Give each field its own key. Names differing only in case are `bynk.types.field_name_case_conflict`.
summary: A field has more than one `@name`, or two fields of a request record read the same wire name.

blurb: A `@name` has to be usable as a key where the record is read. It may not be empty, and on a `cookies` record it must be a cookie name, an RFC 9110 token: no spaces, quotes or separators such as `;` `,` or `=`. A name the request could never carry would make the field unreachable. Use a valid token, such as `__Host-sid`.
summary: A field's `@name` is not a valid name for where the record is read (a cookie name that is not a token, or an empty name).

blurb: `@name` renames the key a request reader looks for. Only a record that is the `cookies`, `query` or `@form`/`@multipart` `body` parameter of an `on http` handler is read that way, so on any other record the annotation would do nothing. Remove it, or make the record that parameter. A record used as a JSON body or result may not carry `@name` either: `bynk.types.field_name_record_not_boundary`.
summary: `@name` is on a field of a record that is not the `cookies`, `query` or `@form`/`@multipart` `body` record of an HTTP handler.

blurb: A record with `@name` fields is read off a request by those names, but its JSON form uses the field names, so using it as a JSON body, a result, a store field, an event or a call argument would make the two forms disagree. It may only be a `cookies`, `query` or `@form`/`@multipart` `body` parameter. Use a second record, without `@name`, for the other position.
summary: A record with `@name` fields is used as a JSON body, a result, a store field, an event or a call argument.

blurb: An inline refinement, `price: Money where Positive`, applies predicates to a value of a base type, or of a refined type over one. A record or a sum has no such value for a predicate to test. Put the refinement on the field that holds the number, inside the record, or declare a refined type and use its name.
summary: An inline field refinement requires a base or refined type.

blurb: A record literal checks each field against the type the declaration gives it, with no implicit conversion, so `y: "0"` for an `Int` field is refused where it is written. Give the field a value of its declared type, or convert it first. A field the type lacks is `bynk.resolve.unknown_field`, and one left out is `bynk.resolve.missing_field`.
summary: A record field was given a value of the wrong type.

blurb: A `File` is one uploaded part of a `@multipart` request, held in memory for the handler that receives it. A record may have a `File` field, alone, in an `Option` or in a `List`, which is how a `@multipart` `body` names its parts. But a `File`, or a record carrying one, is refused as an agent store field or key, an event field, a handler result, or any handler parameter but that `body`. Take the part's `bytes`, and the `filename` and `contentType` you need, in the handler, and keep those.
summary: A `File` (a file part of a multipart request), or a type carrying one, is used where it would be persisted, sent across a boundary or returned.

blurb: `Form.decode[T]` and `Form.encode` read and write the flat `key=value` text a `@form` route handles, so `T` must be a record of fields a form can carry: a `String`, `Int`, `Bool`, `Decimal`, an enum, or a refined or opaque type over one, optionally in an `Option` or a `List`. Form keys have no nesting, so a nested record, or a type that is not a record, is refused. Put the nested record's fields in `T` itself. A `@form` route's own body has the same rule: `bynk.http.form_field_not_stringy`.
summary: `Form.decode` or `Form.encode` names a type that is not a record of form fields (a `String`, `Int`, `Bool`, `Decimal`, an enum, or a refined or opaque type over one, optionally in an `Option` or a `List`).

blurb: A function type can be written only where a value stays in the running program: as a `fn` or lambda parameter, a return, or a local. A value that is serialised, stored or sent has to be data, and a function has no wire form, so a function type in a record field, a sum payload, an event field, a service or agent handler signature, an agent key or store field, a capability operation or an actor identity is refused where it is written. Keep the function out of the type: pass it as a parameter to the `fn` that needs it, or store the data it is built from, such as a name or a number, and rebuild the behaviour on the other side.
summary: A function type appeared in a serialisable or boundary position (a record field, sum payload, service/agent handler signature, capability operation signature, agent state field, or agent key); functions cannot serialise or cross a boundary.

blurb: A guard, as in `pattern if condition => …`, decides whether an arm applies, so it must be a `Bool`: a number or an `Option` is not read as true or false. Say what you mean with a comparison, such as `r > 10`. A guarded arm covers nothing for exhaustiveness, because its guard may fail. The condition of an `if` expression is `bynk.types.if_non_bool_cond`.
summary: A match-arm `if` guard is not a `Bool` expression.

blurb: `RequestHeaders` is the view of one request's headers, given to the handler that is answering it. It is read there and dropped: headers can carry credentials such as `Authorization`, and a copy kept or sent on would outlive the request. It is accepted only as an HTTP handler's `headers` parameter, and refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent key or store field, a capability operation, or any other handler parameter or result. Read the header you need (`headers.get("…")`) and keep that `String`. See also `bynk.types.request_query_at_boundary`.
summary: `RequestHeaders` appears where a value is stored or sent: a field of a type, or a boundary such as a call, a message or an agent.

blurb: A `Connection` is a held resource, built and disposed of in place, so it is never stored or sent: it cannot be a record, sum or event field, or part of a service or agent handler signature. An agent may keep one in its own state, as `Cell[Option[Connection[F]]]` or `Map[K, Connection[F]]`. Keep it there, and pass what you need from it, not the connection.
summary: A held value (`Connection[F]`) appears in a serialisable or boundary position — a held resource is built and disposed in place, never persisted or sent across a boundary (§2.9, real-time track slice 2).

blurb: A held `Connection` is a live resource with an identity: two values are the same connection or they are not, so there is no value to compare. So `==` on one, or on a type that holds one, is refused. Compare an id that you keep next to the connection. A `Stream` has `bynk.types.stream_not_comparable`, and functions and effects have `bynk.types.not_comparable`.
summary: A held value (`Connection[F]`) is compared with `==`/`!=` — held values have identity, not value-equality (§2.9.3, real-time track slice 2).

blurb: Both branches of an `if` can be its value, so they must have one type: their common supertype, where a refined type and its base agree at the base. With a `String` in one branch and an `Int` in the other, the caller has no single type to rely on. Make the branches agree, converting where needed. A `match` whose arms disagree is `bynk.types.match_arm_mismatch`.
summary: The branches of an `if` have different types.

blurb: An `if` chooses a branch on a `Bool`, and Bynk has no truthiness: a number, a string, an `Option` or a list is never read as true or false. Say what you mean with a comparison (`count > 0`), or test an `Option` with `is Some(…)`. A match-arm guard has the same rule, as `bynk.types.guard_not_bool`.
summary: An `if` condition is not a `Bool`.

blurb: An `if` with no `else` has nothing to produce when its condition is false, so Bynk gives that path the value `()`. The `then` branch must therefore be `()` too, or `Effect[()]` for a branch that only performs effects; a branch that yields a `String` would leave the other path without one. Add an `else` that produces a value of the same type, or make the branch a unit effect.
summary: An `if` with no `else` branch has a non-unit then-branch; the missing else defaults to `()`, so the branch must be `()` or `Effect[()]`.

blurb: A `\(…)` hole in a string takes a `String`, `Int`, `Float`, `Bool`, `Decimal`, or a refined type over one of them, and nothing else. A record or sum has no canonical text, and Bynk will not print an unreadable stand-in such as `[object Object]`. An opaque type hides its base, so use `.raw` first. Turn other values into a `String` yourself: `toHex()` or `toBase64()` on `Bytes`, `toString()` on a `Duration`, `toIso()` or `toString()` on an `Instant`, or interpolate the fields of a record, a `ValidationError` or a `DecodeError`.
summary: An interpolation hole holds a value with no string form.

blurb: A `Matches` pattern, and the pattern of a regex method such as `containsRegex`, must be a valid regular expression. The emitted check runs it under JavaScript's `RegExp`, so the compiler validates it with those rules: a pattern the Rust `regex` crate accepts, such as `(?P<name>…)`, may be refused here, and the compiler would otherwise ship a check that throws at run time. A regex method's pattern may open with one inline-flag group of `i`, `m` and `s`, each at most once. Fix the syntax; the note carries the parser's message. A valid but dangerous pattern is `bynk.types.catastrophic_regex`.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z")     // ✗ the class is never closed

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]+")   // ✓
summary: A `Matches` predicate, or a regex method's pattern (`containsRegex`, …), contains an invalid regular expression or malformed inline flags.

blurb: `InRange(lo, hi)` is inclusive at both ends, so it needs `lo <= hi`. With the bounds the wrong way round the refinement admits no value, which is almost certainly a slip, so the compiler refuses it. Swap them; the diagnostic offers that fix. On an `Int` or `Float` the empty range is also reported as `bynk.types.empty_refinement`, which is what contradictory predicates give too. An inverted range in a `match` arm is `bynk.types.empty_range_pattern`.
example:
type Price = Decimal where InRange(100.00d, 0.00d)    // ✗ the minimum is above the maximum

type Price = Decimal where InRange(0.00d, 100.00d)    // ✓
summary: An `InRange` predicate has its bounds inverted.

blurb: `value is Quantity` runs a refined type's predicates against the value. A refined type is a base type plus predicates, so the value must have that base: an `Int` can be checked against `Int where …`, but a `String` has nothing for an `Int` range to test. Check the value against a refined type over its own type, or convert it first, for example by parsing the `String`.
example:
type Quantity = Int where InRange(1, 100)

s is Quantity    // ✗ `s` is a `String`, `Quantity` is over `Int`

n is Quantity    // ✓ `n` is an `Int`
summary: An `is` refinement check is applied to a value of the wrong base type.

blurb: `is` tests a value's variant or refined type, not its value, so `x is 31` would read as a type test while meaning equality. Bynk refuses it rather than let the two readings blur. Compare with `==` instead. In a `match`, a literal is a fine pattern, because a `match` arm tests a value there.
summary: A literal was used on the right of `is`; `is` tests type/refinement, not value equality (use `==`).

blurb: `value is Variant` asks which variant a sum, `Result` or `Option` holds, so its left side must be one of those. On an `Int`, a `String` or a record there is no variant to ask about. To test a number or a string against a refined type, name that type: `n is Quantity`. To compare by value, use `==`. A variant the sum does not have is `bynk.types.is_unknown_variant`.
summary: `is` was applied to a value that is not a sum type.

blurb: `is` tests a value's variant or refined type, not whether a number lies in a range, so `age is 13..19` would read as a type test while comparing values. Bynk refuses it. Compare the bounds, write a `match` arm `13..19`, or declare a refined type with `InRange(13, 19)` and test against that. The literal case is `bynk.types.is_literal_pattern`.
summary: A range pattern was used directly on the right of `is`; `is` tests type/refinement, not value ranges (use `match`, a guard or `InRange`).

blurb: `is` tests a value against a type or a variant. An inline refinement, `_ where Positive`, is a pattern for a `match` arm, and is not accepted after `is`: a rule worth testing is worth a name, which also lets every other place use it. Declare a refined type and write `n is Natural`, or move the test into a `match` arm.
example:
n is _ where Positive    // ✗ not a pattern for `is`

type Natural = Int where Positive

n is Natural             // ✓ name the refinement
summary: A refined (`where`) pattern was used on the right of `is`; refined patterns are `match`-only.

blurb: `l is Amber` asks whether a `Light` is its `Amber` variant, which only means something if `Light` has one. A name that is not a variant of the sum is usually a typo or a variant left over from an earlier version of the type. Use one the type declares. On a value that is not a sum at all, the error is `bynk.types.is_non_sum`.
summary: `is` names a variant the type does not have.

blurb: `Json.encode` and `Json.decode` work on values that have a wire form, and a function does not: a value that can run has no JSON text to stand for it. The codec covers the base types, named types and the built-in containers over them. It does not cover functions, effects, streams or a type that carries one, `bynk.crypto` keys or the error builtins. Encode the data the function produces, or the record that describes it, not the function itself.
summary: A `Json.encode`/`Json.decode` target type cannot pass through the typed JSON codec (functions, effects, streams or a type that carries one, `bynk.crypto` keys, error builtins).

blurb: A `bynk.crypto` `SigningKey` or `VerifyKey` is a handle to a key the platform holds non-extractable, and it lives only for the call that imported it. Storing, serialising, logging or sending it would either leak the secret or mean nothing on the other side, so one cannot be a `store` field, a record or event field, or a handler parameter or result. Keep the key's bytes, such as the PKCS#8 `Bytes`, in `Secrets` or a field, and import the key again with `Crypto.importSigningKey` where you sign. A capability operation may take one.
summary: A `bynk.crypto` `SigningKey` or `VerifyKey` appears in a storable or boundary-crossing position — a key is held non-extractable and lives for the call that imported it, never persisted, logged or sent (standard-library K4).

blurb: `sortBy`, `sortByDescending`, `min` and `max` order a list, or a storage `Query`, by the value the key function returns, so that value needs a total order. A record or sum is not ordered by accident, because opting in makes field and variant order significant. Return a field that is already orderable, or add `derives Ord` to the type. The operators `<` and `>` on an unordered type are `bynk.types.not_orderable`.
summary: A `sortBy`/`sortByDescending`/`min`/`max` key function does not return an orderable type. The key must be an `Ord` type, on a `List` and on a storage `Query` alike.

blurb: A lambda is checked against the function type expected where it is written, such as the parameter it is passed for. It must take the same number of parameters, any annotation on a parameter must match that parameter's type, and its body must produce the result type, because the function it is passed to calls it with that shape and uses what comes back. Change the lambda to fit, or change the function type if that is what is wrong.
summary: A lambda's parameter count, parameter annotations, or body type do not match the expected function type.

blurb: A `let` with a type annotation declares what the binding is, and its value must have exactly that type. The annotation is the contract that later code reads, so a value of another type is refused at the `let`, not where it is later used. Nothing is converted for you: change the value, convert it explicitly, or correct the annotation if the value is what you meant. The same rule governs a function's declared return, which is `bynk.types.return_mismatch`.
summary: A `let` value does not match its type annotation.

blurb: A list has one element type, taken from the context if there is one and otherwise from the first element, and every element must have it. `[1, 2, "3"]` mixes `Int` and `String`, and the error is on the element that disagrees. Make the elements one type, or wrap them in a sum type if the list really holds more than one kind of value. An empty `[]` with no context is `bynk.types.uninferable_element_type`.
summary: A list-literal element has a different type from the list's element type.

blurb: A list pattern such as `[x, ..]` matches a value by its length and its elements, so the value must be a `List[T]`. A `Set`, a `Map`, an `Int` or a record has no such shape, and a record or sum is matched by its own pattern. Convert the value first, as `s.toList()` does for a `Set`, or match on what the value actually is. The same rule applies to a list pattern after `is` and in `let … else`.
summary: A list pattern is matched against a value that is not a `List` (a record, sum, base type, `Set` or `Map`).

blurb: A `match` is an expression, so its arms must produce one type: the least upper bound of their types, where a refined type and its base agree at the base. If one arm gives a `String` and another an `Int`, there is no single type for the caller to rely on. Make the arms agree, converting where needed. The rule also holds for `let … else`, whose `else` must produce the type of the rest of its block.
summary: A `match` arm has a different type from the others.

blurb: `match` chooses between alternatives, so it needs a value that has some: a sum, an enum, a `Result` or `Option`, an `Int`, `String` or `Bool`, or a list matched by list patterns. A `Float` or a function has none, and a record has a single shape, so it can be matched only with a record pattern such as `Point { x, .. }`. Read a field directly, and use `if` to branch on a condition.
summary: `match` was applied to a value that is not a sum type.

blurb: A method was called with a different number of arguments from the number it declares. The count excludes `self`, which the receiver supplies, so `fn Box.adjust(self, delta: Int)` takes one argument. Pass exactly that many. The same code covers the built-in methods of `String`, `List`, `Map` and the other kernel types.
summary: A method was called with the wrong number of arguments.

blurb: A method call names an instance method that the receiver's type does not have. An instance method is a function declared with `self` as its first parameter. A function declared on a type without `self` is static, and is called on the type, as `Counter.zero()`, never on a value. This also fires on a typo, and on a built-in type that has methods but not this one, since only the methods the type documents exist.
summary: Called a method the type does not have.

blurb: A method call needs a type that has methods. A user-declared type does, and so do the built-ins that document them, such as `String` and `List`, but a function value, a `Bool` or `()` has none, so `f.apply(n)` has nothing to look up. A function is called directly, as `f(n)`. For a type that does have methods, a name it lacks is `bynk.types.method_not_found`.
summary: A method was called on a built-in type that has no methods.

blurb: A variant pattern binds its payload either by field name, `Circle(r: x, d: y)`, or by position, `Circle(x, y)`. Mixing the two leaves it unclear which field a bare name takes, so Bynk wants one style in each pattern. Name every field, or none.
summary: A pattern mixes named and positional bindings.

blurb: `MinLength`, `MaxLength` and `Length` count the characters of a string, and a length cannot be below zero, so `MinLength(-1)` would hold for every string and `MaxLength(-1)` for none. The compiler takes a negative argument to be a mistake and refuses it. Give a length of zero or more. A set of predicates that no value can satisfy is `bynk.types.empty_refinement`.
example:
type Short = String where MinLength(-1)    // ✗ a length is never negative

type Short = String where MinLength(8)     // ✓
summary: A length predicate was given a negative value.

blurb: A value that only faults, such as `unreachable("…")` or `todo("…")`, has the bottom type `never returns`, which stands in for any type. If an unannotated `let` or `<-` binding took it, every later use would type-check whatever it was used as, and the type cannot be written in source to say otherwise. Annotate the binding with the type it is meant to have. A lambda that only faults is annotated with a function type.
summary: An unannotated `let` or `<-` binding has a type that is, or contains, the bottom type (`never returns`) because its value only faults (a faulting lambda bound this way included); the type cannot be written in source, so an annotation is needed.

blurb: `Int`, `Float` and `Decimal` are never mixed implicitly, in an operator, a comparison or an `InRange` bound. Each conversion can lose or invent precision, so Bynk makes you write it: `.toFloat()` on an `Int`, `.round()`, `.floor()`, `.ceil()` or `.truncate()` on a `Float`, `Decimal.fromInt(n)` or a decimal literal for a `Decimal`. The same code covers a `Duration` or `Instant` used with an operand it does not support.
summary: `Int`, `Float` and `Decimal` were mixed without an explicit conversion — in an operation, a comparison or refinement bounds.

blurb: A `match` must cover every value its subject can take, so it can never fall off its end. The compiler names a case that no arm covers: add an arm for it, or end the `match` with a wildcard `_` arm. Listing every variant a type has today is not a substitute for `_` where the compiler says one is needed, and where a `match` is too complex for it to prove exhaustive it asks for `_` too.
summary: A `match` does not cover every value.

blurb: A type parameter declared `T: Codable`, on a generic `fn` or a capability operation, accepts only the types `Json.decode` can read. A call that makes `T` a function, an `Effect`, a `Stream` or a type carrying one, a `bynk.crypto` key or `()` is refused, because such a value has no wire form. Pass a plain value, or use a function whose parameter is not `Codable`. Calling `Json.encode` or `Json.decode` on such a type directly is `bynk.types.json_uncodable`.
summary: A type is instantiated at a `Codable`-bounded parameter (of a generic function, or of a capability operation) but is outside the domain `Json.decode` accepts: top-level `()`, a function, `Effect`, `Query`, a `Stream` or a type that carries one, a connection, the HTTP and queue result types, `Asset`, request headers, token claims, or an actor (constrained-generics slice 3).

blurb: `==` and `!=` compare values structurally, which needs a value to compare. A function, an `Effect` and a `Query` are computations, and two of them have no equality. A type that holds one anywhere inside it, in a field, a payload, an element or a generic argument, is refused too. Compare what the computation produces, or the data it was built from. A `Stream` and a held connection have their own codes, `bynk.types.stream_not_comparable` and `bynk.types.held_not_comparable`.
summary: A value compared with `==`/`!=` contains a function, `Effect`, or `Query` somewhere inside it — those have no value equality, so the type is not equality-supporting (type-system §2.3.5, #1652).

blurb: A `Map` key, a `Set` element, or the key of a `distinct`, `distinctBy`, `groupBy` or join, must be a `Key` type, one whose equal values can always be found again. `String`, `Int`, `Bool`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `Bytes` and `Decimal` are, as are `Option` and `List` of a key and records, sums and enums made only of keys. A `Float` never is, at any depth, because `NaN` is not equal to itself, so a key holding one could never be looked up. Key on a type that is: an `Int` count of cents, say, or a `String`.
summary: A `Map` key, `Set` element, or `distinct`/`distinctBy`/`groupBy`/join key, or an argument to a `Key`-bounded parameter, is not `Key`. `String`, `Int`, `Bool`, `Instant`, `Duration`, `Bytes`, `Option`/`List` of a key type, refined and opaque types over them, and records, sums and enums made only of key types are; a `Float` is never one, at any depth, because `NaN` is not equal to itself (constrained-generics slice 2).

blurb: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, and a parameter declared `T: Ord`, need a type with a total order. `Int`, `Float`, `Decimal`, `String`, `Duration`, `Instant` and `Bytes` have one, as do refined types over them, `Option` and `List` of an orderable type, and any type of your own that declares `derives Ord`. `Bool`, `Result`, `Map`, `Set` and functions do not. Your own types are not ordered by accident, because opting in makes declaration order significant: reordering the fields or variants changes how values sort. Add `derives Ord`, or compare a field that is already orderable. A `sortBy`, `min` or `max` key that cannot be ordered is `bynk.types.key_not_orderable`.
summary: A value is ordered (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`), or passed to an `Ord`-bounded parameter, but its type is not `Ord`. `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Duration`, `Instant`, `Bytes`, `Option`/`List` of an orderable type, refined types over those, and types that declare `derives Ord` are; adding `derives Ord` is offered as a fix that is never applied automatically, because it makes declaration order significant (constrained-generics slice 1).

blurb: `Ok(v)` takes its type from where it is used. A return type or annotation of `Result[T, E]` fixes `T`, so `Ok("12")` where `T` is `Int` is refused at the value, with no conversion; so is a value that does not match an `HttpResult[T]` handler's `T`. Pass a `T`, or change the declared type. The error half is `bynk.types.err_value_mismatch`; with nothing to fix `T`, it is `bynk.types.cannot_infer_result_type_params`.
summary: An `Ok` payload has the wrong type.

blurb: An opaque type hides its base representation from everything but the unit that declares it, so no other code can take a `Token` apart or forge one. `.raw` reads the base value and is allowed only there. Elsewhere, use what the defining unit offers: a method or accessor on the type. To make a value, use `Token.of(value)`.
summary: `.raw` on an opaque type was used outside its defining commons.

blurb: `T.unsafe(v)` wraps a base value as an opaque type without checking it, which is sound only where the type's own unit vouches for the value, so it is allowed only in the unit that declares the type. Elsewhere use `T.of(v)`, which returns a `Result` so the check is explicit. Reading the base value back is `bynk.types.opaque_raw_outside`.
summary: `.unsafe` on an opaque type was used outside its defining context.

blurb: An or-pattern, `Walk(steps) | Wait`, runs one arm for either alternative, so every alternative must bind the same names. If `steps` came only from `Walk`, the arm's body would read a name that does not exist when `Wait` matched. Bind the name in every alternative, bind it in none with `_`, or split the alternatives into separate arms. A shared name must also have the same type: see `bynk.types.or_pattern_type_mismatch`.
summary: An or-pattern's alternatives don't all bind the same set of names.

blurb: An or-pattern, `A(n) | B(n)`, runs one arm for either alternative, so a name it binds must mean the same thing in both: the arm's body has only one `n` to use. Here `n` is an `Int` in one alternative and a `String` in the other, so the body could not be checked. A refined type and its base count as different too. Give each alternative its own arm, or bind a value of the same type in both.
summary: An or-pattern's alternatives give a shared binding different types (or refinements).

blurb: A variant pattern takes one binding for each payload field the variant declares, in order, or none to ignore the payload. A different count, or any binding on a variant with no payload, is refused: an extra name has nothing to hold, and a missing one would silently drop a field. Use `_` for a field you do not need, or name the fields you want (`radius: r`). Building a variant with the wrong number of arguments is `bynk.types.variant_arity`.
summary: A pattern binds the wrong number of payload fields.

blurb: A pattern can only match values of the type it describes, so a pattern of another kind than the value being matched can never succeed and is refused. A literal pattern must have the scrutinee's type, so `"one"` cannot match an `Int`. A variant pattern needs a sum value, a record pattern needs that record, and a qualified pattern such as `Status.Active` must name the scrutinee's own type. Match on the type the value has, or convert the value before the `match`. A pattern with the wrong number of bindings is `bynk.types.pattern_arity`.
summary: A pattern's type does not match the matched value.

blurb: A `Matches` pattern runs under a backtracking `RegExp` on untrusted input. Two repetitions in sequence that can match the same characters, as in `\d*\d*`, let the engine split a run between them many ways, so the time grows as a power of the input's length. That is slower to hurt than `bynk.types.catastrophic_regex` but can still stall a handler. A `MaxLength`, `Length` or `IsoDate` predicate that keeps the input short enough makes it the warning `bynk.types.polynomial_regex_capped`; a regex method has no such bound. Rewrite it so the repetitions cannot overlap.
example:
type Digits = String where Matches("\\d*\\d*")    // ✗ two loops over the same digits

type Digits = String where Matches("\\d*")         // ✓ one way to match
summary: A `Matches` pattern can split the same text between repetitions, so matching time grows polynomially with input length, and no length predicate bounds the input small enough for its degree; a regex method's pattern has no bound to excuse it.
A `Matches` pattern's matching time grows polynomially with input length, but a `MaxLength` or `Length` predicate bounds the input small enough for its degree (warning).

blurb: Each predicate checks one kind of value, so it can only refine a base that has such values. `NonEmpty`, `MinLength`, `MaxLength`, `Length`, `Matches` and `IsoDate` apply to a `String`, and `NonNegative`, `Positive` and `InRange` to an `Int`, `Float` or `Decimal`. A mismatch would test something the base cannot have. Change the base type to suit the predicate, or choose the predicate that suits the base.
example:
type Code = Int where NonEmpty         // ✗ `NonEmpty` is a `String` predicate

type Code = String where NonEmpty      // ✓
summary: A predicate does not apply to the type's base (e.g. a string predicate on an `Int`).

blurb: A `Query[T]` is a lazy read over an agent's stored data: nothing runs until a terminal such as `.collect()` executes it, in the agent that owns the data. Persisted or sent, it would be a description of a read with nothing to read from. A helper may take or return one, but it is refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent key or store field, a capability operation, or a handler's parameter or result. Run it and keep or send the `List` or `Option` it gives. A `Stream` has its own rule: `bynk.types.stream_at_boundary`.
summary: A `Query` type appears in a storable or boundary-crossing position — a query is built and executed in place, never persisted or sent (ADR 0115).

blurb: `?` returns the `Err` from the enclosing function as it is, so its error type must be one the function declares: a `String` error cannot escape a function whose errors are `Int`. The only automatic conversion is a declared embedding, where the function's error is a sum type with an `embeds` clause for the inner one. Otherwise convert the error before the `?` with `.mapErr(…)`, or change the function's error type.
summary: `?` propagates an error type incompatible with the function's.

blurb: `?` unwraps an `Ok` and returns early from the function on an `Err`, so it needs a `Result[T, E]`: a plain `Int` has no error to return. The one other operand it takes is an `Option`, in an `HttpResult` handler. Apply `?` to the call that produces the `Result`, not to a value already unwrapped. To turn an `Option` into a `Result` elsewhere, use `.okOr(err)`.
summary: `?` was applied to a non-`Result` value.

blurb: `?` on an `Option` turns `None` into an early return, which needs somewhere to return it to. In a handler that returns an `HttpResult`, `None` becomes a `NotFound` response. Elsewhere an `Option` has no error to carry, so `?` is refused. Say what absence means with `.okOr(err)`, which makes a `Result`, and put `?` after that.
summary: `?` lifts an `Option` only inside a handler returning `HttpResult` (`None` becomes `NotFound`); elsewhere use `.okOr(err)`.

blurb: `?` returns early with the `Err`, so the function around it must be able to return one: its return type has to be a `Result`, or an `Effect` of one. In a function returning `Int` the error has nowhere to go. Change the return type to `Result[T, E]` and wrap the final value in `Ok`, or deal with the `Result` where it arises, with a `match` or `.getOrElse(…)`.
summary: `?` used in a function that does not return a `Result`.

blurb: A range pattern `lo..hi` matches an `Int` by comparing it with two bounds. It is not offered for a `Float`, because `NaN` is neither inside nor outside a range, nor for a `String`; both are left out on purpose. Compare with `<` and `>=` in an `if` instead. An empty range is `bynk.types.empty_range_pattern`.
summary: A range pattern (`lo..hi`) was matched against a scrutinee that is not an `Int`.

blurb: A record pattern, `Order { total, .. }`, takes a record apart by its fields, so the name before the braces must be a record type. A sum, an enum, a refined or opaque type and a built-in have no fields to name. Match a sum or an enum by its variants, and read an opaque or built-in value through its methods.
summary: A record pattern names a type that is not a record (a sum, enum, refined or opaque type, or a built-in).

blurb: A regex method checks its pattern when the program compiles, to reject one that can take catastrophic time on crafted input (ReDoS). A pattern built at run time would escape that check, so it must be a string literal. Write the pattern in place, as an ordinary or a raw string, `r"\d+"`. To look for text that varies, use `contains`, which takes plain text.
summary: A regex method's pattern (`matchesRegex`, `containsRegex`, `findRegex`, `findAllRegex`, `replaceRegex`, `splitRegex`) is not a string literal, so its ReDoS check cannot run at compile time.

blurb: A `BoundaryRejection` is the router's account of a request it refused before any handler ran: a malformed or oversized body, an unsupported media type, a wrong method. `on rejected` reads it to render the answer, and it is accepted only as that handler's parameter. It is refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent store field, a capability operation, or any other handler's parameter or result. Match on it in `on rejected` and keep what you need, such as the detail text, as a `String`.
summary: `BoundaryRejection` appears where a value is stored or sent: a field of a type, or a boundary such as a call, a message or an agent.

blurb: `RequestCookies` is the raw view of one request's cookies, the `cookies` parameter of a handler that needs a name a record field cannot spell, such as `__Host-sid`. Cookies often carry session credentials, so the view is read where the request arrives and never kept. It is accepted only as an HTTP handler's `cookies` parameter, and refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent key or store field, a capability operation, or any other handler parameter or result. Read the cookie you need (`cookies.get("sid")`) and keep that `String`.
summary: `RequestCookies` appears where a value is stored or sent: a field of a type, or a boundary such as a call, a message or an agent.

blurb: `RequestQuery` is the raw view of one request's query string, the `query` parameter of a handler that reads keys it does not know in advance. It is read where the request arrives and then dropped: a copy kept or sent on would outlive the request. It is accepted only as an HTTP handler's `query` parameter, and refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent key or store field, a capability operation, or any other handler parameter or result. Read the value you need (`query.get("q")`) and keep that `String`.
summary: `RequestQuery` appears where a value is stored or sent: a field of a type, or a boundary such as a call, a message or an agent.

blurb: The value a function or handler body ends with does not have the declared return type, and the compiler compares the two exactly. Either change the body so it produces the declared type, or change the declared return type to match what the body produces. A refined type is the same rule with one extra step: an `Int` is not an `Age`, because `Age` carries a rule the `Int` has not been checked against. Build the refined value with `.of`, which checks the predicate and returns a `Result`, and declare that `Result` as the return type.
example:
fn count() -> Int { "three" }       // ✗ a `String` where an `Int` is declared

fn count() -> Int { 3 }              // ✓ the body has the declared type

type Age = Int where InRange(0, 150)

fn parse(n: Int) -> Age { n }                           // ✗ an `Int` is not an `Age`

fn parse(n: Int) -> Result[Age, ValidationError] {      // ✓ checked by `.of`
    Age.of(n)
}
summary: A returned value does not match the declared return type.

blurb: A rounding mode is written `RoundingMode.<mode>` where the rounding happens, as the mode argument of a `Decimal`'s `round` or `div`. It is not a value: it cannot be bound to a name, stored or passed around, so the rounding at each call is visible at that call. Write the mode at the call. A mode that is not a `RoundingMode.<mode>` at all is `bynk.types.unknown_rounding_mode`.
example:
let mode = RoundingMode.HalfUp         // ✗ a mode is not a value

price.round(2, RoundingMode.HalfUp)    // ✓ written where it rounds
summary: `RoundingMode.<mode>` was used outside the mode argument of a `Decimal`'s `round` or `div`. A mode is read where the rounding happens and is not a first-class value (#2622).

blurb: `select[T]` and `firstAs[T]` write the `SELECT` and the column list themselves, from the fields of the row record `T`, so the SQL you give is only the rest, starting at `FROM`. That way the columns are spelt once and cannot drift from the type. Start at `FROM`. A query that cannot (a `WITH` or a parenthesised one) is read with `all` and `Json.decodeSql`, which take the whole statement.
example:
let _ <- Orders.select[Order]("SELECT id, total FROM orders", [])    // ✗ the compiler writes `SELECT`

let _ <- Orders.select[Order]("FROM orders", [])                      // ✓
summary: A `D1`, `Postgres` or `MySql` `select[T]` or `firstAs[T]` statement does not start at `FROM` (for example it begins with `SELECT`, `WITH` or a parenthesis); the compiler writes the `SELECT` and column list from `T`.

blurb: `sequenceAll` and `sequenceTry` fold a `List[Result[T, E]]` into one `Result`, so every element must already be a `Result`. A list of plain values has no failures to collect. Map each element through a function that returns a `Result` first, as in `xs.map(check).sequenceAll()`. `sequenceAll` gathers every error, and `sequenceTry` stops at the first.
summary: `sequenceAll`/`sequenceTry` was called on a list whose elements are not `Result`s. They collect a `List[Result[T, E]]`.

blurb: `Some(v)` takes its type from the surrounding `Option[T]`, the annotation or the function's return type, so `Some("a")` where `T` is `Int` is refused at the value, with no conversion. Pass a `T`, or change the declared type. With nothing to say what the `Option` holds, a bare `None` is `bynk.types.cannot_infer_option_type_param`.
summary: A `Some` payload has the wrong type.

blurb: The SQL of a `D1`, `Postgres` or `MySql` call must be a string literal, or a `String` constant bound to one, so it is fixed when the program compiles and no request data can become part of the statement: that is how SQL injection happens. An interpolated string, a parameter or a `let` binding is refused. Put the value in the parameter list, as `?1` with `Text(id)`, which is always bound and never spliced in.
example:
let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = '\(id)'", [])         // ✗ built at run time

let _ <- Orders.all("SELECT id FROM orders WHERE id = ?1", [Text(id)])      // ✓ bound
summary: A `D1` or `Postgres` statement's SQL (the first argument of `all`, `first`, `run`, `select` or `firstAs`, or the `sql` of a `SqlStatement` or a `PgStatement`) is neither a string literal nor a bare reference to a `String` constant bound to one, so data could be spliced into it instead of bound as a `SqlValue` or `PgValue` parameter (standard-library P4c, Hyperdrive H1 and H3).

blurb: `select[T]`, `firstAs[T]` and `Json.decodeSql` read each SQL row into a record, and a column holds only a plain value. So `T` must be a record whose fields are `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Bool` or `Bytes`, or a refined or opaque type over one, or an `Option` of either (Postgres and MySQL also read `Decimal`); a nested record, a list or an enum has no column to read. `T` is the row itself, so `select[List[Row]]` is refused too. Flatten the record.
summary: `Json.decodeSql[T]`'s (or `select[T]`'s, `firstAs[T]`'s) `T` is not a SQL row: a record whose fields are `Int`, `Float`, `String`, `Bool` or `Bytes` (or a refined or opaque type over one, or an `Option` of either), or a `List` of such records (standard-library P4c). A `Postgres` row may also hold a `Decimal` or an `Instant` (Hyperdrive H3).

blurb: A `SqlStatement`, `PgStatement` or `MySqlStatement` is a statement a database capability runs, whose SQL the compiler requires to be a literal, so that request data is only ever bound as a parameter. One restored from storage or received from a caller would carry SQL that was never a literal, so it is refused as a record, sum or event field, an agent store field, a handler parameter or result, or a `Json` codec target. A capability operation's signature may name one. Keep or send the values instead, and build the statement where it runs.
summary: A `bynk.cloudflare` `SqlStatement`, `PgStatement` or `MySqlStatement` appears in a storable or boundary-crossing position, or as a `Json` codec target — a statement from outside would carry SQL that was never a literal (standard-library P4c).

blurb: A `Stream[T]` is a live, lazily read source, built and consumed where it is made. It cannot be persisted or serialised, so it cannot be a service or agent handler parameter or result, a store field or an event field, nor can a record or sum that carries one in a field, at any depth. Drain it with `collect()` and send or keep the resulting `List`. A capability operation may take or return a stream, since its provider runs in the caller's own isolate, and a `@raw` HTTP handler's `body` may be a `Stream[Bytes]`, the request body as it arrives.
summary: A `Stream` type, or a record or sum carrying one in a field, appears in a storable or boundary-crossing position — a stream is a live value-over-time source, never persisted or sent across a boundary (real-time track slice 0; #2623 admits it in capability signatures and record fields).

blurb: A `Stream` is a source of values over time, read once, so two of them have no value to compare. `==` on one, or on a type that holds one, is refused. Read the streams first, with `collect`, and compare the lists, or compare the data each was built from. Functions and effects have `bynk.types.not_comparable`, and a held connection has `bynk.types.held_not_comparable`.
summary: A `Stream` value is compared with `==`/`!=` — a stream is a live value-over-time source, not a comparable value (real-time track slice 0).

blurb: An operator or a built-in method was given an operand of a type it does not accept: `==` between an `Int` and a `String`, `!` on a number, `&&` on something that is not a `Bool`. Types are compared exactly, with no implicit conversion, so values of different types are never equal and never silently coerced. Make the operands the same type, or convert one explicitly. A `Float` and an `Int` mixed in arithmetic is the separate code `bynk.types.no_numeric_coercion`.
summary: An operator or built-in method got an operand of a type it does not accept, or two operands that had to match did not.

blurb: An empty `[]`, `List.empty()`, `Set.empty()` or `Map.empty()` has no elements to take a type from, and the compiler will not guess, because the element type becomes part of the type of everything the collection touches. Give it one: annotate the binding, as `let xs: List[Int] = []`, or use the empty value where a type is expected, such as an argument or a return value.
summary: An empty `[]` (or `List.empty()` / `Map.empty()`) has no expected type to infer its element type from.

blurb: After a refinement, the only annotation Bynk knows is `@example("…")`, a sample value that the compiler checks against the refinement. Any other name is refused rather than ignored, so a misspelling cannot pass as a comment. Use `@example`, or delete the annotation. `@example` is accepted only on `Matches` and `IsoDate`.
example:
type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @sample("ABC")     // ✗ no annotation `@sample`

type Code = String where Matches("[A-Z]{3}") @example("ABC")    // ✓
summary: An annotation after a refinement is not `@example`.

blurb: A field access names a field the value's type does not declare. A record's fields are fixed by its type declaration, so `p.z` on a `Point` of `x` and `y` is refused. This is usually a typo, or a value of a different type from the one intended. Building a record with a field it lacks is the sibling code `bynk.resolve.unknown_field`.
summary: Referenced a field the record type does not declare.

blurb: When a variant pattern names its bindings, as in `Circle(radius: r)`, each name must be a payload field the variant declares: `Circle` has no `diameter`. Use the declared field name, or bind by position, `Circle(r)`. A count of bindings that does not fit the payload is `bynk.types.pattern_arity`.
summary: A pattern names a field the variant does not have.

blurb: `Decimal`'s `round` and `div` must be told how to break a tie, and the choice is part of the money arithmetic, so it is named, not defaulted: write `RoundingMode.<mode>` as the last argument, where the mode is one of `Down`, `Up`, `Floor`, `Ceiling`, `HalfUp`, `HalfDown` or `HalfEven`. A number, a string or a variable is refused. A mode kept in a binding is `bynk.types.rounding_mode_position`.
example:
price.round(2, 1)                        // ✗ not a rounding mode

price.round(2, RoundingMode.HalfEven)    // ✓
summary: A `Decimal` `round` or `div` was not given a rounding mode written `RoundingMode.<mode>`; the modes are `Down`, `Up`, `Floor`, `Ceiling`, `HalfUp`, `HalfDown` and `HalfEven` (#2622).

blurb: `HttpResult` is a built-in type with a fixed set of variants, the HTTP statuses a handler can answer with, such as `Ok`, `Created`, `NotFound` and `ServerError`. `HttpResult.Nope` names one that does not exist, usually a misspelling or a status the set does not include. Pick one of the listed variants. A type you declared yourself is checked by `bynk.resolve.unknown_static_member`.
example:
HttpResult.Nope        // ✗ no such variant

HttpResult.NotFound    // ✓
summary: A name after `HttpResult.` that is not one of its variants. An unknown member of a type you declared is `bynk.resolve.unknown_static_member`.

blurb: A pattern on a sum value can only name the variants its type declares, so `Square(side)` against a `Shape` with no `Square` could never match and is refused. This is usually a typo, a variant that was never added, or a value of a different type from the one intended. Fix the name, add the variant to the type, or match on the right value. A pattern of the wrong kind altogether is `bynk.types.pattern_type_mismatch`.
summary: A pattern names a variant the sum type does not have.

blurb: A `match` arm can never run, because the arms before it already match every value it would match. The usual cause is a wildcard `_` placed before more specific arms: arms are tried in order, so the wildcard takes everything and the rest are dead code, which Bynk refuses rather than let hide a mistake. Put the specific arms first and the wildcard last, or delete the arm. A guarded arm covers nothing, since its guard may fail.
summary: A `match` arm is unreachable.

blurb: A variant is built like a call, with one argument for each payload field it declares, so `Circle(radius: Int)` takes one and a variant with no payload is written bare. A different number of arguments is refused at the construction. Pass one value for each declared field, or change the type declaration if the variant should carry more. The same code covers the built-in `QueueResult` and `HttpResult` constructors. A `match` arm with the wrong number of bindings is the separate code `bynk.types.pattern_arity`.
summary: A variant constructor got the wrong number of arguments for its payload fields (a pattern with the wrong number of bindings is `bynk.types.pattern_arity`).

blurb: A variant with a payload is built by calling it, with its payload as arguments. Written bare, `Circle` is not a value, since nothing fills `radius`; only a variant with no payload can stand alone. Call it with one argument per field, as `Circle(10)`. The qualified form `Shape.Circle` is refused in the same way. A call with the wrong number of arguments is `bynk.types.variant_arity`.
summary: A variant requiring a payload was used without one.

blurb: A variant's payload fields have declared types and are checked like function parameters: `Circle("big")` for `radius: Int` is refused at the argument, with no conversion. Pass a value of the field's type. For a generic sum the type argument is inferred from the arguments first, and the check applies to the result. The wrong number of arguments is `bynk.types.variant_arity`.
summary: A variant payload has the wrong type.

blurb: A unit that `uses` a commons gets what it declares (types, functions, constants, assets and embeds) in scope under their own names, with no prefix. If two commons it uses both declare the same name, a mention of it could mean either, so the compiler refuses the second `uses`. `uses` has no `as` rename yet. Rename one of the declarations, drop one of the `uses`, or mark the declaration `private` if only its own commons needs it, since a `private` declaration is never imported and so never conflicts.
example:
// billing.bynk
commons billing

type Amount = Int where Positive

// shipping.bynk
commons shipping

type Amount = Int where NonNegative    // both declare `Amount`
type Postage = Int where NonNegative   // ✓ renamed

// orders.bynk
commons orders

uses billing
uses shipping                          // ✗ `Amount` is also declared by `billing`
summary: Two commons a unit `uses` declare the same type, function, constant, asset or embed; or a value crosses between a unit's code and an imported declaration's position whose type the unit shadows; or a reference names an import the unit's own declaration shadows.

blurb: `uses` brings another commons into scope. A commons' own declarations are already there, so using itself adds nothing, and a unit that depends on itself is a cycle of length one. Delete the clause, or, if you meant another commons, name it. The mirror of this for contexts is `bynk.consumes.self_reference`.
summary: A commons `uses` itself.

blurb: `uses` is for shared types and functions, and those live in a commons. A context is something to depend on: it has services to call and capabilities to use, and that is `consumes`. Replace `uses` with `consumes`. The mirror of this is `bynk.consumes.target_is_commons`.
summary: `uses` targets a context instead of a commons.

blurb: `uses` brings a commons' types, functions and constants into scope, so it must name a commons in the project, and no unit of that name exists. Check the spelling against the `commons` line of the unit you mean. If the unit is a context, `uses` is the wrong clause: that is `bynk.uses.target_is_context`.
example:
// money.bynk
commons money

type Amount = Int where NonNegative

// shop.bynk
context shop

uses mony                        // ✗ no commons `mony`
uses money                       // ✓ the commons' declared name
summary: `uses` names a commons that does not exist.

blurb: A `for all` over a declared type draws values from it, but an agent is not a value: a state that satisfies every invariant need not be one the agent can reach. So an agent cannot be a `for all` binding. To test an agent over generated input, bind a `History` of it, which drives real handler calls and so reaches only real states.
summary: A `for all`/`Val` cannot generate an agent — fabricated agent states need not be reachable.

blurb: `Val[T]` takes at most one argument, the pin: `Val[Age]` lets the compiler choose a value, `Val[Age](20)` fixes it. `Val` makes one value of one type, so a second argument has no meaning. Pass one pin or none.
summary: `Val[T]` was given the wrong number of pin arguments.

blurb: `Val[T]` fabricates a value for a test from the declaration of `T`. That is not yet done for each instantiation of a generic type, so `Val` refuses one whether it is written bare, `Val[Box]`, or applied, `Val[Box[Int]]`. The type itself is fine, and may cross a boundary through its codec; only fabrication is missing. Build the value yourself instead: a record literal for a generic record, one of its variants for a generic sum.
summary: A `Val[…]` fabricates a value of a generic type; per-instantiation value fabrication is not yet wired (ADR 0197). The type itself may cross a boundary through its monomorphised codec (v0.174). Named `bynk.generics.generic_record_at_boundary` before #3379.

blurb: A pinned `Val[T](…)` is checked against the refinement of `T` at compile time, and this literal breaks it, so the test would build a value the type does not allow. Pin a value that satisfies the refinement, or drop the pin and let `Val[T]` choose one. To test that an invalid value is refused, call `T.of(…)` and expect an `Err`.
summary: A pinned `Val[T]` value violates the type's refinement.

blurb: In a test, a bare `Val[T]` fabricates a valid value of `T`. It can do that for most refinements (`Positive` gives `1`, `MinLength(3)` a string of length three) but not for a `Matches` pattern or `IsoDate`, so it refuses rather than guess; the same goes for a record or sum that reaches one. A `for all` over such a type is refused too. Pin a value, `Val[Code]("abc")`, which is checked against the refinement, or give the type an `@example` and use bare `Val`. See the `bynk.val.*` codes for pins that are not literals or do not satisfy the type.
summary: A bare `Val[T]` cannot generate a value (e.g. a `Matches` string); pin one.

blurb: `Val[T]` fabricates a value that merely satisfies `T`. That is what a test wants and what running code must not do, so `Val` is allowed only in test code. In a function or handler, take the value as a parameter or build it properly, for instance with `Age.of(20)`. See `bynk.val.needs_pin` for a bare `Val` that a test cannot generate.
summary: `Val[T]` was used outside a test case body.

blurb: A pin on `Val[T]` is checked against the refinement of `T` when the program compiles, so it must be a literal of `T`'s base type. A name or a call has no value at that point. Write the literal in place. For a computed value, build it with `Age.of(…)` and `?`, which fails the case if the value is not valid.
summary: A `Val[T]` pin argument is not a compile-time literal.

blurb: A pinned `Val[T](lit)` is accepted only for a refined type, where the literal is checked against the refinement. A sum, record or opaque type takes no pin, so one is refused. Use bare `Val[T]`, which builds the first variant, or every field, itself, or construct the value directly with a variant or a record literal. A pin that is not a literal at all is `bynk.val.pin_not_literal`.
summary: A pin was given for a type kind that does not support pinning.

blurb: `Val[T]` fabricates a value of the type it names, so the name must resolve to a type the suite can see. A misspelt name stops here, before anything else about the value can be checked. Fix the spelling, or declare the type in the target unit or the suite. The same code covers a `for all` binder whose type does not resolve.
summary: `Val[T]` names a type that does not resolve.

blurb: `Val[T]` fabricates a value from a type declaration: a refinement, a sum, a record or an opaque type. A built-in type such as `Int` or `String`, a `List` or a function type has no declaration to draw from, so `Val` refuses it. Write the value, `20`, or declare a type for it, which `Val` can then fabricate.
example:
type Age = Int where InRange(0, 150)

let n = Val[Int]   // ✗ a built-in type
let a = Val[Age]   // ✓ a declared type
summary: `Val[T]` cannot fabricate a value for this kind of type.

blurb: A public declaration may not mention a `private` type of its own unit in its signature: a public function's parameters and return, a public type's fields and variant payloads, a public constant's type, or a context's `exports` list. A unit that `uses` the commons could neither name that type nor build a value of it, so the function would be half-usable. Make the type public, or make the declaration `private` too. Services, agents and capabilities are not checked here; a context's `exports` governs them.
summary: A public declaration's signature names a `private` type of its own unit, which an importer could neither name nor build.

blurb: A `private` function, type, constant, asset or embed (or a `private` method) is visible only within its own unit, across all of that unit's files, and to the unit's suites. It is never visible through `uses`, so a unit that uses the commons cannot name it. The compiler reports that the name is private, not that it is unknown, so you know it exists. `private` keeps a helper out of the public surface, so it can change without breaking anyone. Call the commons' public function that does the job, or, if the item really belongs to the public surface, remove `private` where it is declared.
summary: A reference from another unit names a `private` declaration, which is visible only within its own unit and that unit's suites.

A `messages` block in a commons is `private`. A bundle whose `@reference` block is private is never negotiated by a context that uses the commons, and `private` on another block of a bundle whose reference is public has no effect (warning).

blurb: `private` hides a `fn`, `type`, `messages`, `asset`, `embed` or `const` from the units that import its commons or context. It does not apply to a service, agent, capability, provider, actor or event, or to anything in an adapter: how far those reach is decided by a context's `exports` and `consumes`, and an adapter's `exports`. Remove `private`. See `bynk.visibility.private_item` for using something that is private.
example:
private service total { … }        // ✗ `private` does not apply to a service
service total { … }                // ✓ reach is governed by `exports`
summary: `private` modifies a declaration it does not apply to: anything but a `fn`, `type`, `messages`, `asset`, `embed` or `const` in a commons or context.
