The in-browser compiler could not strip the emitted TypeScript to JavaScript.

blurb: `within` hands the effect it abandons on a timeout to the execution context, and an agent handler has none. Call it from the service handler that calls the agent, so the agent's work is bounded from outside. For a slow call out, `FetchOptions.timeout` bounds it inside the agent. The same rule holds for `bynk.race.in_agent_handler`.
summary: `e.within(d)` was used in an agent handler, which has no execution context to hand the abandoned effect to.

blurb: `within` hands the effect it abandons on a timeout to the execution context, and only an effectful body has one: a pure function never runs an effect at all. Change the enclosing function's return type to `Effect[…]` so its body can run it. The same rule holds for `bynk.race.in_pure_context`.
summary: `e.within(d)` was used in a pure (non-effectful) context.

blurb: `within` hands the effect it abandons on a timeout to the execution context, which only a service handler's body, or a function's it calls, has. A WebSocket handler, a provider operation and a test `case` have none. Move the `within` into a service handler or a function, and have the case call that, simulating a slow call with `stub … after`. In an agent handler the rule is `bynk.within.in_agent_handler`.
summary: `e.within(d)` was used outside a service handler's body and outside a function (in a provider operation, a WebSocket handler or a test `case` body), where no execution context exists.

blurb: `within` returns `Result[_, TimedOut]`, and `TimedOut` is declared in `bynk`, so a unit that wants `within` has to consume it. Without that the result type names a type the unit cannot see. Add `consumes bynk { TimedOut }` to the unit, or add `TimedOut` to its existing `consumes bynk { … }` list.
summary: `e.within(d)` yields `Result[_, TimedOut]`, but the unit does not consume `bynk`, so `TimedOut` is not in scope.

blurb: The connection's principal is verified once, by `on open`'s `by`, and carried for the life of the connection; `on message` and `on close` read it and never verify again. So their `by` must name the same actor as `on open`'s, or the same members of an actor sum. The binder names may differ. Change the lifecycle handler's `by` to match `on open`.
summary: A WebSocket `on message`/`on close` handler's `by` clause does not name the same actor(s) as `on open`'s — the connection's principal is verified once, at `on open`, and carried for its life, so the lifecycle handlers must be the same single actor or the same actor-sum members (binder names may differ).

blurb: A WebSocket `on message` handler is called with a decoded inbound frame, so it needs exactly one parameter of the service's `in:` type. Any other parameters are route values recovered from the connection. Add the frame parameter. A route value whose type differs from `on open`'s is `bynk.ws.route_param_mismatch`.
summary: A WebSocket `on message` handler does not have exactly one parameter of the service's inbound (`in:`) frame type — the decoded frame (real-time track slice 3b-iii).

blurb: A WebSocket `on open` cannot declare `given` capabilities. It only accepts the upgrade and hands the connection to an agent; on Workers it runs inside the Durable Object that holds the connection, where there is no composition root to supply capabilities. Put the work that needs a capability in the agent handler the connection is transferred to, which carries its own `given`.
summary: A WebSocket `on open` handler declares `given` capabilities — unsupported at v1, since on Workers the handler runs inside the connection-hosting Durable Object, which has no composition root to supply them (real-time track slice 3b).

blurb: On the Workers target, a `from websocket` service's `on open` is hosted inside the Durable Object of the agent it hands the connection to, and that method is emitted from the file the service and the agent share. When a context is split over several files, each is emitted on its own, so a service in one file that transfers to an agent in another would be routed to the agent's Durable Object and never handled there: the upgrade would answer `404`. The compiler refuses the layout. Put the service in the agent's file, or build for `--target bundle`, where the open is an ordinary method and the layout works.
summary: On the Workers target, a WebSocket `on open` handler transfers its `connection` to an agent declared in a different file of the same context — the open is hosted in the agent's Durable Object, which is emitted from the agent's own file, so the upgrade would never be handled; the service and the agent must share a file.

blurb: On Workers the upgrade is routed to the Durable Object that hosts the connection before the `on open` body runs, so the edge has to work out the agent's key on its own. A route parameter, a `const` of the context or of a commons it `uses`, or a literal can be evaluated there. A key computed in the body, such as a `let`, cannot, because the body has not run. Key the agent by a parameter of `on open`, a constant, or a literal. The bundle target runs the body first, so it does not check this.
summary: On the Workers target, the key of a WebSocket `on open` handler's connection transfer is not a route parameter, a constant of the context or of a commons it uses, or a literal — the upgrade is routed to the hosting Durable Object before the body runs, so the edge must be able to evaluate the key on its own.

blurb: A WebSocket `on open` must hand its `connection` to exactly one agent, unconditionally, as `Room(room).join(user.identity, connection)`. On Workers the upgrade is routed to that agent's Durable Object, which holds the connection, so it needs a single target the compiler can find. Neither none nor several will do, and a transfer inside an `if` or a `match` is not found. A connection left undisposed is `bynk.held.leak`; a transfer whose key the edge cannot compute is `bynk.ws.open_transfer_key`.
summary: A WebSocket `on open` handler does not transfer its `connection` into exactly one agent, so the Workers upgrade has no single Durable Object to route to (real-time track slice 3b).

blurb: `on message` and `on close` are not given a fresh URL: their route values are recovered, in order, from what `on open` accepted. So the leading parameters of each must have the same types as `on open`'s, in the same order. A different type at some position would reinterpret one route value as another. Match the types of `on open`'s parameters; the names may differ. A missing frame parameter is `bynk.ws.message_frame_param`.
summary: A WebSocket `on message`/`on close` route parameter does not match the `on open` parameter at the same position — route values are recovered positionally from the connection, so they must be a type-compatible prefix of the `on open` parameters (real-time track slice 3b-iii).
